[{:db/id 17592186133906 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-c3b9fdd0-8dab-5a0b-9e88-9a8e531bca1d" "question-cb3d3dae-b723-59f7-8d1b-568e2e8664df"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-c3b9fdd0-8dab-5a0b-9e88-9a8e531bca1d" :question/id #uuid "c3b9fdd0-8dab-5a0b-9e88-9a8e531bca1d" :question/math-academy-id "q-139771" :question/problem "$$
x={R}^{-1}\,\bbox[5px,border:1px solid black]{\phantom{A}}\,b
$$

Let $A=QR$  be a QR decomposition of an $m\times n$ matrix $A$ with linearly independent columns, and the expression above gives the least-squares solution of $Ax=b.$ What is the missing part of the equation?" :question/worked-solution "The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the normal equation

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b.
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Then, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $R$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by ${R}^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}^{-1}\cdot Rx & ={R}^{-1}\cdot {Q}^{T}b \\ x & ={R}^{-1}\,\,{Q}^{T}\,\,b.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing part of the equation is ${Q}^{T}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-9cd33a2a-4f98-5342-9ba4-5873365eeaa6"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-9cd33a2a-4f98-5342-9ba4-5873365eeaa6" :answer-field/id #uuid "9cd33a2a-4f98-5342-9ba4-5873365eeaa6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-2aaeec0e-9d7d-51b5-8e98-ca8703231590" :answer-field/choices ["answer-b7edffd0-66a0-5c75-bcc7-1841cf561f2f" "answer-e8c7732e-ce78-5352-8708-b204edd3100c" "answer-5a928cee-21d3-53ca-ace1-76f33e1c43e5" "answer-ac5cc7e5-983e-54c2-88c3-dc3f7ef1cb76" "answer-2aaeec0e-9d7d-51b5-8e98-ca8703231590"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b7edffd0-66a0-5c75-bcc7-1841cf561f2f" :answer/id #uuid "b7edffd0-66a0-5c75-bcc7-1841cf561f2f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(Q-I)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e8c7732e-ce78-5352-8708-b204edd3100c" :answer/id #uuid "e8c7732e-ce78-5352-8708-b204edd3100c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "A" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5a928cee-21d3-53ca-ace1-76f33e1c43e5" :answer/id #uuid "5a928cee-21d3-53ca-ace1-76f33e1c43e5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "Q" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ac5cc7e5-983e-54c2-88c3-dc3f7ef1cb76" :answer/id #uuid "ac5cc7e5-983e-54c2-88c3-dc3f7ef1cb76" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{A}^{-1}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2aaeec0e-9d7d-51b5-8e98-ca8703231590" :answer/id #uuid "2aaeec0e-9d7d-51b5-8e98-ca8703231590" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{Q}^{T}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-cb3d3dae-b723-59f7-8d1b-568e2e8664df" :question/id #uuid "cb3d3dae-b723-59f7-8d1b-568e2e8664df" :question/math-academy-id "q-139772" :question/problem "$$

"Given the QR decomposition $A=QR,$ find the least-squares solution to $Ax=b,$ where

$$
Q=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}],\,R=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}3 & -4 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$" :question/worked-solution "The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ is orthogonal, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Finally, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}3 & -4 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}}x & =\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}]}}\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]}} \\ [\begin{aligned}3 & -4 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]x & =[\begin{aligned}-11 \\ 10\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}=-11 \\ 2{x}_{2}=10.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=5.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}-4(5) & =-11 \\ 3{x}_{1} & =9 \\ {x}_{1} & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the least-squares solution to $Ax=b$ is $[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 5\end{aligned}].$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields "c07b8d08-df25-5edc-8755-7d7271698aeb" :question/math-academy-id "q-157078" :question/problem "Given the QR decomposition $A=QR,$ find the least-squares solution to $Ax=b,$ where

$$
Q=\frac{1}{\sqrt{70}}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5} & \sqrt{2} \\ 3\sqrt{5} & 3\sqrt{2} \\ 2\sqrt{5} & -5\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}],\,R=\frac{1}{\sqrt{70}}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5} & 2\sqrt{5} \\ 0 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$" :question/worked-solution "The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Finally, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{70}}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5} & 2\sqrt{5} \\ 0 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]}}x & =\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{70}}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5} & 3\sqrt{5} & 2\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{2} & 3\sqrt{2} & -5\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]}}\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}} \\ [\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5} & 2\sqrt{5} \\ 0 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]x & =[\begin{aligned}-10\sqrt{5} \\ -10\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5}{x}_{1}+2\sqrt{5}{x}_{2}=-10\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{2}{x}_{2}=-10\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=-10.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5}{x}_{1}+2\sqrt{5}(-10) & =-10\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{5}{x}_{1} & =10\sqrt{5} \\ {x}_{1} & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the least-squares solution to $Ax=b$ is $[\begin{aligned}10 \\ -10\end{aligned}].$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186188179 :question/problem "What is $0.2 \,\textrm{kg}$ expressed in $\textrm g?$" :question/worked-solution "We start by recalling the conversion table for mass units. 

| Name | Symbol | Conversion |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kilogram | $\textrm{kg}$ | $1\,\textrm{kg} = 1\,000\,\textrm{g}$ |
| Gram | $\textrm{g}$ | Base Unit |
| Milligram | $\textrm{mg}$ | $1\,000\,\textrm{mg} = 1\,\textrm{g}$ |

There are $1000\,\textrm g$ per $\textrm{kg},$ which we can write as follows:

$$
\dfrac{1000\,\textrm g}{\textrm{kg}}
$$

This is our conversion factor.

Now, multiplying $0.2\,\textrm{kg}$ by our conversion factor, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}0.2\,\text{kg} & =0.2\,\text{kg}\cdot \frac{1\,000\,\text{g}}{\text{kg}} \\  & =0.2\,\cancel{\text{kg}}\cdot \frac{1\,000\,\text{g}}{\cancel{\text{kg}}} \\  & =0.2\cdot 1\,000\,\text{g} \\  & =200\,\text{g}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $0.2\,\textrm{kg}$ is equivalent to $200 \,\text{g}.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186188244 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-6ef2597c-1ce8-509f-a9ab-036304f6968d" "question-706f7978-b984-597c-b5ee-5c4df365adea"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186188180 :question/problem "What is $2.25 \,\textrm{g}$ expressed in $\textrm{mg}?$" :question/worked-solution "We start by recalling the conversion table for mass units. 

| Name | Symbol | Conversion |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kilogram | $\textrm{kg}$ | $1\,\textrm{kg} = 1\,000\,\textrm{g}$ |
| Gram | $\textrm{g}$ | Base Unit |
| Milligram | $\textrm{mg}$ | $1\,000\,\textrm{mg} = 1\,\textrm{g}$ |

There are $1000\,\textrm {mg}$ per $\textrm{g},$ which we can write as follows:

$$
\dfrac{1000\,\textrm{mg}}{\textrm{g}}
$$

This is our conversion factor.

One type of problem where units can help is converting between different units of measurement. 

For example, let's use units to convert $0.03\,\textrm{kg}$ into grams. We start by recalling the conversion table for mass units. 

| Name | Symbol | Conversion |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kilogram | $\textrm{kg}$ | $1\,\textrm{kg} = 1\,000\,\textrm{g}$ |
| Gram | $\textrm{g}$ | Base Unit |
| Milligram | $\textrm{mg}$ | $1\,000\,\textrm{mg} = 1\,\textrm{g}$ |

Since we're converting from kilograms to grams, we need a conversion between these two units. According to our table, there are $1000\,\textrm g$ per $\textrm{kg}.$ We can write this ratio as a fraction, as follows:

$$
\dfrac{1000\,\textrm g}{\textrm{kg}}
$$

This is our **conversion factor.** It's important to write the conversion factor with the units included.

To convert $0.03 \,\textrm{kg}$ to grams, we multiply this quantity by our conversion factor as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}0.03\,\text{kg} & =0.03\,\text{kg}\cdot \frac{1\,000\,\text{g}}{\text{kg}}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the kilogram units $(\textrm{kg})$ cancel, leaving only gram units $(\textrm{g}).$ Consequently, our expression can be simplified as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}0.03\,\text{kg} & =0.03\,\text{kg}\cdot \frac{1\,000\,\text{g}}{\text{kg}} \\  & =0.03\,\cancel{\text{kg}}\cdot \frac{1\,000\,\text{g}}{\cancel{\text{kg}}} \\  & =0.03\cdot 1\,000\,\text{g} \\  & =30\,\text{g}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $0.03 \,\textrm{kg}$ is equivalent to $30 \,\text{g}.$

Note the following:

- When multiplying by the conversion factor, the units we want to remove should *always* cancel, and the units we wish to keep should *always* remain. If this isn't the case, we've made a mistake somewhere.

- We can think of the conversion factor as equivalent to the number $1,$ and multiplying a quantity by $1$ doesn't change it. Therefore, multiplying $0.03\,\textrm{kg}$ by the conversion factor doesn't change the *size* of the quantity, though it does change the units.

Finally, notice that, in this example, we've converted from a "larger" unit of mass $(\textrm{kg})$ to a smaller one $(\textrm{g}).$ We'll see how to use units to convert from smaller units of mass to larger units later in this lesson." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186189495 :tutorial/content "We've seen how to use units to convert from larger units of mass to smaller ones. Let's now learn how to convert from smaller units to larger ones.

For example, suppose we want to convert $600\,\textrm{mg}$ to grams. We start by recalling the conversion table for mass units. 

| Name | Symbol | Conversion |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kilogram | $\textrm{kg}$ | $1\,\textrm{kg} = 1\,000\,\textrm{g}$ |
| Gram | $\textrm{g}$ | Base Unit |
| Milligram | $\textrm{mg}$ | $1\,000\,\textrm{mg} = 1\,\textrm{g}$ |

There are $1000\,\textrm {mg}$ per $\textrm{g},$ which we can write as follows:

$$
\dfrac{1000\,\textrm{mg}}{\textrm{g}}
$$

However, since we're converting from a smaller unit of mass $(\textrm{mg})$ to a larger one $(\textrm{g}),$ we construct our conversion factor by taking the *reciprocal* of the above:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{g}}{1000\,\textrm{mg}}
$$

Now, multiplying $600 \,\textrm{mg}$ by our conversion factor, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}600\,\text{mg} & =600\,\text{mg}\cdot \frac{\text{g}}{1\,000\,\text{mg}} \\  & =600\,\cancel{\text{mg}}\cdot \frac{\text{g}}{1\,000\,\cancel{\text{mg}}} \\  & =600\cdot \frac{\text{g}}{1\,000} \\  & =\frac{600}{1000}\,\text{g} \\  & =0.6\,\text{g}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $600 \,\textrm{mg}$ is equivalent to $0.6\,\text{g}.$

Note the following: 

- When we say that grams are a "larger unit of mass" than milligrams, this simply means that $1\,\textrm g$ is a larger mass than $1\,\textrm{mg}.$

- If you forget to take the reciprocal to find the conversion factor, the units will not cancel when you multiply. This indicates that a mistake has occurred. In such cases, it's best to double-check that you're using the correct conversion factor." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186188462 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186122468 :answer-field/choices 17592186122469] [:db/retract 17592186122468 :answer-field/choices 17592186122470] [:db/retract 17592186122468 :answer-field/choices 17592186122471] [:db/retract 17592186122468 :answer-field/choices 17592186122472] [:db/retract 17592186122468 :answer-field/choices 17592186122473] [:db/retract 17592186122414 :answer-field/choices 17592186122416] [:db/retract 17592186122414 :answer-field/choices 17592186122419] {:db/id 17592186124464 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-726c12fc-e2ed-50f3-8cd6-76ed12fb7e44" "question-056dc885-9ad1-5245-b1aa-85becac66885"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124978 :question/problem "Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)=2x+4y+5xy$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(2,1).$" :question/worked-solution "A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(2,1)$, can be found by computing $∇f(2,1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x+4y+5xy)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x+4y+5xy)\text{ }j \\  & =(5y+2)\text{ }i+(5x+4)\text{ }j \\ ∇f(2,1) & =(5\cdot 1+2)\text{ }i+(5\cdot 2+4)\text{ }j \\  & =7i+14j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇f(2,1)}{‖∇f(2,1)‖} & =\frac{7i+14j}{\sqrt{{7}^{2}+(14)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{7i+14j}{7\sqrt{5}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}(i+2\,j)\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186122468 :answer-field/correct "answer-cef8e14b-ece7-51a1-921e-23d70f9d2c98" :answer-field/choices ["answer-3c60959a-01b7-53b2-91be-83d1b906ea40" "answer-144e5910-b093-5cd4-abe0-394d07cded53" "answer-91e9dfc1-cddb-5022-b3ab-97f0a0267baa" "answer-cef8e14b-ece7-51a1-921e-23d70f9d2c98" "answer-812ac18a-9cbd-56eb-aadd-016577600a1e"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3c60959a-01b7-53b2-91be-83d1b906ea40" :answer/id #uuid "3c60959a-01b7-53b2-91be-83d1b906ea40" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "7\,i+7\,j" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-144e5910-b093-5cd4-abe0-394d07cded53" :answer/id #uuid "144e5910-b093-5cd4-abe0-394d07cded53" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "7\,i-12\,j" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-91e9dfc1-cddb-5022-b3ab-97f0a0267baa" :answer/id #uuid "91e9dfc1-cddb-5022-b3ab-97f0a0267baa" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}(2\,i+j)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-cef8e14b-ece7-51a1-921e-23d70f9d2c98" :answer/id #uuid "cef8e14b-ece7-51a1-921e-23d70f9d2c98" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}(i+2\,j)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-812ac18a-9cbd-56eb-aadd-016577600a1e" :answer/id #uuid "812ac18a-9cbd-56eb-aadd-016577600a1e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "i-4j" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124969 :question/problem "Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)=2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-y$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(0,1).$" :question/worked-solution "A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(x,y)=(0,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(0,1):$

$$

\frac{∇f(0,1)}{‖∇f(0,1)‖}=\frac{3\,j}{3}=j

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(0,0,\sqrt{e})$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,0,\sqrt{e}).$  

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,0,\sqrt{e}):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}))i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}))j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}))k \\  & =\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\text{ }i+\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\text{ }j+\frac{2z}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\text{ }k \\ ∇f(0,0,\sqrt{e}) & =\frac{2(0)}{(0)^{2}+(0)^{2}+(\sqrt{e})^{2}}\text{ }i+\frac{2(0)}{(0)^{2}+(0)^{2}+(\sqrt{e})^{2}}\text{ }j+\frac{2\sqrt{e}}{(0)^{2}+(0)^{2}+(\sqrt{e})^{2}}\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{e}}{e}k\end{aligned}
$$

The parametric equations for the normal line to $f(x,y,z)$ at a point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ are given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={x}_{0}+{f}_{x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})t, \\ y & ={y}_{0}+{f}_{y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})t, \\ z & ={z}_{0}+{f}_{z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametic equations  for the normal line to our surface that  passes through the point $(0,0,\sqrt{e})$ can be written as 
 

$$
x=0,\,y=0,\,z=\sqrt{e}+\frac{2t\sqrt{e}}{e}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-c615bb4c-1597-5b7b-a91f-2e2776baf55b"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "056dc885-9ad1-5245-b1aa-85becac66885" :question/math-academy-id "q-131125" :question/problem "Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface ${x}^{2}-{y}^{2}=4-4z$ at the point $(0,2,2).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2} & =4-4z \\ {x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+4z & =4\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+4z$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=4.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(0,2,2)$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,2,2).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,2,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+4z)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+4z)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+4z)k \\  & =2x\,i-2y\,j+4\,k \\ ∇f(0,2,2) & =2(0)\,i-2(2)\text{ }j+4\,k \\  & =-4\,j+4\,k \\  & =⟨0,-4,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(0,2,2)$ and passes through the point $(0,2,2)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨0,2,2⟩+t\,∇f(0,2,2)=⟨0,2,2⟩+t\,⟨0,-4,4⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-5dba8cbc-5d08-5d14-930e-b1a41b746cb3"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186125735 :tutorial/content "Given a function $z=f(x,y)$, if both partial derivatives $f_x,$ $f_y$ exist and are continuous in a neighborhood of a point $P(x_0,y_0)$ in the domain of the function, and if $\nabla \! f(x_0,y_0) \neq \mathbf 0,$ then we have the following result:

*$\nabla \! f(x_0,y_0)$ is a normal vector to the level curve $C$ that passes through the point $P.$ *

This property is one of the most important facts in multivariable calculus since it gives a fundamental  link between
calculus and geometry!

Let's illustrate this property with a concrete example. Consider the paraboloid $z = f (x, y)=  x^2 + y^2$ and the level curve $\color{red}C$ of $f(x,y)$ corresponding to the point $P(1,-1).$  It is easy to see that  $\color{red}C$ is a circle of radius $\sqrt{2}$ with equation $x^2+y^2 = 2.$ 

![](images/f2/f2461dbfcde2403e6ed7de9d6288d33a4deb52319d35b7036628c3fa8b3789dc.png)

In this particular instance, the property says that

*$\nabla \! f(1,-1)$ is a normal vector to the level curve $\color{red}C$ that passes through the point $P(1,-1).$ *

![](images/48/481b68af522b9144e232d9c775f734cd998b31a21571cbfd983c23d0f68c3688.png)

Looking at the situation in the $xy$-plane, we see the following:

![](images/ce/ceb353d5164d6aa089a37e77c9469d747ef4430e363e42f9d35ee6d769d9a4e4.png)

Let's verify that $\nabla f(1,-1)$ is a normal line to the level curve $C$ at the point $P(1,-1).$

- First, computing the gradient, we find that $\nabla f = \langle 2x, 2y \rangle.$ Therefore, 

$$
\nabla f(1,-1) = \langle 2, -2 \rangle.
$$

- Then, using elementary calculus, we can show that the equation of the tangent to $C$ at $P$ is $y=x-2.$ Since this line has slope $m=1,$ it follows that the vector $\langle 1,1 \rangle$  is parallel to the level curve.

- Finally, taking the dot product between the gradient and the tangent vector, we obtain

$$
\nabla f(1,-1)\cdot  \langle 1,1 \rangle = \langle 2, -2\rangle \cdot \langle 1,1 \rangle = 0.
$$

This means that $\nabla f(1,-1)$ is *perpendicular* to the tangent line to $C$ at $(1,-1).$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186125740 :tutorial/content "The same property holds true in the case of three or more variables. In general, if $f$ is a differentiable real-valued function of $n$ variables, $\mathbf y$ is a point in the domain of $f,$ and if  the  gradient vector is nonzero, i.e., 

$$
\nabla f (\mathbf y)= \left \langle f_{x_1}(\mathbf y), f_{x_2}(\mathbf y), \cdots, f_{x_n}(\mathbf y)\right \rangle \neq \mathbf 0,
$$

then we have the following result:

*$\nabla f (\mathbf y)$ is a normal vector to the level surface $f(x_1,x_2, \cdots, x_n) =f(\mathbf y)$ at $\mathbf y.$*

To illustrate, let's consider the function  

$$
w = f (x, y, z)= \dfrac 1 2\left(x^2 + y^2 + z^2-1\right).
$$

 

The level surface corresponding to $w=0$ is the sphere $\mathcal S$ with equation $x^2 + y^2 +z^2 =1.$ 

The point $P(0,0,1)$ lies on $\mathcal S.$ Computing $\nabla f(0,0,1),$ we get

$$
\eqalign{
\nabla f(x,y,z) &= \langle f_x, \: f_y, \:f_z\rangle \[5pt]
&= \dfrac12\langle2x, \: 2y, \: 2z\rangle\[5pt]
&= \langle x, \: y, \: z\rangle\[10pt]

\nabla f(0,0,1) &= \langle 0,\: 0,\: 1 \rangle.
}
$$

Now clearly, $\nabla f (0,0, 1)$ is perpendicular to $\mathcal S$ at the point $(0,0,1).$

![](images/88/88bf25de31ae3318379865cdf2590c15216cb984cbf3948f975caa47317be664.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124731 :activity/expected-seconds 1260.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186098995 :answer-field/choices 17592186098996] [:db/retract 17592186098995 :answer-field/choices 17592186098997] [:db/retract 17592186098995 :answer-field/choices 17592186098998] [:db/retract 17592186098995 :answer-field/choices 17592186098999] [:db/retract 17592186098995 :answer-field/choices 17592186099000] [:db/retract 17592186098983 :answer-field/choices 17592186098984] [:db/retract 17592186098983 :answer-field/choices 17592186098985] [:db/retract 17592186098983 :answer-field/choices 17592186098986] [:db/retract 17592186098983 :answer-field/choices 17592186098987] [:db/retract 17592186098983 :answer-field/choices 17592186098988] [:db/retract 17592186098989 :answer-field/choices 17592186098992] [:db/retract 17592186098989 :answer-field/choices 17592186098993] [:db/retract 17592186098989 :answer-field/choices 17592186098994] [:db/retract 17592186098989 :answer-field/choices 17592186098990] [:db/retract 17592186098989 :answer-field/choices 17592186098991] {:db/id 17592186100840 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-9c0fb2ee-81ac-5d75-ab41-5ee64f815cef" "question-ac9bf5e8-0b9b-5a4e-90d8-e2b158eca7f5" "question-c7823091-db8e-5d0b-aebf-c2f82fe402a4" "question-edfe2065-c6c9-560e-b435-e28eacd51b92"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186100650 :question/problem "We wish to construct a cylindrical can with a base but no lid. Our cylinder must have an exact volume of $27\pi\, \textrm{in}^3.$ What is the radius of the cylinder that gives the smallest surface area?" :question/worked-solution "First, let's draw a picture of a cylinder. Let $r$ be the radius, and $h$ the height.

![](images/ad/adb9c56132e8f346a07a9a644cd364c2347ad8c551a3c9bd4842b7067eb1d050.png)

We wish to minimize the surface area

$$
S= 2\pi r h + \pi r^2.
$$

We know that the volume is fixed at $27\pi \, \textrm{in}^3,$ so we also have the constraint condition

$$
27\pi = \pi r^2 h.
$$

Now, by making $h$ the subject of the constraint equation, we have that

$$
h = \dfrac{27}{ r^2}.
$$

Plugging the above into our expression for $S,$ we obtain

$$
\eqalign{
S(r)& = 2\pi r \left(\dfrac{27}{ r^2}\right) + \pi r^2\
 & = \dfrac{54\pi}{r} +  \pi r^2.}
$$

We want to minimize $S,$ so we need to differentiate $S$ and set the derivative equal to zero. The derivative is 

$$
S'(r) = -\dfrac{54\pi}{r^2} + 2\pi r.
$$

Setting the derivative equal to zero and solving for $r$ gives a stationary point, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(r) & =0 \\ -\frac{54\pi }{{r}^{2}}+2\pi r & =0 \\ 2\pi r & =\frac{54\pi }{{r}^{2}} \\ 2\pi {r}^{3} & =54\pi  \\ {r}^{3} & =27 \\ r & =\sqrt[3]{27} \\ r & =3\,\text{in}\end{aligned}
$$

Using a calculator, we can verify that if $r <   3$ then $S'(r) <         0,$ and if $r > 3$ then $S'(r) > 0,$ which means that the stationary point $r=3$ is indeed a minimum of $S(r).$

We need to create a cylindrical tin with no lid using $108\pi \,{cm}^{2}$ of a metal sheet. What is the radius $r$ of the cylinder that has the largest volume?" :question/worked-solution "First, let $r$ be the radius and $h$ be the height of the cylinder.

We wish to maximize the volume

$$
V=\pi {r}^{2}h.
$$

We know that the surface area is fixed at $108\pi \,{cm}^{2},$ so we also have the constraint equation

$$
2\pi rh+\pi {r}^{2}=108\pi .
$$

Now, by making $h$ the subject of the constraint equation, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi rh & =108\pi -\pi {r}^{2} \\ h & =\frac{108\pi -\pi {r}^{2}}{2\pi r} \\ h & =\frac{108-{r}^{2}}{2r}.\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging the above into our expression for $V,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}V(r) & =\pi {r}^{2}\times \frac{108-{r}^{2}}{2r} \\ V(r) & =\frac{(108r-{r}^{3})\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to maximize $V,$ so we need to differentiate $V$ and set the derivative equal to zero. The derivative is 

$$
{V}^{′}(r)=\frac{(108-3{r}^{2})\pi }{2}.
$$

Setting the derivative equal to zero and solving for $r$ gives a stationary point, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}^{′}(r) & =0 \\ \frac{(108-3{r}^{2})\pi }{2} & =0 \\ 108 & =3{r}^{2} \\ {r}^{2} & =36 \\ r & =6\,\text{cm}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that, in the last step, we only considered the positive root because the radius $r$ must be positive.

Finally, we confirm that $r=6$ is a maximum using the second derivative test. The second derivative ${V}^{″}(r)$ is

$$
{V}^{″}(r)=\frac{-6\pi r}{2}=-3\pi r,
$$

and we can see that ${V}^{″}(6)<0.$ So, the stationary point $r=6$ is indeed a maximum of $V(r).$

Therefore, the cylinder with the largest volume has a radius of $r=6\,\text{cm}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-54b8aa91-91b7-5693-ae56-dd9da1291bd2"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-54b8aa91-91b7-5693-ae56-dd9da1291bd2" :answer-field/id #uuid "54b8aa91-91b7-5693-ae56-dd9da1291bd2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-e91eb110-0036-519e-961d-9bf3cbe43d1b" :answer-field/choices ["answer-1af90d32-167e-5dde-80d0-f28ac27d5b95" "answer-6499d744-86b6-5872-9564-ad470372e5cf" "answer-e91eb110-0036-519e-961d-9bf3cbe43d1b" "answer-6b30217d-8f98-5d80-acc4-6367a9a59089" "answer-e89826da-5376-54ed-8486-970425f19ba4"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1af90d32-167e-5dde-80d0-f28ac27d5b95" :answer/id #uuid "1af90d32-167e-5dde-80d0-f28ac27d5b95" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3\,\text{cm}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6499d744-86b6-5872-9564-ad470372e5cf" :answer/id #uuid "6499d744-86b6-5872-9564-ad470372e5cf" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3\sqrt{6}\,\text{cm}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e91eb110-0036-519e-961d-9bf3cbe43d1b" :answer/id #uuid "e91eb110-0036-519e-961d-9bf3cbe43d1b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "6\,\text{cm}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6b30217d-8f98-5d80-acc4-6367a9a59089" :answer/id #uuid "6b30217d-8f98-5d80-acc4-6367a9a59089" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "6\sqrt{3}\,\text{cm}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e89826da-5376-54ed-8486-970425f19ba4" :answer/id #uuid "e89826da-5376-54ed-8486-970425f19ba4" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "9\,\text{cm}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186101277 :question/problem "![](images/50/50853fcaa44ff9b7d80e708e546275286541afc0b6ed05c4ca87ea3175364c09.png)

We need to create a cylindrical tin with no lid using $48\pi \,{cm}^{2}$ of sheet metal. What is the largest possible volume of the cylinder?" :question/worked-solution "First, let $r$ be the radius and $h$ be the height of the cylinder.

We wish to maximize the volume

$$
V=\pi {r}^{2}h.
$$

We know that the surface area is fixed at $48\pi \,{cm}^{2},$ so we also have the constraint equation

$$
2\pi rh+\pi {r}^{2}=48\pi .
$$

Now, by making $h$ the subject of the constraint equation, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi rh & =48\pi -\pi {r}^{2} \\ h & =\frac{48\pi -\pi {r}^{2}}{2\pi r} \\ h & =\frac{48-{r}^{2}}{2r}.\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging the above into our expression for $V,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}V(r) & =\pi {r}^{2}\times \frac{48-{r}^{2}}{2r} \\ V(r) & =\frac{(48r-{r}^{3})\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to maximize $V,$ so we need to differentiate $V$ and set the derivative equal to zero. The derivative is 

$$
{V}^{′}(r)=\frac{(48-3{r}^{2})\pi }{2}.
$$

Setting the derivative equal to zero and solving for $r$ gives a stationary point, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}^{′}(r) & =0 \\ \frac{(48-3{r}^{2})\pi }{2} & =0 \\ 48 & =3{r}^{2} \\ {r}^{2} & =16 \\ r & =4\,\text{cm}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that, in the last step, we only considered the positive root because the radius $r$ must be positive.

Finally, we confirm that $r=4$ is a maximum using the second derivative test. The second derivative ${V}^{″}(r)$ is

$$
{V}^{″}(r)=\frac{-6\pi r}{2}=-3\pi r,
$$

and we can see that ${V}^{″}(4)<0.$ So, the stationary point $r=4$ is indeed a maximum of $V(r).$

So the cylinder with the largest volume has a radius of $r=4\,\text{cm}.$

Finally, to find the largest volume, we substitute $r=4\,\text{cm}$ into the equation for the volume $V:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V(4) & =\frac{(48(4)-(4)^{3})\pi }{2} \\  & =\frac{(192-64)\pi }{2} \\  & =\frac{128\pi }{2} \\  & =64\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the largest possible volume of the cylinder is $V=64\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186098983 :answer-field/correct "answer-37d90ecc-799c-5966-9485-4403e472a148" :answer-field/choices ["answer-9a21a290-1231-5251-ae15-843e314d1d5a" "answer-a0205964-c271-505f-ba22-0f2acac8f600" "answer-37d90ecc-799c-5966-9485-4403e472a148" "answer-961c2b95-dc93-5b57-bf9b-e581d63cdc5b" "answer-9fcdc104-93f0-5be0-ac43-65beeb6f88d2"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9a21a290-1231-5251-ae15-843e314d1d5a" :answer/id #uuid "9a21a290-1231-5251-ae15-843e314d1d5a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "46\pi \,{cm}^{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a0205964-c271-505f-ba22-0f2acac8f600" :answer/id #uuid "a0205964-c271-505f-ba22-0f2acac8f600" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "58\pi \,{cm}^{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-37d90ecc-799c-5966-9485-4403e472a148" :answer/id #uuid "37d90ecc-799c-5966-9485-4403e472a148" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "64\pi \,{cm}^{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-961c2b95-dc93-5b57-bf9b-e581d63cdc5b" :answer/id #uuid "961c2b95-dc93-5b57-bf9b-e581d63cdc5b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "72\pi \,{cm}^{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9fcdc104-93f0-5be0-ac43-65beeb6f88d2" :answer/id #uuid "9fcdc104-93f0-5be0-ac43-65beeb6f88d2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "81\pi \,{cm}^{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186101278 :question/problem "![](images/38/38883c7cc4bfe8c9ecccadfcc2d0c75ff66f79b19ff697c15ddbe53f4c63dbab.png)

{{field-1}} $\text{yd}$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's draw a picture of a cylinder. Let $r$ be the radius, and $h$ the height.

![](images/55/55de2c06ea57724513e450cbf49a0477d63cd75bac601d5d95f0ba7e366852ff.png)

We wish to minimize the manufacturing cost. We can express the manufacturing cost $C$ in terms of $r$ and $h$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =2\pi rh\cdot 7.50+\pi {r}^{2}\cdot 2.50 \\  & =15\pi rh+2.5\pi {r}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We know that the volume is fixed at $\frac{125}{3}\pi \,{\text{yd}}^{3},$ so we also have the constraint condition

$$
\frac{125}{3}\pi =\pi {r}^{2}h.
$$

Now, by making $h$ the subject of the constraint equation, we have that

$$
h=\frac{125}{3{r}^{2}}.
$$

Plugging the above into our expression for $C,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}C(r) & =15\pi r(\frac{125}{3{r}^{2}})+2.5\pi {r}^{2} \\  & =\frac{625\pi }{r}+2.5\pi {r}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We want to minimize $C,$ so we need to differentiate $C$ and set the derivative equal to zero. The derivative is 

$$
{C}^{′}(r)=-\frac{625\pi }{{r}^{2}}+5\pi r.
$$

 

Setting the derivative equal to zero and solving for $r$ gives a stationary point, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}^{′}(r) & =0 \\ -\frac{625\pi }{{r}^{2}}+5\pi r & =0 \\ 5\pi r & =\frac{625\pi }{{r}^{2}} \\ 5\pi {r}^{3} & =625\pi  \\ {r}^{3} & =125 \\ r & =\sqrt[3]{125} \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Using a calculator, we can verify that if $r<5$ then ${C}^{′}(r)<0,$ and if $r>5$ then ${C}^{′}(r)>0,$ which means that the stationary point $r=5$ is indeed a minimum of $C(r).$

Therefore, the container with the smallest manufacturing cost has radius $r=5\,\text{yd}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-9dc3b0ba-69af-5706-afb5-6c4ce41ddf74"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-9dc3b0ba-69af-5706-afb5-6c4ce41ddf74" :answer-field/id #uuid "9dc3b0ba-69af-5706-afb5-6c4ce41ddf74" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-217e50a3-d416-5fd8-8e38-c8d5e7424bf9" :answer-field/choices ["answer-217e50a3-d416-5fd8-8e38-c8d5e7424bf9"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-217e50a3-d416-5fd8-8e38-c8d5e7424bf9" :answer/id #uuid "217e50a3-d416-5fd8-8e38-c8d5e7424bf9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-ebb08e7a-2131-5a36-9f64-7c4d80a5d168" :question/id #uuid "ebb08e7a-2131-5a36-9f64-7c4d80a5d168" :question/math-academy-id "q-85731" :question/problem "A manufacturer wishes to build a cylindrical tank with a base but no lid. ![](images/33/339a377a68f93c78cf99b0f58333ab26c24bff91509dd707d22981d773ef077c.png)

This is yet another type of optimization problem. Let's remind ourselves of the general strategy for optimization problems.

1\. Draw a diagram of the situation, introducing variables where necessary.

2\. Write down the equation of the quantity that you're trying to maximize or minimize. This is the objective function, and it might include more than one variable.

3\. Write down the constraint equation.

4\. Use the constraint equation to write the objective function in terms of a single variable only.

5\. Differentiate the objective function, set it equal to zero, and solve for the stationary points.

6\. Test each stationary point using the second derivative test. Or you can use the first derivative test if it's easier.

In the following examples, we'll need to use the formulas for a cylindrical can's volume $V$ and surface area $S.$ For a cylinder with radius $r$ and height $h,$ its volume is given by the formula

$$
V = \pi r^2 h.
$$

If the cylinder is closed at both ends, its surface area $S$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}S=2\pi rh+2\pi {r}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

If the cylinder is closed at only one end, its surface area $S$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}S=2\pi rh+\pi {r}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186101069 :activity/expected-seconds 1380.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186101627 :step/math-academy-id 641455 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186101628 :step/math-academy-id 641456 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186101629 :step/math-academy-id 641460 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186101788 :step/math-academy-id 641465 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064237 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-d7abcd6f-c9ce-5a9a-8667-2f8c0c4481fa" "question-0629bbb0-2921-5d85-ab43-d50c29c16b81"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186063973 :question/problem "Find the values of $x$ that satisfy $2x - 5 \leq 1$ and $7x +11 < -3.$" :question/worked-solution "To solve compound "and" inequalities, we solve each inequality separately and then find their intersection.

- We start by solving $3x + 9 \geq 0\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+9 & \ge 0 \\ 3x+9-9 & \ge 0-9 \\ 3x & \ge -9 \\ \frac{3x}{3} & \ge \frac{-9}{3} \\ x & \ge -3\end{aligned}
$$

The solution to this inequality is shown on the number line below.

![](images/51/5127629c09f32bb8ed7872b476322d6973e44e82be7977492c8dd0967d3cb0ec.png)

- Then, we solve $2x \leq -2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & \le -2 \\ \frac{2x}{2} & \le \frac{-2}{2} \\ x & \le -1\end{aligned}
$$

The solution to this inequality is shown on the number line below.

![](images/35/35e30bc9c45b08793d847c8750698f7d9dab781438405239ed4483ce82f2dcfb.png)

To find the values of $x$ that satisfy both inequalities, we find where the two solutions overlap:

![](images/fe/fe4c223767cb06d9d620d32f5e668c7305688b3870bf0317304c56b11053e19f.png)

$$

Substituting the expression for $z$ into the equation of the hyperboloid, we obtain: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+{y}^{2}-\frac{((-2-3y)+2)^{2}}{3} & =-1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+{y}^{2}-\frac{9{y}^{2}}{3} & =-1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-2{y}^{2} & =-1 \\ {x}^{2}-4{y}^{2} & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

"Find the point(s) of the intersection of the sphere ${x}^{2}+(y+4)^{2}+(z-2)^{2}=9$ and the line $x=y+1=\frac{z-2}{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write the equation of our line in parametric form:

$$
\frac{x}{1}=\frac{y+1}{1}=\frac{z-2}{2}=t\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}x=t \\ y=t-1 \\ z=2t+2,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Substituting the above expressions for $x$, $y$, and $z$ into the equation of the sphere, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+(y+4)^{2}+(z-2)^{2} & =9 \\ (t)^{2}+((t-1)+4)^{2}+((2t+2)-2)^{2} & =9 \\ (t)^{2}+(t+3)^{2}+(2t)^{2} & =9 \\ {t}^{2}+({t}^{2}+6t+9)+4{t}^{2} & =9 \\ 6{t}^{2}+6t+9 & =9 \\ 6{t}^{2}+6t & =0 \\ t(t+1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we get the solutions $t=0$ and $t=-1.$ 

Now, we substitute our solutions back into the equations of the line.

- For $t=0$, we have

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=(0)=0 \\ y=(0)-1=-1 \\ z=2(0)+2=2,\end{aligned}
$$

so the first point is $(0,-1,2).$

- For $t=-1$, we have

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=(-1)=-1 \\ y=(-1)-1=-2 \\ z=2(-1)+2=0,\end{aligned}
$$

so the second point is $(-1,-2,0).$

Therefore, the points of intersection are $(0,-1,2)$ and $(-1,-2,0).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-6a536d68-bf2d-5dad-99bc-e23331bfdfe7"] to eliminate the variable $z.$ First, we solve the equation of the plane for $z$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-z & =8\,⟹\,z=2x-8\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the expression for $z$ into the equation of the ellipsoid, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2(x-4)^{2}}{3}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{9}+\frac{(2x-8)^{2}}{3} & =1 \\ \frac{2(x-4)^{2}}{3}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{9}+\frac{(2(x-4))^{2}}{3} & =1 \\ \frac{2(x-4)^{2}}{3}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{9}+\frac{4(x-4)^{2}}{3} & =1 \\ 2(x-4)^{2}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-4)^{2}}{1/2}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{9} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the projection of the intersection is the ellipse $\frac{(x-4)^{2}}{1/2}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{9}=1.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields the elliptic cone ${x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}=4{z}^{2}$ and the line $\frac{x+1}{2}=y=z+2.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write the equation of our line in the parametric form:

$$
\frac{x+1}{2}=y=z+2=t\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}x=2t-1 \\ y=t \\ z=t-2,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Substituting the above expressions for $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ into the equation of the elliptic cone, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2} & =4{z}^{2} \\ (2t-1)^{2}+3{t}^{2} & =4(t-2)^{2} \\ 4{t}^{2}-4t+1+3{t}^{2} & =4({t}^{2}-4t+4) \\ 4{t}^{2}-4t+1+3{t}^{2} & =4{t}^{2}-16t+16 \\ 3{t}^{2}+12t-15 & =0 \\ 3({t}^{2}+4t-5) & =0 \\ 3(t+5)(t-1) & =0 \\ t & =-5,1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute our solutions back into the equations of the line.

- For $t=-5,$ we have

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=2(-5)-1=-11 \\ y=-5 \\ z=-5-2=-7,\end{aligned}
$$

so the first point is $(-11,-5,-7).$

- For $t=1,$ we have

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=2(1)-1=1 \\ y=1 \\ z=1-2=-1,\end{aligned}
$$

so the second point is $(1,1,-1).$

Therefore, the points of intersection are $(-11,-5,-7)$ and $(1,1,-1).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields :question/id #uuid "30a2be53-ad1e-54e7-8cc2-2924faaf8e17" :question/math-academy-id "q-161795" :question/problem "Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T,$ defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}u+\operatorname{cos}⁡w \\ v \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡u+w\end{aligned}].
$$" :question/worked-solution "For a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=u+\operatorname{cos}⁡w,\,y(u,v,w)=v,\,z(u,v,w)=\operatorname{cos}⁡u+w.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡u & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =0, & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡u & 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =1(-1)^{2+2}|\begin{aligned}1 & -\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡u & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =1-\operatorname{sin}⁡u\,\operatorname{sin}⁡w.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-2d0df2e4-d380-5912-bac6-465760a259a6"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}u+v\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +w\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 3v \\ u\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +w\end{aligned}].
$$

You may assume that $\theta $ is a fixed constant." :question/worked-solution "For a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=u+v\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +w\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,y(u,v,w)=3v,\,z(u,v,w)=u\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +w.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =3 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =0, & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}1 & \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =3(-1)^{2+2}|\begin{aligned}1 & \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =3(1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =3{cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-7d304d66-3b35-5b7a-a10d-e4c98f3bf8ff"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 9.$ Express your answer in interval notation." :question/worked-solution "We start by solving $6x-1 \leq 2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}6x-1 & \le 2 \\ 6x & \le 3 \\ x & \le \frac{3}{6} \\ x & \le \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/dd/dd2c101e02e14a147371bc1b822f3bc86081dd0059ac50ae1f9131909e73e3ad.png)

Then, we solve $5x -1 > 9\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}5x-1 & >9 \\ 5x & >10 \\ x & >2\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/8b/8b252e1c42dcac87072a33b33460a887b6ec3bfa0d1511f05a004935df1911ca.png)

To graph the values of $x$ that satisfy either inequality, we overlay the two graphs on the same number line:

![](images/ac/ac44f335b135463820ec0db9bc04470769fee7aabc8717edcc351893b6d8de47.png)

Therefore, the final solution is $x \leq \dfrac{1}{2}$ or $x >2.$ We can write this using interval notation as

$$
\begin{aligned}(-\infty ,\frac{1}{2}]\cup (2,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186115321 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-4351a80f-5497-5bde-b1ce-3fcb89da7609"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186115153 :question/problem "Find all the values of $x$ that satisfy $12x+8 > 44$ or $5x+3 \leq 28.$" :question/worked-solution "We start by solving $12x+8 > 44\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}12x+8 & >44 \\ 12x & >36 \\ x & >3\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/e9/e9eec85ca2dd2a9fd01db97a5f281d16fd958e143e048f7ff3c5e7a87dd33f0a.png)

Then, we solve $5x+3 \leq 28\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}5x+3 & \le 28 \\ 5x & \le 25 \\ x & \le 5\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}8x+7 & \le -9 \\ 8x & \le -16 \\ x & \le -2\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/12/12c34a5af230afb788ddd8c689ef0e9b29c5c5adaf35a1e81099453436cf7f3f.png)

To graph the values of $x$ that satisfy either inequality, we overlay the two graphs on the same number line:

![](images/bc/bc365364192f3784c565ebcb819a5f37885830f93510029647d39883217987cb.png)

Therefore, the final solution is $x\le 2.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186112434 :answer-field/correct 17592186112435 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186116417 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find all of the values of $x$ that satisfy *either* $4x+2 < 6$ *or* $2x \geq 8.$

To do this, we solve each inequality individually and then compute the union of the two solutions.

We start by solving $4x+2 < 6\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}4x+2 & <6 \\ 4x & <4 \\ x & <1\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/0d/0d36b8e68d9fd0b33b255502860481eeb525b60382029b17434bfb072cc39da2.png)

Then, we solve $2x \geq 8\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & \ge 8 \\ x & \ge 4\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/ed/edf5665b7cab7f51e3f252601a96d43c6f0cbfc64e5c9b8da81f0ef09d7b2f5a.png)

To graph the values of $x$ that satisfy either inequality, we overlay the two graphs on the same number line:

![](images/5c/5c60839a626f2ba8a0fe4a24f4011af0fa52c00d79fbf80039bcfdbdf0a612c7.png)

Thus, the final solution is $x < 1$ or $x \geq 4.$ We can write this using interval notation as

$$
(-\infty, 1) \cup [4,\infty).
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186115415 :activity/expected-seconds 720.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186172106 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-7f9f9f92-90ae-5c14-9ede-c5718a2ba70e" "question-33a01272-f3c9-5c47-b349-cebcb033572c"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-7f9f9f92-90ae-5c14-9ede-c5718a2ba70e" :question/id #uuid "7f9f9f92-90ae-5c14-9ede-c5718a2ba70e" :question/math-academy-id "q-159628" :question/problem "Consider a sample of size ${n}_{1}=54$ from a population with standard deviation ${\sigma }_{1}=3.7$ and a sample of size ${n}_{2}=77$ from a population with standard deviation ${\sigma }_{2}=1.2.$ Given that the samples are independent and the sample means are ${\overset{―}{x}}_{1}=23$ and  ${\overset{―}{x}}_{2}=12,$ find a $99%$ confidence interval for the difference ${\mu }_{1}-{\mu }_{2}$ between the corresponding population means.

*Hint: Use the fact that $P(Z>2.576)=0.005,$ where $Z∼N(0,1).$*" :question/worked-solution "Notice that

- the samples are independent,

- both sample sizes are "sufficiently large," i.e., $\ge 30,$ and

- both population variances are known.

As a result, given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the difference ${\mu }_{1}-{\mu }_{2}$ between the corresponding population means can be written as

$$
({\overset{―}{x}}_{1}-{\overset{―}{x}}_{2})\pm E
$$

where 

- $E={z}_{\alpha /2}\sqrt{\frac{{\sigma }_{1}^{2}}{{n}_{1}}+\frac{{\sigma }_{2}^{2}}{{n}_{2}}}$ is the margin of error,

- ${\overset{―}{x}}_{1}$ and ${\overset{―}{x}}_{2}$ are the sample means, ${\mu }_{1}$ and ${\mu }_{2}$ are the population means, ${\sigma }_{1}^{2}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}^{2}$ are the population variances,  ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are the sample sizes,

- $P(Z>{z}_{\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2}$ and $Z∼N(0,1).$

Now, to construct the confidence interval, we proceed as follows:

- **Step 1.** Find the point estimate:

$$
{\overset{―}{x}}_{1}-{\overset{―}{x}}_{2}=23-12=11
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the margin of error. Since we are interested in finding a $99%$ confidence interval, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.99=0.01\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.005.
$$

We are given that $P(Z>2.576)=0.005.$ As a result, 

$$
{z}_{\alpha /2}={z}_{0.005}=2.576.
$$

Now, we can compute the margin of error:

$$
E=2.576\cdot \sqrt{\frac{{3.7}^{2}}{54}+\frac{{1.2}^{2}}{77}}≈1.344
$$

- **Step 3.** Construct the $99%$ confidence interval for the difference between the population means:

$$
\begin{aligned} & 11\pm 1.344\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-05a48ccb-a74e-541e-97fa-2294603b02e6"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "The lengths of traditional baguettes and brown baguettes made at a particular French bakery have standard deviations of $4\,\text{cm}$ and $3\,\text{cm},$ respectively. The baker wants to determine whether the population mean ${\mu }_{x}$ of the lengths of traditional baguettes is larger than the population mean ${\mu }_{y}$ of the lengths of brown baguettes. He constructs a $90%$ confidence interval for the difference between the population means.

Given that the baker sampled $50$ traditional baguettes and $40$ brown baguettes and found that their mean lengths were $65\,\text{cm}$ and $63.5\,\text{cm},$ respectively, which of the following statements are true?

I. The end-points of the $90%$ confidence interval for the difference between the population means are approximately $1.5\pm 1.421.$

II. All values contained within the $90%$ confidence interval are positive.

III. The confidence interval data suggests that ${\mu }_{x}>{\mu }_{y}.$

*Hint: Given a random variable $Z∼N(0,1),$ the table below shows the $z$-scores ${z}_{p}$ such that $P(Z>{z}_{p})=p$ for some particular values of $p.$*

| $p$ | $0.100$ | $0.050$ | $0.025$ | $0.010$ | $0.005$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${z}_{p}$ | $1.282$ | $1.645$ | $1.960$ | $2.326$ | $2.576$ |" :question/worked-solution "Notice that

- the samples are independent,

- both sample sizes are "sufficiently large," i.e., $\ge 30,$ and

- both population variances are known.

As a result, given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the difference ${\mu }_{1}-{\mu }_{2}$ between the corresponding population means can be written as

$$
({\overset{―}{x}}_{1}-{\overset{―}{x}}_{2})\pm E
$$

where 

- $E={z}_{\alpha /2}\sqrt{\frac{{\sigma }_{1}^{2}}{{n}_{1}}+\frac{{\sigma }_{2}^{2}}{{n}_{2}}}$ is the margin of error,

- ${\overset{―}{x}}_{1}$ and ${\overset{―}{x}}_{2}$ are the sample means, ${\mu }_{1}$ and ${\mu }_{2}$ are the population means, ${\sigma }_{1}^{2}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}^{2}$ are the population variances,  ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are the sample sizes,

- $P(Z>{z}_{\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2}$ and $Z∼N(0,1).$

Now, to construct the confidence interval, we proceed as follows:

- **Step 1.** Find the point estimate:

$$
{\overset{―}{x}}_{1}-{\overset{―}{x}}_{2}=65-63.5=1.5
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the margin of error. Since we are interested in finding a $90%$ confidence interval, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.90=0.1\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.05.
$$

We also need to find the $z$-score value ${z}_{0.05}$ such that $P(Z>{z}_{0.05})=0.05,$ where $Z∼N(0,1).$
From the percentage points table of the normal distribution, we obtain that ${z}_{0.05}=1.645:$  

| $p$ | $0.100$ | $0.050$ | $0.025$ | $0.010$ | $0.005$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${z}_{p}$ | $1.282$ | $1.645$ | $1.960$ | $2.326$ | $2.576$ |

 

Now, we can compute the margin of error:

$$
E=1.645\cdot \sqrt{\frac{{4}^{2}}{50}+\frac{{3}^{2}}{40}}≈1.214
$$

- **Step 3.** Construct the confidence interval:

$$
\begin{aligned} & 1.5\pm 1.214\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. The end-points of our confidence interval are $1.5\pm 1.214.$

- Statement II is true. All values within the confidence interval are positive:

$$
(1.5-1.214,\,1.5+1.214)=(0.286,\,2.714)
$$

- Statement III is true. Since all values within the confidence interval are positive, this suggests that ${\mu }_{x}>{\mu }_{y}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-5eb63ba3-c644-5698-927f-01d281fe6523"] :db/ensure :question/problem "The scores of girls and boys on a national post-high school exam have standard deviations of $3$ points and $4$ points, respectively. Officials sampled $111$ girls and $115$ boys and found that their mean scores on the test were $74$ points and $73.4$ points, respectively. Which of the following statements are true?

({\overset{―}{x}}_{1}-{\overset{―}{x}}_{2})\pm E
$$

- $P(Z>{z}_{\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2}$ and $Z∼N(0,1).$

- **Step 1.** Find the point estimate:

$$
{\overset{―}{x}}_{1}-{\overset{―}{x}}_{2}=74-73.6=0.6
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the margin of error. Since we are interested in finding a $95%$ confidence interval, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.95=0.05\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.025.
$$

We also need to find the $z$-score value ${z}_{0.025}$ such that $P(Z>{z}_{0.025})=0.025,$ where $Z∼N(0,1).$
From the percentage points table of the normal distribution, we obtain that ${z}_{0.025}=1.960:$ 

| $p$ | $0.100$ | $0.050$ | $0.025$ | $0.010$ | $0.005$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${z}_{p}$ | $1.282$ | $1.645$ | $1.960$ | $2.326$ | $2.576$ |

 

Now, we can compute the margin of error:

$$
E=1.960\cdot \sqrt{\frac{{3}^{2}}{111}+\frac{{4}^{2}}{115}}≈0.920
$$

- **Step 3.** Construct the confidence interval:

\begin{aligned} & 0.6\pm 0.920\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now examine our statements.

:question/problem "A study of body weight conducted on two age groups of women, X and Y, yields standard deviations of ${\sigma }_{x}=8\,\text{lb}$ and ${\sigma }_{y}=10\,\text{lb},$ respectively.
A researcher wants to determine whether the population mean ${\mu }_{x}$ of the weights of group X is smaller than the population mean ${\mu }_{y}$ of the weights of group Y. She decides to construct a $90%$ confidence interval for the difference between the population means.

The researcher sampled $50$ women from group X and $55$ from group Y, finding that their mean weights are $58\,lb$ and $64\,lb,$  respectively. Which of the following statements are true?  

I. The end-points of the $90%$ confidence interval for the difference between the population means are approximately $-6\pm 2.895.$

II. All values contained within the $90%$ confidence interval are negative.

III. The confidence interval data suggests that ${\mu }_{x}<{\mu }_{y}.$

*Hint: Given a random variable $Z∼N(0,1),$ the table below shows the $z$-scores ${z}_{p}$ such that $P(Z>{z}_{p})=p$ for some particular values of $p.$*

| $p$ | $0.100$ | $0.050$ | $0.025$ | $0.010$ | $0.005$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${z}_{p}$ | $1.282$ | $1.645$ | $1.960$ | $2.326$ | $2.576$ |" :question/worked-solution "Notice that

- the samples are independent,

- both sample sizes are "sufficiently large," i.e., $\ge 30,$ and

- both population variances are known.

As a result, given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the difference ${\mu }_{1}-{\mu }_{2}$ between the corresponding population means can be written as

$$
({\overset{―}{x}}_{1}-{\overset{―}{x}}_{2})\pm E
$$

where 

- $E={z}_{\alpha /2}\sqrt{\frac{{\sigma }_{1}^{2}}{{n}_{1}}+\frac{{\sigma }_{2}^{2}}{{n}_{2}}}$ is the margin of error,

- ${\overset{―}{x}}_{1}$ and ${\overset{―}{x}}_{2}$ are the sample means, ${\mu }_{1}$ and ${\mu }_{2}$ are the population means, ${\sigma }_{1}^{2}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}^{2}$ are the population variances,  ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are the sample sizes,

- $P(Z>{z}_{\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2}$ and $Z∼N(0,1).$

Now, to construct the confidence interval, we proceed as follows:

- **Step 1.** Find the point estimate:

$$
{\overset{―}{x}}_{1}-{\overset{―}{x}}_{2}=58-64=-6
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the margin of error. Since we are interested in finding a $90%$ confidence interval, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.90=0.1\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.05.
$$

We also need to find the $z$-score value ${z}_{0.05}$ such that $P(Z>{z}_{0.05})=0.05,$ where $Z∼N(0,1).$
From the percentage points table of the normal distribution, we obtain that ${z}_{0.05}=1.645:$  

| $p$ | $0.100$ | $0.050$ | $0.025$ | $0.010$ | $0.005$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${z}_{p}$ | $1.282$ | $1.645$ | $1.960$ | $2.326$ | $2.576$ |

 

Now, we can compute the margin of error:

$$
E=1.645\cdot \sqrt{\frac{{8}^{2}}{50}+\frac{{10}^{2}}{55}}≈2.895
$$

- **Step 3.** Construct the confidence interval:

$$
\begin{aligned} & -6\pm 2.895\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. The end-points of our confidence interval are $-6\pm 2.895.$

- Statement II is true. All values within the confidence interval are negative:

$$
(-6-2.895,\,-6+2.895)=(-8.895,\,-3.105)
$$

- Statement III is true. Since all values within the confidence interval are negative, this suggests that ${\mu }_{x}<{\mu }_{y}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-63a3ec7b-79e1-5862-a616-14f2961b8754"] :db/ensure $$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t-{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨4-2t,3{t}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})=c⟨2,1⟩.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =c⟨2,1⟩ \\ ⟨4-2t,3{t}^{2}⟩ & =c⟨2,1⟩ \\ ⟨4-2t,3{t}^{2}⟩ & =⟨2c,c⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4-2t=2c \\ 3{t}^{2}=c\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we obtain that $c=2-t.$ Substituting in the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{t}^{2} & =2-t \\ 3{t}^{2}+t-2 & =0 \\ (3t-2)(t+1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $⟨2,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the points corresponding to $t=-1,\frac{2}{3}.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-1) & =⟨4(-1)-(-1)^{2},(-1)^{3}⟩=⟨-5,-1⟩ \\ r(\frac{2}{3}) & =⟨4(\frac{2}{3})-{(\frac{2}{3})}^{2},{(\frac{2}{3})}^{3}⟩=⟨\frac{20}{9},\frac{8}{27}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨2,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the points $(-5,-1)$ and $(\frac{20}{9},\frac{8}{27}).$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $F(x)$ is an even function. So, the Fourier series of its $2L$-periodic extension has the form

$$
\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{L}).
$$

In our case, $L=3$ and we are already given the coefficients ${a}_{0}$ and ${a}_{n}$ for $n\ge 1.$ Thus, the Fourier series of $f(x)$ is given by

$$
f(x)∼-2+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{72(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Now, notice that 

- the function $F$ is continuously differentiable on $(-3,3),$

- continuous on $[-3,3),$ and

- satisfies $F(-3)=F(3),$ if we extend the value at $x=3$ using the formula $F(x)=-2{x}^{2}+4.$

Therefore, the $6$-periodic extension $f$ is $\text{continuous}$ and $\text{piecewise smooth}$ on $R,$ so we may differentiate its Fourier series term-by-term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-2{x}^{2}+4) & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-2)+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{72(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})) \\ -4x & ∼0+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{72(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}\cdot (-\frac{n\pi }{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})) \\ -4x & ∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{-24(-1)^{n+1}}{n\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\ -4x & ∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{24(-1)^{n}}{n\pi }\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})\end{aligned}

$$
\boxed{\,2\,}÷\frac{1}{3}=\boxed{\,6\,}
$$

"4a460e59-a60e-5c01-b0d6-ac09a000a8e4" :question/math-academy-id "q-159874" :question/problem "Suppose ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{5}$ is an I.I.D random sample with ${X}_{i}∼\text{Exp}(\theta )$ and unknown rate parameter $\theta .$ For a particular sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{5},$ you're given that 

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{5}{x}_{i}=4.5.
$$

Find the likelihood function of the sample.

*Hint: The probability density function for an exponential random variable is given by* 

$$
f(x;\theta )=\theta {e}^{-\theta x},\,x\ge 0.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed continuous random variables with probability density function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is

$$
L(\theta )=P({X}_{1}={x}_{1},{X}_{2}={x}_{2},…,{X}_{n}={x}_{n})={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\,\theta ).
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=5$ independent exponential random variables with unknown parameter $\theta ,$ for which the probability density function is

$$
f(x;\theta )=\theta {e}^{-\theta x},\,x\ge 0.
$$

We can calculate the likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & ={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}\theta {e}^{-\theta {x}_{i}} \\  & ={\theta }^{n}\,{e}^{-\theta \sum {x}_{i}} \\  & ={\theta }^{n}\,{e}^{-S\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

where $S={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}.$ 

We are told that $S={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}=4.5$ and $n=5.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & ={\theta }^{5}\,{e}^{-4.5\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-afa1de34-af75-5f8e-b326-c843f5d31eb8"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id For a particular sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3},{x}_{4},$ you're given that 

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{4}{x}_{i}=8.98,\,{\sum }_{i=1}^{4}{x}_{i}^{2}=29.4.
$$

Given that the likelihood function of the sample is

$$
L(\theta )=\frac{1}{4{\pi }^{2}}\,{e}^{\,g(\theta )},
$$

what is the expression for $g(\theta )?$

*Hint: The probability density function for a normal random variable with mean $\theta $ and variance $1$ is given by* 

$$
f(x;\theta )=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed continuous random variables with probability density function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is

$$
L(\theta )=P({X}_{1}={x}_{1},{X}_{2}={x}_{2},…,{X}_{n}={x}_{n})={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\,\theta ).
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=4$ independent normal random variables with unknown mean $\theta $ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=1,$ for which the probability density function is

$$
f(x;\theta )=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

We can calculate the likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & ={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\  & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-\sum ({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}/2} \\  & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-(\sum {x}_{i}^{2}-2\theta \sum {x}_{i}+n{\theta }^{2})/2} \\  & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-(C-2S\theta +n{\theta }^{2})/2}\end{aligned}
$$

where $S={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}$ and $C={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2}.$

We are told that $S={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}=8.98,$ $C={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2}=29.4,$ and $n=4.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & =(2\pi )^{-4/2}\,{e}^{-(29.4-2(8.98)\theta +4{\theta }^{2})/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4{\pi }^{2}}\,{e}^{\,-14.7\,+\,8.98\theta \,-\,2{\theta }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
g(\theta )=-14.7+8.98\theta -2{\theta }^{2}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e9645430-c3dd-5a0d-a5c2-2b90bb8a3076"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},{X}_{3},{X}_{4}$ is an I.I.D random sample with ${X}_{i}∼N(\theta ,1),$  where $\theta $ is an unknown mean.  Given that the likelihood function of the sample $0.3,\,1.2,\,-2.6,\,0.4$ is

$$
L(\theta )=\frac{1}{4{\pi }^{2}}\,{e}^{\,g(\theta )},
$$

what is the expression for $g(\theta )?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed continuous random variables with probability density function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is

$$
L(\theta )=P({X}_{1}={x}_{1},{X}_{2}={x}_{2},…,{X}_{n}={x}_{n})={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\,\theta ).
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=4$ independent normal random variables with unknown mean $\theta $ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=1,$ for which the probability density function is

$$
f(x;\theta )=\frac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-\frac{1}{2}{(\frac{x-\theta }{\sigma })}^{2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

We can calculate the likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & ={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\  & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-\sum ({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}/2} \\  & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-(\sum {x}_{i}^{2}-2\theta \sum {x}_{i}+n{\theta }^{2})/2} \\  & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-(C-2S\theta +n{\theta }^{2})/2}\end{aligned}
$$

where $S={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}$ and $C={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2}.$

For our sample, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}S & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} \\  & =0.3+1.2+(-2.6)+0.4 \\  & =-0.7 \\ C & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2} \\  & =(0.3)^{2}+(1.2)^{2}+(-2.6)^{2}+(0.4)^{2} \\  & =8.45\end{aligned}
$$

and $n=4.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & =(2\pi )^{-4/2}\,{e}^{-(8.45-2(-0.7)\theta +4{\theta }^{2})/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4{\pi }^{2}}\,{e}^{\,-4.225\,-\,0.7\theta \,-\,2{\theta }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
g(\theta )=-4.225-0.7\theta -2{\theta }^{2}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-5f8fd110-202a-5667-bf26-f7d318d06cc6"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186193027 :question/problem "Let $f(x)$ be positive and strictly increasing for $x\in [1,4],$ and differentiable for $x\in (1,4).$ Suppose we approximate the area under the curve $y=g(x)=x\cdot f(x)$ over the interval $[1,4]$ using a left Riemann sum. Given that $g(x)>0,$ which of the following statements must be true?

I. ${f}^{′}(x)>0$

II. ${g}^{′}(x)>0$

III. The Riemann sum underestimates the true area." :question/worked-solution "We're given that $g(x)=x\cdot f(x)>0.$ Now, recall the following:

- If $g(x)$ is strictly increasing, the left Riemann sum gives an *underestimate* of the area under the curve $y=g(x).$

- If $g(x)$ is strictly decreasing, the left Riemann sum gives an *overestimate* of the area under the curve $y=g(x).$

Let's now consider each statement in turn:

- Statement II is true. Differentiating $g(x)=x\cdot f(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(x) & =(x)^{′}\cdot f(x)+x\cdot {f}^{′}(x) \\  & =f(x)+x\cdot {f}^{′}(x).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x)$ is positive and strictly increasing over the interval $(1,4),$ we have 

$$
x>0,\,f(x)>0,\,{f}^{′}(x)>0.
$$

Hence, we obtain

$$
{g}^{′}(x)={{f(x)}_{⏟}}_{>0}+{{x}_{⏟}}_{>0}\cdot {{{f}^{′}(x)}_{⏟}}_{>0}={{f(x)}_{⏟}}_{>0}+{{x\cdot {f}^{′}(x)}_{⏟}}_{>0}>0.
$$

- Statement III is true. Since ${g}^{′}(x)>0,$ the function $g(x)$ is strictly increasing. Therefore, the left Riemann sum gives an *underestimate* of the area under the curve $y=x\cdot f(x).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186190048 :answer-field/correct 17592186190053 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192712 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-95ecf8d2-2252-5516-85e1-ebd3d6544d2a" "question-3dca0c4b-ab3e-5cab-b892-e8bf877045ac"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-95ecf8d2-2252-5516-85e1-ebd3d6544d2a" :question/id #uuid "95ecf8d2-2252-5516-85e1-ebd3d6544d2a" :question/math-academy-id "q-149419" :question/problem "The table below gives the values of a positive, continuous function $f(x)$ over the closed interval $[0,15].$

"question-597bb006-761e-5b6e-a002-be65431d8129" :question/id #uuid "597bb006-761e-5b6e-a002-be65431d8129" :question/math-academy-id "q-149505" :question/problem "Let $f(x)$ be negative and strictly increasing for $x\in [0,1],$ and differentiable for $x\in (0,1).$ Suppose we approximate the area under the curve $y=g(x)=({x}^{2}-2)\cdot f(x)$ over the interval $[0,1]$ using a right Riemann sum. Given that $g(x)>0,$ which of the following statements must be true?

I. ${f}^{′}(x)>0$

II. ${g}^{′}(x)>0$

III. The Riemann sum underestimates the true area." :question/worked-solution "We're given that $g(x)=({x}^{2}-2)\cdot f(x)>0.$ Now, recall the following:

- If $g(x)$ is strictly increasing, the right Riemann sum gives an *overestimate* of the area under the curve $y=g(x).$

- If $g(x)$ is strictly decreasing, the right Riemann sum gives an *underestimate* of the area under the curve $y=g(x).$

Let's now consider each statement in turn:

- Statement I is true. Since $f(x)$ is strictly increasing, we have ${f}^{′}(x)>0.$

- Statement II is false. Differentiating $g(x)=({x}^{2}-2)\cdot f(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(x) & =({x}^{2}-2)^{′}\cdot f(x)+({x}^{2}-2)\cdot {f}^{′}(x) \\  & =2x\cdot f(x)+({x}^{2}-2)\cdot {f}^{′}(x).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x)$ is negative and strictly increasing over the interval $(0,1),$ we have 

$$
2x>0,\,f(x)<0,\,{x}^{2}-2<0,\,{f}^{′}(x)>0.
$$

Hence, we obtain

$$
{g}^{′}(x)={{2x}_{⏟}}_{>0}\cdot {{f(x)}_{⏟}}_{<0}+{{({x}^{2}-2)}_{⏟}}_{<0}\cdot {{{f}^{′}(x)}_{⏟}}_{>0}={{2x\cdot f(x)}_{⏟}}_{<0}+\,{{{x}^{2}\cdot {f}^{′}(x)}_{⏟}}_{<0}<0.
$$

- Statement III is true. Since ${g}^{′}(x)<0,$ the function $g(x)$ is strictly decreasing. Therefore, the right Riemann sum gives an *underestimate* of the area under the curve $y=({x}^{2}-2)\cdot f(x).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-bda027a4-fbea-5ab2-9b7c-09170115f2b8"] :db/ensure
