$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -4 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}}}x & =\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}}}\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}}} \\ \begin{bmatrix}2 & -4 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}x & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 6\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}=2 \\ 3{x}_{2}=6.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get $x_2=2.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-4(2) & =2 \\ 2{x}_{1} & =10 \\ {x}_{1} & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the least-squares solution to $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ is ![](images/72/723835f5ecb612e7d79c29ada9cc05241ffd4f233e29c9ed9a643994580a8c36.svg)" :tutorial/id #uuid "5fcac262-421e-57b7-b038-713427320ff4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6150 :tutorial/title "Using QR Factorization to Solve a Least-Squares Problem"} :step/id #uuid "f3959285-3101-555f-96a2-bd9e95bfe12e" :step/math-academy-id 37330 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134702}}] :activity/title "Finding a Least-Squares Solution Using QR Factorization" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186134028} {:db/id 17592186134701 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135061 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the least-squares problem for the system

$$
A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}.
$$

We can use QR factorization to construct the least-squares solution of this system. Recall that finding the QR factorization of $A$ means expressing $A$ in the form

$$
A = QR,
$$

where

- $Q$ has orthonormal columns, and

- $R$ is an upper triangular matrix with positive entries on its main diagonal.

To see how QR factorization can be used to solve a least-squares problem, we first recall that the least-squares solution satisfies the normal equation

$$
A^T A \mathbf{x} = A^T \mathbf{b}.
$$

Substituting $A = QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, we have $Q^T Q = I.$ Therefore, the above equation becomes

$$
R^TR\mathbf{x} = R^TQ^T\mathbf{b}.
$$

Since $R^T$ is invertible, pre-multiplying our equation by $(R^T)^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b\end{aligned}
$$

which simplifies as

$$
R \mathbf{x} = Q^T \mathbf{b}.  \qquad\qquad (\ast)
$$

The least-squares solution $\hat{\mathbf x}$ can now be found by solving this equation using back-substitution or row operations. This is usually the fastest way.

If we want an explicit formula for the least-squares solution, then we note that since $R$ is invertible, pre-multiplying $(\ast)$ by $R^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}^{-1}\cdot Rx & ={R}^{-1}\cdot {Q}^{T}b\end{aligned}
$$

which simplifies as

$$
\mathbf{x} = R^{-1} Q^T \mathbf{b}.
$$

The least-squares solution is unique if $A$ has linearly independent columns." :tutorial/id #uuid "7a9501fc-fdbc-5905-ad31-e3c6c2767a33" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3639 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "733946c8-bb91-5523-9be6-6e334aa51df6" :step/math-academy-id 20276 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134887}} {:db/id 17592186135061 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the least-squares problem for the system

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

$$

$$

$$

which gives the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}\sqrt{14}{x}_{1}+3\sqrt{14}{x}_{2}=-3\sqrt{14} \\ 3\sqrt{3}{x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{\begin{aligned}3\sqrt{2}{x}_{1}-4\sqrt{2}{x}_{2}=38\sqrt{2} \\ 2{x}_{2}=-10.\end{aligned}

$$

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y) = (1,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+x)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+x)\,j \\  & =(2x+0+1)\,i+(0+4y+0)\,j \\  & =(2x+1)\,i+4y\,j \\ ∇f(1,1) & =(2(1)+1)\,i+4(1)\,j \\  & =3\,i+4\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since we want a unit normal vector, we normalize $\nabla f(1,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇f(1,1)}{‖∇f(1,1)‖} & =\frac{3\,i+4\,j}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{4}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(3\,i+4\,j)\end{aligned}

$∇f(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\text{ }j \\  & =2x\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j \\ ∇f(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}) & =2(-\frac{1}{2})\text{ }i+2(\frac{1}{2})\text{ }j \\  & =-i+j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇f(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})}{‖∇f(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})‖} & =\frac{-i+j}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{-i+j}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(i-j)\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186338930 :question/id #uuid "436e814d-020d-5b28-b909-495bbb1c431a" :question/math-academy-id "q-71374" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186124461 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d5baf28d-c2c0-57bd-9433-c47043009f0d" :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Normal Vector to a Level Curve"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "049b7f23-d6a7-5be3-a6ca-ac19b8a84234" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-j" :db/id 17592186336070} {:answer/id #uuid "123c36c6-7310-581c-8de4-b675e090dc56" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "i+i" :db/id 17592186336203} {:answer/id #uuid "4b49d759-d015-5843-b6e9-3497dc09edfe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "i-i" :db/id 17592186336730} {:answer/id #uuid "6e16ffd6-406d-50b5-9b6a-0f4b899fc6bd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-i" :db/id 17592186337009} {:answer/id #uuid "ccd3f738-ef19-5d09-afcb-04a5b6bdd7fa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}(-2i+i)" :db/id 17592186337828}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "6e16ffd6-406d-50b5-9b6a-0f4b899fc6bd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-i" :db/id 17592186337009} :answer-field/id #uuid "60184a90-8959-560b-aa4a-378830d13dbb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186338445}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)=x+3y-2xy$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(\frac{3}{2},1).$" :question/worked-solution "A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(\frac{3}{2},1)$, can be found by computing $∇f(\frac{3}{2},1).$

:question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)={e}^{x+y}+x+y$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(0,0).$" :question/worked-solution "A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(0,0)$, can be found by computing $∇f(0,0).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(0,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{x+y}+x+y)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x+y}+x+y)\text{ }j \\  & =({e}^{x+y}+1)\text{ }i+({e}^{x+y}+1)\text{ }j \\ ∇f(0,0) & =({e}^{0+0}+1)\text{ }i+({e}^{0+0}+1)\text{ }j \\  & =2i+2j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(0,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇f(0,0)}{‖∇f(0,0)‖} & =\frac{2i+2j}{\sqrt{(2)^{2}+(2)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2i+2j}{2\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(i+j)\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186383153 :question/id #uuid "cee7213b-050a-5cea-8e38-6fcbc59025d4" :question/math-academy-id "q-129892"} {:db/id 17592186383160 :question/id #uuid "3b2f7fab-cebe-519a-83e3-a0831cac289d" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Equation of the Normal Line to a Plane Curve Using the Gradient"}] :question/problem "Consider the plane curve $\dfrac{x^2}9 + \dfrac {y^2}{16}=1.$ Find an equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(0, 4).$" :question/worked-solution "To find the equation of the normal line, we first find the equation of a normal vector, and then write the equation of the line that is parallel to the normal vector.

To obtain a normal vector, we write our curve as a level curve and then compute the gradient. Bringing all the terms of our equation to one side, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-1 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y) = \dfrac{x^2}9 + \dfrac {y^2}{16} - 1,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$   

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(0,4)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f(0,4).$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-1)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-1)j \\  & =\frac{2x}{9}\text{ }i+\frac{y}{8}\text{ }j \\ ∇f(0,4) & =\frac{2(0)}{9}\text{ }i+\frac{(4)}{8}\text{ }j \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\text{ }j \\  & =⟨0,\,\frac{1}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\nabla f(0,4)= \left\langle 0, \:\dfrac12 \right\rangle$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(0,4).$

Now, remember that the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\mathbf{v} = \langle v_x, v_y \rangle$ and passes through the point $(x_0,y_0)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{x-{x}_{0}}=\frac{{v}_{y}}{{v}_{x}}\end{aligned}
$$

or, equivalently,

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{y}(x-{x}_{0}) & ={v}_{x}(y-{y}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\nabla f(0,4)= \left\langle 0, \:\dfrac12 \right\rangle,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(x-0) & =0(y-4) \\ \frac{1}{2}x & =0 \\ x & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that the equation of the normal line to the ellipse $\dfrac{x^2}9 + \dfrac {y^2}{16}=1$ at the point $(0,4)$ is $x=0.$"} {:db/id 17592186124971 :question/id #uuid :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}6xy & =5{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} \\ 0 & =5{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-6xy\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=5{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-6xy$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(1,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(5{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-6xy)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(5{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-6xy)\,j \\  & =(10x-6y)\,i+(2y-6x)\,j \\ ∇f(1,1) & =(10-6(1))\,i+(2(1)-6)\,j \\  & =4\,i-4\,j \\  & =⟨4,-4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(1,1)=⟨4,-4⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(1,1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-1}{4} & =\frac{y-1}{-4} \\ x-1 & =-y+1 \\ x+y-2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186125190 :question/id #uuid "cb219d72-040d-55dd-90ca-3f831acb4d64" :question/math-academy-id "q-65173" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "034d9a67-8763-5c70-b5b9-7febdebfdaf9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3x-5y+1=0" :db/id 17592186496664} {:answer/id #uuid "132dcf6f-8423-544a-b9b0-4fe0220a1869" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-x-3y+5=0" :db/id 17592186496700} {:answer/id #uuid "6cc0248f-f177-570e-9398-26b743d6c5ad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2x-2y+3=0" :db/id 17592186496894} {:answer/id #uuid "9a929f5c-99d1-523a-aabc-fdf5eb4c7f18" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4x+5y-3=0" :db/id 17592186496982} {:answer/id #uuid "bc272b8f-4ab5-5f01-8506-f12b4f57de0b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-5x-4y+1=0" :db/id 17592186497043}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186496982} :answer-field/id #uuid "22b9919e-c058-55c4-a73e-14ca053dbdce" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186123740}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Consider the plane curve $xy={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-7.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(2,-1).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}xy & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-7 \\ 0 & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,-1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,-1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,-1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7)\,j \\  & =(2x-y)\,i+(2y-x)\,j \\ ∇f(2,-1) & =(2(2)-(-1))\,i+(2(-1)-2)\,j \\  & =5\,i-4\,j \\  & =⟨5,-4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(2,-1)=⟨5,-4⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,-1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-2}{5} & =\frac{y-(-1)}{-4} \\ -4(x-2) & =5(y+1) \\ -4x-5y+8-5 & =0 \\ -4x-5y+3 & =0 \\ 4x+5y-3 & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186265960 :question/id #uuid "c80428ab-daca-506e-aca7-d4e40b0d604c" :question/math-academy-id "q-130718" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "076ccae2-d102-5ad8-b1c2-ac28978e3e97" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-3y=0" :db/id 17592186263068} {:answer/id #uuid "1b3882de-2108-52bf-b5e1-4c3304b9a5c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-y-2=0" :db/id 17592186263257} {:answer/id #uuid "a00ce4f7-3888-5dba-a972-b715615f1421" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+y-4=0" :db/id 17592186264362} {:answer/id #uuid "cf2a0770-0459-500c-aa32-352ae1667e03" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+3y-6=0" :db/id 17592186264813} {:answer/id #uuid "d493ac59-d9ae-5896-bd9e-006d111d56b9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x+y-7=0" :db/id 17592186264850}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186264362} :answer-field/id #uuid "cb7e101e-fe81-5db4-a578-c892744685d7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186265605}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Consider the plane curve ${x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}=6.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(3,1).$" :question/worked-solution "If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-3{y}^{2},$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=6.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(3,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(3,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(3,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =2x\,i-6y\,j \\ ∇f(3,1) & =2(3)\,i-6(1)\,j \\  & =6\,i-6\,j \\  & =⟨6,-6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(3,1)=⟨6,-6⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(3,1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-3}{6} & =\frac{y-1}{(-6)} \\ -6(x-3) & =6(y-1) \\ -(x-3) & =y-1 \\ -x+3 & =y-1 \\ x+y-4 & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186265961 :question/id #uuid "d42d4bf9-4eef-57b6-b4ed-d5448bfe2b61" :question/math-academy-id "q-130723" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186124462 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "3b2f7fab-cebe-519a-83e3-a0831cac289d" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Equation of the Normal Line to a Plane Curve Using the Gradient"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0029eb5c-a868-5b35-b213-3fa6e3a04a1d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2x-y-5=0" :db/id 17592186263005} {:answer/id #uuid "2d9853cb-1b4d-5d99-b740-f207d47a13c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "x-3y-5=0" :db/id 17592186263384} {:answer/id #uuid "62cb3b0d-c5e0-5140-9b14-0b73eecbc9ac" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "x+y-1=0" :db/id 17592186263854} {:answer/id #uuid "70e32100-046e-5e0e-b9f2-eac7fe211b6f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "x-2y-4=0" :db/id 17592186263976} {:answer/id #uuid "b5d5900d-9aee-5b56-aa97-4e95d9c8f10a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "x+2y=0" :db/id 17592186264575}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "0029eb5c-a868-5b35-b213-3fa6e3a04a1d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2x-y-5=0" :db/id 17592186263005} :answer-field/id #uuid "263638a6-9832-58e0-a5f7-da0d13d29e2d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186265316}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Consider the plane curve $4xy+2{x}^{2}=x+2y.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(2,-1).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side: 

$$
\begin{aligned}4xy+2{x}^{2} & =x+2y \\ 4xy+2{x}^{2}-x-2y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=4xy+2{x}^{2}-x-2y$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$   

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,-1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,-1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4xy+2{x}^{2}-x-2y)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(4xy+2{x}^{2}-x-2y)\,j \\  & =(4y+4x-1)\,i+(4x-2)\,j \\ ∇f(2,-1) & =(4(-1)+4(2)-1)\,i+(4(2)-2)\,j \\  & =3\,i+6\,j \\  & =⟨3,6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 Hence, $∇f(2,-1)=⟨3,6⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,-1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-2}{3} & =\frac{y-(-1)}{6} \\ 6(x-2) & =3(y+1) \\ 2(x-2) & =y+1 \\ 2x-4 & =y+1 \\ 2x-y-5 & =0\end{aligned}

17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Consider the plane curve ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(2,0).$" :question/worked-solution "If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=4.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,0).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =2x\,i+2y\,j \\ ∇f(2,0) & =2(2)\,i+2(0)\,j \\  & =4\,i \\  & =⟨4,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(2,0)=⟨4,0⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,0).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-{x}_{0}){v}_{y}-(y-{y}_{0}){v}_{x} & =0 \\ (x-2)0-(y-0)4 & =0 \\ -4y & =0 \\ y & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186338933 :question/id #uuid "2de4f7e4-2884-5220-a39a-17359a9ea964" :question/math-academy-id "q-71388"} {:db/id 17592186338934 :question/id #uuid 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Consider the plane curve ${y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}=4xy.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(-1,-3).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2} & =4xy \\ {y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4xy & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4xy$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(-1,-3)$ can be found by computing $∇f(-1,-3).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(-1,-3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4xy)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4xy)\,j \\  & =(6x-4y)\,i+(2y-4x)\,j \\ ∇f(-1,-3) & =(6(-1)-4(-3))\,i+(2(-3)-4(-1))\,j \\  & =6\,i-2\,j \\  & =⟨6,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(-1,-3)=⟨6,-2⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(-1,-3).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-(-1)}{6} & =\frac{y-(-3)}{-2} \\ (-2)(x+1) & =6(y+3) \\ -2x-2 & =6y+18 \\ 6y+2x+20 & =0 \\ 3y+x+10 & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186338936 :question/id #uuid "47afea57-2ac6-5bfd-8472-520b5199e74f" :question/math-academy-id "q-71393" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186124462 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "3b2f7fab-cebe-519a-83e3-a0831cac289d" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Equation of the Normal Line to a Plane Curve Using the Gradient"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "923db4e3-1672-5a50-9581-8d103a4e9394" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "x+2y-2=0" :db/id 17592186337357} {:answer/id #uuid "a0ca54cd-1662-5f06-ad4a-139620f93cc6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-x+y-1=0" :db/id 17592186337484} {:answer/id #uuid "a201c603-2105-5c16-ac28-6ea1909ee0e3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "x+y-1=0" :db/id 17592186337500} {:answer/id #uuid "f0aa3752-46b2-55e2-872a-d4d7eb4de111" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "x+y+1=0" :db/id 17592186338139} {:answer/id #uuid "f7b5b220-5b4e-5b43-8acc-b11f2fdd7f50" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "x-y+1=0" :db/id 17592186338205}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "a201c603-2105-5c16-ac28-6ea1909ee0e3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "x+y-1=0" :db/id 17592186337500} :answer-field/id #uuid "a093c235-9586-5c2c-a6e1-6f61aa48334d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186338573}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Consider the plane curve $\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)=2xy.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(0,1).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y) & =2xy \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2xy & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2xy$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(0,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2xy)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2xy)\,j \\  & =(\frac{1}{x+y}-2y)\,i+(\frac{1}{x+y}-2x)\,j \\ ∇f(0,1) & =(\frac{1}{0+1}-2(1))\,i+(\frac{1}{0+1}-2(0))\,j \\  & =-i+j \\  & =⟨-1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(0,1)=⟨-1,1⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(0,1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-0}{-1} & =\frac{y-1}{1} \\ -x & =y-1 \\ x+y-1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186373125 :question/id #uuid "03866640-0a40-5a70-8301-d2aa021aa524" :question/math-academy-id "q-71394"} {:db/id 17592186385515 :question/id #uuid "50913094-4471-56fc-97f7-275492373a24" :question/math-academy-id "q-71386"} {:db/id 17592186385522 :question/id #uuid "4a6c1cae-376e-5dfa-b07c-5886b3b91c3f" :question/math-academy-id "q-71389"} {:db/id 17592186406787 :question/id #uuid "ef115c0b-3981-5c8f-8e9d-f41c20799c2d" :question/math-academy-id "q-130719" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1a1d5e01-e81c-5544-a929-055747dc7f77" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+y-3=0" :db/id 17592186406774} {:answer/id #uuid "82778c6a-7758-50ec-ad08-3720a9d490ae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x-y-3=0" :db/id 17592186406777} {:answer/id #uuid "cdae5c41-27fa-5c55-9f46-cceeabd59a1a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x+y-5=0" :db/id 17592186406779} {:answer/id #uuid "dbcc8cce-7237-5eb6-ac41-6a5901ea8c81" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+2y-4=0" :db/id 17592186406780} {:answer/id #uuid "ecf6508f-66f3-52c3-8fbf-477ac88383db" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-y-1=0" :db/id 17592186406783}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186406779} :answer-field/id #uuid "f9e7ba4e-7d61-5628-8ce5-894dfba410f8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186406785}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Consider the plane curve $2y-x=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y}).$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(2,1).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}2y-x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y})-2y+x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y})-2y+x,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y})-2y+x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y})-2y+x)j \\  & =(\frac{2y}{x}\cdot \frac{1}{2y}+1)i+(\frac{2y}{x}\cdot (-\frac{x}{2{y}^{2}})-2)j \\  & =(\frac{1}{x}+1)i+(-\frac{1}{y}-2)j \\ ∇f(2,1) & =(\frac{1}{2}+1)i+(-\frac{1}{1}-2)j \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\,i-3\,j \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{2},-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(3,1)=⟨\frac{3}{2},-3⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-2}{(\frac{3}{2})} & =\frac{y-1}{(-3)} \\ -3(x-2) & =\frac{3}{2}(y-1) \\ -6(x-2) & =3(y-1) \\ -2(x-2) & =y-1 \\ -2x+4 & =y-1 \\ 2x+y-5 & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186423051 :question/id #uuid "6f16c0b1-b80b-5067-adaf-a65b04fb7bb4" :question/math-academy-id "q-130721" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "364ddf2b-cdd1-5e21-88c2-478a7d637e32" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x+3y-4=0" :db/id 17592186423045} {:answer/id #uuid "415a3975-289f-5c0a-aa48-bc85b813f82a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x-y-4=0" :db/id 17592186423046} {:answer/id #uuid "6321cb0e-8e68-5a7b-9a36-ac871cc17b89" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+2y-2=0" :db/id 17592186423047} {:answer/id #uuid "82ce7cc2-be21-5dc4-9b04-e941ddd03d24" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-3y-2=0" :db/id 17592186423048} {:answer/id #uuid "ba63a292-9d83-540d-ac68-00ce4812ebb4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+3y-2=0" :db/id 17592186423049}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186423048} :answer-field/id #uuid "02401848-522e-501b-82ff-6e5cb3f48ab9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186423050}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Consider the plane curve ${e}^{{x}^{2}y}={y}^{2}-{x}^{3}+9.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(2,0).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{{x}^{2}y} & ={y}^{2}-{x}^{3}+9 \\ {e}^{{x}^{2}y}-{y}^{2}+{x}^{3} & =9\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={e}^{{x}^{2}y}-{y}^{2}+{x}^{3}$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=9.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,0).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,0):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{{x}^{2}y}-{y}^{2}+{x}^{3})i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{{x}^{2}y}-{y}^{2}+{x}^{3})j \\  & =(2xy{e}^{{x}^{2}y}+3{x}^{2})i+({x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{2}y}-2y)j \\ ∇f(2,0) & =(2(2)(0){e}^{({2}^{2})(0)}+3({2}^{2}))i+(({2}^{2}){e}^{({2}^{2})(0)}-2(0))j \\  & =12\,i+4\,j \\  & =⟨12,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(2,0)=⟨12,4⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,0).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-2}{12} & =\frac{y-0}{4} \\ 4(x-2) & =12y \\ x-2 & =3y \\ x-3y-2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186124463 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124267 :question/id #uuid "d3222782-abc1-5cd3-bceb-27e0585f9e09" :question/math-academy-id "e-3434"} :knowledge-point/id of the normal line to the surface $z = \ln (x^2 - xy)$ at the point $\left(2, 1, \ln 2 \right).$" :question/worked-solution "To find the equation of the normal line, we first find the equation of a normal vector, and then write the equation of the line that is parallel to the normal vector.

To obtain a normal vector, we write our curve as a level curve and then compute the gradient. Bringing all the terms of our equation to one side, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-xy) \\ 0 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-xy)-z\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z) = \ln (x^2 - xy) - z,$ our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $\left(2, 1, \ln 2 \right)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f(2,1,\ln 2){:}$  

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-xy)-z)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-xy)-z)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-xy)-z)k \\  & =(\frac{2x-y}{{x}^{2}-xy})\text{ }i+(\frac{1}{y-x})\text{ }j-\text{ }k \\ ∇f(2,1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & =(\frac{2\cdot 2-1}{{2}^{2}-2\cdot 1})\text{ }i+(\frac{1}{1-2})\text{ }j-\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{3}{2}i-\,j-k \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{2},-1,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, remember that the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\mathbf v = \langle v_x, v_y, v_z \rangle$ and passes through the point $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\nabla f(2,1,\ln 2)= \left\langle  \dfrac {3} {2}, -1, -1\right  \rangle,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-2}{(\frac{3}{2})}=\frac{y-1}{-1}=\frac{z-\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{-1} \\ \frac{x-2}{3}=\frac{y-1}{-2}=\frac{z-\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{-2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048850} {:db/id 17592186049485} {:db/id 17592186124973 :question/id #uuid "967a9051-3e85-5612-827f-8db0c0985ba4" :question/math-academy-id "q-36343"} {:db/id 17592186125074 $$
\begin{aligned}z & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y) \\ 0 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, if we set $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z$, then our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(1,-1,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,-1,0).$

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,-1,0):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z)k \\  & =\frac{2}{2x+y}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{2x+y}\text{ }j-1\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,-1,0) & =\frac{2}{2(1)+(-1)}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{2(1)+(-1)}\text{ }j-k \\  & =2\text{ }i+\,j-k \\  & =⟨2,\,1,\,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by using the symmetric form of the equation of the line that is parallel to the vector $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$,  we get: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-(-1)}{1}=\frac{z-0}{-1} \\ \frac{x-1}{2}=y+1=-z\end{aligned}

$(2,1,2).$" :question/worked-solution "Let's set $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+y-4z}.$ Then, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=1.$     

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(2,1,2)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,1,2).$

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,1,2):$    

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+y-4z})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+y-4z})\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+y-4z})\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{2x}{\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+y-4z}}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+y-4z}}\text{ }j-\frac{2}{\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+y-4z}}\text{ }k \\ ∇f(2,1,2) & =\frac{2\cdot 2}{\sqrt{2\cdot {2}^{2}+1-4\cdot 2}}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2\cdot {2}^{2}+1-4\cdot 2}}\text{ }j-\frac{2}{\sqrt{2\cdot {2}^{2}+1-4\cdot 2}}\text{ }k \\  & =4\text{ }i+\frac{1}{2}\text{ }j-2\text{ }k \\  & =⟨4,\,\frac{1}{2},\,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by using the symmetric form of the equation of the line that is parallel to the vector $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$,  we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-2}{4}=\frac{y-1}{\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{z-2}{-2} \\ \frac{x-2}{4}=2y-2=\frac{2-z}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186403468 :question/id #uuid "ca7dad4d-8007-5c21-9019-38d66b5366c7" :question/math-academy-id "q-71407"} {:db/id 17592186405132 :question/id #uuid "a7c74ce4-3c4e-5ea4-ab88-89558065f279" :question/math-academy-id "q-36754"} {:db/id 17592186497401 :question/id #uuid "ca2288f3-367d-50c0-9754-21f3665fdec7" :question/math-academy-id "q-71406" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "367ab4f2-93bc-5938-9462-dc0e018dd590" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "r=⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩+t\,⟨1,0,1⟩" :db/id 17592186496776} {:answer/id #uuid "399e3797-afa8-52bc-9d91-1f755a50f199" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "r=⟨1,0,1⟩+t\,⟨1,1,1⟩" :db/id 17592186496783} {:answer/id #uuid "d59ec8f6-4eba-53b8-a3b8-5a5f6ce7e72d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "r=⟨1,0,1⟩+t\,⟨\frac{1}{2},0,\frac{1}{2}⟩" :db/id 17592186497104} {:answer/id #uuid "db86fc5b-7216-54fe-8379-494c5e62c9fd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "r=⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩+t\,⟨\frac{1}{2},0,\frac{1}{2}⟩" :db/id 17592186497123} {:answer/id #uuid "fbc71725-cf86-521b-8c43-ec05f48b2500" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "r=⟨1,0,1⟩+t\,⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩" :db/id 17592186497200}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186497200} :answer-field/id #uuid "631be222-c76c-5ee5-9b25-874887015acd" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186497263}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface $\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-xyz$ at the point $(1,0,1).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-xyz \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2).$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(1,0,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,0,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)k \\  & =(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+yz)\text{ }i+(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+xz)\text{ }j+(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+xy)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,0,1) & =(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(0)(1))\,i+(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(1)(1))\text{ }j+(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(1)(0))\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,i+\frac{3}{2}\,j+\frac{1}{2}\,k \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(1,0,1)$ and passes through the point $(1,0,1)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨1,0,1⟩+t\,∇f(1,0,1)=⟨1,0,1⟩+t\,⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$"} {:db/id 17592186049390} {:db/id 17592186049511} {:db/id 17592186050885} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0029eb5c-a868-5b35-b213-3fa6e3a04a1d" :answer/type :topic/math-academy-id 1939} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186125298 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125735 :tutorial/content "Given a function $z=f(x,y)$, if both partial derivatives $f_x,$ $f_y$ exist and are continuous in a neighborhood of a point $P(x_0,y_0)$ in the domain of the function, and if $\nabla \! f(x_0,y_0) \neq \mathbf 0,$ then we have the following result:

*$\nabla \! f(x_0,y_0)$ is a normal vector to the level curve $C$ that passes through the point $P.$*

This property is one of the most important facts in multivariable calculus since it gives a fundamental link between calculus and geometry!

Let's illustrate this property with a concrete example. Consider the paraboloid $z = f (x, y)= x^2 + y^2$ and the level curve $\color{red}C$ of $f(x,y)$ corresponding to the point $P(1,-1).$ It is easy to see that $\color{red}C$ is a circle of radius $\sqrt{2}$ with equation $x^2+y^2 = 2.$

![](images/f2/f2461dbfcde2403e6ed7de9d6288d33a4deb52319d35b7036628c3fa8b3789dc.png)

In this particular instance, the property says that

*$\nabla \! f(1,-1)$ is a normal vector to the level curve $\color{red}C$ that passes through the point $P(1,-1).$*

![](images/48/481b68af522b9144e232d9c775f734cd998b31a21571cbfd983c23d0f68c3688.png)

Looking at the situation in the $xy$-plane, we see the following:

![](images/ce/ceb353d5164d6aa089a37e77c9469d747ef4430e363e42f9d35ee6d769d9a4e4.png)

Let's verify that $\nabla f(1,-1)$ is a normal line to the level curve $C$ at the point $P(1,-1).$

- First, computing the gradient, we find that $\nabla f = \langle 2x, 2y \rangle.$ Therefore, $$\nabla f(1,-1) = \langle 2, -2 \rangle.$$
- Then, using elementary calculus, we can show that the equation of the tangent to $C$ at $P$ is $y=x-2.$ Since this line has slope $m=1,$ it follows that the vector $\langle 1,1 \rangle$ is parallel to the level curve.
- Finally, taking the dot product between the gradient and the tangent vector, we obtain $$\nabla f(1,-1)\cdot \langle 1,1 \rangle = \langle 2, -2\rangle \cdot \langle 1,1 \rangle = 0.$$

This means that $\nabla f(1,-1)$ is *perpendicular* to the tangent line to $C$ at $(1,-1).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "68a96106-e224-5989-af04-8d464b6e58d5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2499 :tutorial/title holds true in the case of three or more variables. In general, if $f$ is a differentiable real-valued function of $n$ variables, $\mathbf y$ is a point in the domain of $f,$ and if the gradient vector is nonzero, i.e.,

$$\nabla f (\mathbf y)= \left \langle f_{x_1}(\mathbf y), f_{x_2}(\mathbf y), \cdots, f_{x_n}(\mathbf y)\right \rangle \neq \mathbf 0,$$

then we have the following result:

*$\nabla f (\mathbf y)$ is a normal vector to the level surface $f(x_1,x_2, \cdots, x_n) =f(\mathbf y)$ at $\mathbf y.$*

To illustrate, let's consider the function

$$w = f (x, y, z)= \dfrac 1 2\left(x^2 + y^2 + z^2-1\right).$$

The level surface corresponding to $w=0$ is the sphere $\mathcal S$ with equation $x^2 + y^2 +z^2 =1.$

The point $P(0,0,1)$ lies on $\mathcal S.$ Computing $\nabla f(0,0,1),$ we get

$$\eqalign{ \nabla f(x,y,z) &= \langle f_x, \: f_y, \:f_z\rangle \[5pt] &= \dfrac12\langle2x, \: 2y, \: 2z\rangle\[5pt] &= \langle x, \: y, \: z\rangle\[10pt] \nabla f(0,0,1) &= \langle 0,\: 0,\: 1 \rangle. }$$

Now clearly, $\nabla f (0,0, 1)$ is perpendicular to $\mathcal S$ at the point $(0,0,1).$

$z=f(x,y)$, if both partial derivatives $f_x,$ $f_y$ exist and are continuous in a neighborhood of a point $P(x_0,y_0)$ in the domain of the function, and if $\nabla \! f(x_0,y_0) \neq \mathbf 0,$ then we have the following result:

*$\nabla \! f(x_0,y_0)$ is a normal vector to the level curve $C$ that passes through the point $P.$*

This property is one of the most important facts in multivariable calculus since it gives a fundamental link between calculus and geometry!

Let's illustrate this property with a concrete example. Consider the paraboloid $z = f (x, y)= x^2 + y^2$ and the level curve $\color{red}C$ of $f(x,y)$ corresponding to the point $P(1,-1).$ It is easy to see that $\color{red}C$ is a circle of radius $\sqrt{2}$ with equation $x^2+y^2 = 2.$

![](images/f2/f2461dbfcde2403e6ed7de9d6288d33a4deb52319d35b7036628c3fa8b3789dc.png)

In this particular instance, the property says that

*$\nabla \! f(1,-1)$ is a normal vector to the level curve $\color{red}C$ that passes through the point $P(1,-1).$*

![](images/48/481b68af522b9144e232d9c775f734cd998b31a21571cbfd983c23d0f68c3688.png)

Looking at the situation in the $xy$-plane, we see the following:

![](images/ce/ceb353d5164d6aa089a37e77c9469d747ef4430e363e42f9d35ee6d769d9a4e4.png)

Let's verify that $\nabla f(1,-1)$ is a normal line to the level curve $C$ at the point $P(1,-1).$

- First, computing the gradient, we find that $\nabla f = \langle 2x, 2y \rangle.$ Therefore, $$\nabla f(1,-1) = \langle 2, -2 \rangle.$$
- Then, using elementary calculus, we can show that the equation of the tangent to $C$ at $P$ is $y=x-2.$ Since this line has slope $m=1,$ it follows that the vector $\langle 1,1 \rangle$ is parallel to the level curve.
- Finally, taking the dot product between the gradient and the tangent vector, we obtain $$\nabla f(1,-1)\cdot \langle 1,1 \rangle = \langle 2, -2\rangle \cdot \langle 1,1 \rangle = 0.$$

This means that $\nabla f(1,-1)$ is *perpendicular* to the tangent line to $C$ at $(1,-1).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "68a96106-e224-5989-af04-8d464b6e58d5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2499 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "35b375f8-a01b-56db-97b7-ac88f2a7883a" :step/math-academy-id 11200 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125306}} {:db/id 17592186125735 :tutorial/content "Given a function $z=f(x,y)$, if both partial derivatives $f_x,$ $f_y$ exist and are continuous in a neighborhood of a point $P(x_0,y_0)$ in the domain of the function, and if $\nabla \! f(x_0,y_0) \neq \mathbf 0,$ then we have the following result:

17592186125740 :tutorial/content "The same property holds true in the case of three or more variables. In general, if $f$ is a differentiable real-valued function of $n$ variables, $\mathbf y$ is a point in the domain of $f,$ and if the gradient vector is nonzero, i.e.,

$$\nabla f (\mathbf y)= \left \langle f_{x_1}(\mathbf y), f_{x_2}(\mathbf y), \cdots, f_{x_n}(\mathbf y)\right \rangle \neq \mathbf 0,$$

then we have the following result:

*$\nabla f (\mathbf y)$ is a normal vector to the level surface $f(x_1,x_2, \cdots, x_n) =f(\mathbf y)$ at $\mathbf y.$*

To illustrate, let's consider the function

$$w = f (x, y, z)= \dfrac 1 2\left(x^2 + y^2 + z^2-1\right).$$

The level surface corresponding to $w=0$ is the sphere $\mathcal S$ with equation $x^2 + y^2 +z^2 =1.$

The point $P(0,0,1)$ lies on $\mathcal S.$ Computing $\nabla f(0,0,1),$ we get

$$\eqalign{ \nabla f(x,y,z) &= \langle f_x, \: f_y, \:f_z\rangle \[5pt] &= \dfrac12\langle2x, \: 2y, \: 2z\rangle\[5pt] &= \langle x, \: y, \: z\rangle\[10pt] \nabla f(0,0,1) &= \langle 0,\: 0,\: 1 \rangle. }$$

Now clearly, $\nabla f (0,0, 1)$ is perpendicular to $\mathcal S$ at the point $(0,0,1).$

:question/math-academy-id "q-71397" :question/problem "For the function $f(x,y,z)=2{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}-xy$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-2,-3,1).$" :question/worked-solution "A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-2,-3,1)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(-2,-3,1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(-2,-3,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}-xy)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}-xy)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(2{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}-xy)\,k \\  & =(4x-y)\text{ }i-x\text{ }j+2z\text{ }k \\ ∇f(-2,-3,1) & =(4(-2)-(-3))\,i-(-2)\,j+2(1)\,k \\  & =-5\,i+2\,j+2\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $-5\,i+2\,j+2\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-2,-3,1).$"} :step/id #uuid "6c546df4-95bc-53a6-8314-f63e977926a5" :step/next {:db/id 17592186406789}} {:db/id 17592186406789 :step/content {:db/id 17592186406787 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1a1d5e01-e81c-5544-a929-055747dc7f77" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+y-3=0" :db/id 17592186406774} {:answer/id #uuid "82778c6a-7758-50ec-ad08-3720a9d490ae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x-y-3=0" :db/id 17592186406777} {:answer/id #uuid "cdae5c41-27fa-5c55-9f46-cceeabd59a1a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x+y-5=0" :db/id 17592186406779} {:answer/id #uuid "dbcc8cce-7237-5eb6-ac41-6a5901ea8c81" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+2y-4=0" :db/id 17592186406780} {:answer/id #uuid "ecf6508f-66f3-52c3-8fbf-477ac88383db" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-y-1=0" :db/id 17592186406783}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186406779} :answer-field/id #uuid "f9e7ba4e-7d61-5628-8ce5-894dfba410f8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186406785}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "ef115c0b-3981-5c8f-8e9d-f41c20799c2d" :question/math-academy-id "q-130719" :question/problem "Consider the plane curve $2y-x=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y}).$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(2,1).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}2y-x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y})-2y+x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y})-2y+x,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y})-2y+x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y})-2y+x)j \\  & =(\frac{2y}{x}\cdot \frac{1}{2y}+1)i+(\frac{2y}{x}\cdot (-\frac{x}{2{y}^{2}})-2)j \\  & =(\frac{1}{x}+1)i+(-\frac{1}{y}-2)j \\ ∇f(2,1) & =(\frac{1}{2}+1)i+(-\frac{1}{1}-2)j \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\,i-3\,j \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{2},-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(3,1)=⟨\frac{3}{2},-3⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-2}{(\frac{3}{2})} & =\frac{y-1}{(-3)} \\ -3(x-2) & =\frac{3}{2}(y-1) \\ -6(x-2) & =3(y-1) \\ -2(x-2) & =y-1 \\ -2x+4 & =y-1 \\ 2x+y-5 & =0\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}2y-x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y})-2y+x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y})-2y+x,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y})-2y+x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y})-2y+x)j \\  & =(\frac{2y}{x}\cdot \frac{1}{2y}+1)i+(\frac{2y}{x}\cdot (-\frac{x}{2{y}^{2}})-2)j \\  & =(\frac{1}{x}+1)i+(-\frac{1}{y}-2)j \\ ∇f(2,1) & =(\frac{1}{2}+1)i+(-\frac{1}{1}-2)j \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\,i-3\,j \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{2},-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(3,1)=⟨\frac{3}{2},-3⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-2}{(\frac{3}{2})} & =\frac{y-1}{(-3)} \\ -3(x-2) & =\frac{3}{2}(y-1) \\ -6(x-2) & =3(y-1) \\ -2(x-2) & =y-1 \\ -2x+4 & =y-1 \\ 2x+y-5 & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "854e10c9-a2d4-5612-8167-ef459f663827" :step/next {:db/id 17592186406790}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1a1d5e01-e81c-5544-a929-055747dc7f77" :answer/type {:db/id $$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{{x}^{2}y} & ={y}^{2}-{x}^{3}+9 \\ {e}^{{x}^{2}y}-{y}^{2}+{x}^{3} & =9\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={e}^{{x}^{2}y}-{y}^{2}+{x}^{3}$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=9.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,0).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,0):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{{x}^{2}y}-{y}^{2}+{x}^{3})i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{{x}^{2}y}-{y}^{2}+{x}^{3})j \\  & =(2xy{e}^{{x}^{2}y}+3{x}^{2})i+({x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{2}y}-2y)j \\ ∇f(2,0) & =(2(2)(0){e}^{({2}^{2})(0)}+3({2}^{2}))i+(({2}^{2}){e}^{({2}^{2})(0)}-2(0))j \\  & =12\,i+4\,j \\  & =⟨12,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(2,0)=⟨12,4⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,0).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-2}{12} & =\frac{y-0}{4} \\ 4(x-2) & =12y \\ x-2 & =3y \\ x-3y-2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "68e1c4ea-40a6-5a21-ae75-071da89109f6" :step/next {:db/id 17592186423052}} {:db/id 17592186423055 :step/content {:db/id 17592186373006 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9dd151b9-79f9-5a66-8557-365b16a9535a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y+1}{2}=-z" :db/id 17592186373008} {:answer/id #uuid "e407b4cd-b0e3-5ef2-a3e1-1c2c4a208e39" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-1=\frac{y}{2}=-z" :db/id 17592186373009} {:answer/id #uuid "2042c239-c608-579c-a356-780f349dc015" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x-1}{2}=y+1=-z" :db/id 17592186373010} {:answer/id #uuid "e11362e5-c68a-5d93-8627-d0fe7c1b9816" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-1=\frac{y+1}{2}=z" :db/id 17592186373011} {:answer/id #uuid "dad753bd-efc6-5cc5-bf02-04d7fe01e2cb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x+1}{2}=\frac{y-1}{2}=z" :db/id 17592186373012}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186373010} :answer-field/id #uuid "f074ec94-f4ab-59e4-98e4-6833b7d43d47" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186373007}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "a1e0fe3a-1bd3-5ee4-ab1a-74e46b29c2c8" :question/math-academy-id "q-36351" :question/problem "Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $z=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)$ at the point $(1,-1,0).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$

$$

 

So, if we set $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z$, then our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(1,-1,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,-1,0).$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z)k \\  & =\frac{2}{2x+y}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{2x+y}\text{ }j-1\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,-1,0) & =\frac{2}{2(1)+(-1)}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{2(1)+(-1)}\text{ }j-k \\  & =2\text{ }i+\,j-k \\  & =⟨2,\,1,\,-1⟩\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-xyz \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2).$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(1,0,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,0,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)k \\  & =(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+yz)\text{ }i+(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+xz)\text{ }j+(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+xy)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,0,1) & =(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(0)(1))\,i+(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(1)(1))\text{ }j+(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(1)(0))\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,i+\frac{3}{2}\,j+\frac{1}{2}\,k \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(1,0,1)$ and passes through the point $(1,0,1)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨1,0,1⟩+t\,∇f(1,0,1)=⟨1,0,1⟩+t\,⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$"} :step/id #uuid "bf1f0a54-a2e4-5d5b-9366-b7874e2b2325" :step/next {:db/id 17592186497425}}] :activity/title "The Gradient as a Normal Vector" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045464 :db/ident :activity.type/review} :db/id 17592186496648} {:db/id 17592186497419 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125190 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "034d9a67-8763-5c70-b5b9-7febdebfdaf9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3x-5y+1=0" :db/id 17592186496664} {:answer/id #uuid "132dcf6f-8423-544a-b9b0-4fe0220a1869" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-x-3y+5=0" :db/id 17592186496700} {:answer/id #uuid "6cc0248f-f177-570e-9398-26b743d6c5ad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2x-2y+3=0" :db/id 17592186496894} {:answer/id #uuid "9a929f5c-99d1-523a-aabc-fdf5eb4c7f18" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4x+5y-3=0" :db/id 17592186496982} {:answer/id #uuid "bc272b8f-4ab5-5f01-8506-f12b4f57de0b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-5x-4y+1=0" :db/id 17592186497043}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186496982} :answer-field/id #uuid "22b9919e-c058-55c4-a73e-14ca053dbdce" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186123740}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "cb219d72-040d-55dd-90ca-3f831acb4d64" :question/math-academy-id "q-65173" :question/problem "Consider the plane curve $xy={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-7.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(2,-1).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}xy & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-7 \\ 0 & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7\end{aligned}
$$

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-xyz \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2).$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(1,0,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,0,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)k \\  & =(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+yz)\text{ }i+(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+xz)\text{ }j+(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+xy)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,0,1) & =(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(0)(1))\,i+(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(1)(1))\text{ }j+(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(1)(0))\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,i+\frac{3}{2}\,j+\frac{1}{2}\,k \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(1,0,1)$ and passes through the point $(1,0,1)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨1,0,1⟩+t\,∇f(1,0,1)=⟨1,0,1⟩+t\,⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$"} :step/id #uuid "bf1f0a54-a2e4-5d5b-9366-b7874e2b2325" :step/next {:db/id 17592186497425}} {:db/id 17592186497425 :step/content {:db/id 17592186265960 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "076ccae2-d102-5ad8-b1c2-ac28978e3e97" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-3y=0" :db/id 17592186263068} {:answer/id #uuid "1b3882de-2108-52bf-b5e1-4c3304b9a5c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-y-2=0" :db/id 17592186263257} {:answer/id #uuid "a00ce4f7-3888-5dba-a972-b715615f1421" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+y-4=0" :db/id 17592186264362} {:answer/id #uuid "cf2a0770-0459-500c-aa32-352ae1667e03" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+3y-6=0" :db/id 17592186264813} {:answer/id #uuid "d493ac59-d9ae-5896-bd9e-006d111d56b9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x+y-7=0" :db/id 17592186264850}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186264362} :answer-field/id #uuid "cb7e101e-fe81-5db4-a578-c892744685d7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186265605}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "c80428ab-daca-506e-aca7-d4e40b0d604c" :question/math-academy-id "q-130718" :question/problem "Consider the plane curve ${x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}=6.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(3,1).$" :question/worked-solution "If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-3{y}^{2},$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=6.$

"39738d1a-2b58-58e7-8b93-fae76501045c" :knowledge-point/title "Minimizing the Surface Area of a Cylinder With a Fixed Volume"}] :question/problem "We wish to construct a cylindrical can with a base but no lid. Our cylinder must have an exact volume of $27\pi\, \textrm{in}^3$. What is the radius of the cylinder that gives the smallest surface area?" :question/worked-solution "First, let's draw a picture of a cylinder. Let $r$ be the radius, and $h$ the height.

![](images/ad/adb9c56132e8f346a07a9a644cd364c2347ad8c551a3c9bd4842b7067eb1d050.png)

We wish to minimize the surface area

$$
S= 2\pi r h + \pi r^2
$$

We know that the volume is fixed at $27\pi \, \textrm{in}^3$, so we also have the constraint condition

$$
27\pi = \pi r^2 h
$$

Now, by making $h$ the subject of the constraint equation, we have that

$$
h = \dfrac{27}{r^2}
$$

Plugging the above into our expression for $S$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} S(r)& = 2\pi r \left(\dfrac{27}{r^2}\right) + \pi r^2 \\ & = \dfrac{54\pi}{r} + \pi r^2. \end{aligned}
$$

We want to minimize $S$, so we need to differentiate $S$ and set the derivative equal to zero. The derivative is

$$
S'(r) = -\dfrac{54\pi}{r^2} + 2\pi r
$$

Setting the derivative equal to zero and solving for $r$ gives a stationary point, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
S^{′}(r) &= 0 \\
- \frac{54π}{r^{2}} + 2πr &= 0 \\
2πr &= \frac{54π}{r^{2}} \\
2πr^{3} &= 54π \\
r^{3} &= 27 \\
r &= \sqrt[3]{27} \\

What is the radius $r$ of the cylinder that has the largest volume?

![](images/a2/a2916167b3c8d4169339280fe67a0018b5d09a9784260cf6488cd6825753b2b9.png)" :question/worked-solution "First, let $r$ be the radius and $h$ be the height of the cylinder.

We wish to maximize the volume

$$
V = \pi r^2 h
$$

We know that the surface area is fixed at $25\pi\,\mathrm{cm^2}$, so we also have the constraint equation

$$
2\pi r h + \pi r^2 = 25\pi
$$

Now, by making $h$ the subject of the constraint equation, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}
2πrh &= 25π - πr^{2} \\
h &= \frac{25π - πr^{2}}{2πr} \\
h &= \frac{25 - r^{2}}{2r}
\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging the above into our expression for $V$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
V(r) &= πr^{2} \cdot \frac{25 - r^{2}}{2r} \\
V(r) &= ((25r - r^{3})π)/(2)
\end{aligned}
$$

We want to maximize $V$, so we need to differentiate $V$ and set the derivative equal to zero. The derivative is

$$
V'(r) = \frac{(25 - 3 r^2)\pi}{2}
$$

Setting the derivative equal to zero and solving for $r$ gives a stationary point, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
V^{′}(r) &= 0 \\
((25 - 3r^{2})π)/(2) &= 0 \\
25 &= 3r^{2} \\
r^{2} &= \frac{25}{3} \\
r &= \frac{5\sqrt{3}}{3}cm
\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we only considered the positive root in the last step because the radius $r$ must be positive.

Finally, we confirm that

$$
r = \dfrac{5\sqrt{3}}{3}
$$

is a maximum using the second derivative test. The second derivative is

$$
V''(r) = -3\pi r
$$

and we can see that

$$
V''\left(\dfrac{5\sqrt{3}}{3} \right) < 0
$$

So, the stationary point

$$
r=\dfrac{5\sqrt{3}}{3}
$$

is indeed a maximum of $V(r)$.

Therefore, the cylinder with the largest volume has a radius of

$$
r=\dfrac{5\sqrt{3}}{3} \, \textrm{cm}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186101277 :question/id #uuid "28541c18-bc9f-5800-8a64-d3d3ece27f6e" :question/math-academy-id "q-18444" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186100841 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a8fae559-f88f-50ec-a1f0-a7cfeb319d19" :knowledge-point/title "Maximizing the Volume of a Cylinder With a Fixed Surface Area"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "84537527-8aad-5079-96d5-367c58417266" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "72πcm^{3}" :db/id 17592186098984} {:answer/id #uuid "bb349210-57fd-5a97-ade4-91b18e7bd0cc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "58πcm^{3}" :db/id 17592186098985} {:answer/id #uuid "c747ebc0-007f-588b-bd5f-bba27ed13dc0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "46πcm^{3}" :db/id 17592186098986} {:answer/id #uuid "10beb0e4-5b03-534d-b076-f843369f0e2f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "64πcm^{3}" :db/id 17592186098987} {:answer/id #uuid "5416a513-8bd9-5615-a645-5fe545fd93fd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "81πcm^{3}" :db/id 17592186098988}] :answer-field/id #uuid "1be58fdc-55c3-5738-97fc-4b0fc03a148f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186098983}] :question/problem "![](images/50/50853fcaa44ff9b7d80e708e546275286541afc0b6ed05c4ca87ea3175364c09.png)

The tank must have an exact volume of $18\pi\,\mathrm{m}^3$.
To make the tank, the manufacturer uses two materials:

- a metal sheet that costs $\[math]1.50$ per $\mathrm{m}^2$ for the lateral surface,
- a metal sheet that costs $\[/math]0.50$ per $\mathrm{m}^2$ for the base and lid.

What is the radius of the tank that gives the smallest possible manufacturing cost?" :question/worked-solution "First, let's draw a picture of a cylinder. Let $r$ be the radius, and $h$ the height.

![](images/d7/d72b9a87e460f841bbd135fd16806607c16aa0b37b2279727bd7d9eeeb9c6982.png)

We wish to minimize the manufacturing cost. We can express the manufacturing cost $C$ in terms of $r$ and $h$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
C &= 2πrh \cdot 1.5 + 2πr^{2} \cdot 0.5 \\
&= 3πrh + πr^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

We know that the volume is fixed at $18\pi\,\textrm{m}^3$, so we also have the constraint condition

$$
18\pi = \pi r^2 h
$$

Now, by making $h$ the subject of the constant equation, we have that

$$
h = \dfrac{18}{r^2}
$$

Plugging the above into our expression for $C$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
C(r) &= 3πr(\frac{18}{r^{2}}) + πr^{2} \\
&= \frac{54π}{r} + πr^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

We want to minimize $C$, so we need to differentiate $C$ and set the derivative equal to zero. The derivative is

$$
C'(r) = -\dfrac{54\pi}{r^2} + 2\pi r
$$

Setting the derivative equal to zero and solving for $r$ gives a stationary point, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
C^{′}(r) &= 0 \\
- \frac{54π}{r^{2}} + 2πr &= 0 \\
2πr &= \frac{54π}{r^{2}} \\
2πr^{3} &= 54π \\
r^{3} &= 27 \\
r &= \sqrt[3]{27} \\
r &= 3m
\end{aligned}
$$

Using a calculator, we can verify that if $r < 3$ then $C'(r) < 0$, and if $r > 3$ then $C'(r) > 0$, which means that the stationary point $r = 3$ is indeed a minimum of $C(r)$.

Therefore, the tank with the smallest manufacturing cost has radius

$$
r = 3\,\textrm{m}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186101235 :question/id #uuid "c2e8ae7e-3d78-5804-9cd0-c56bbfa61291" :question/math-academy-id "q-16255"} {:db/id 17592186101553 :question/id #uuid [{:db/id 17592186101627 :step/content {:db/id 17592186102011 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to construct a cylindrical container with a fixed volume, yet we wish to use as little material as possible to minimize our production costs.

![](images/33/339a377a68f93c78cf99b0f58333ab26c24bff91509dd707d22981d773ef077c.png)

This is yet another type of optimization problem. Let's remind ourselves of the general strategy for optimization problems.

1. Draw a diagram of the situation, introducing variables where necessary.
2. Write down the equation of the quantity that you're trying to maximize or minimize. This is the objective function, and it might include more than one variable.
3. Write down the constraint equation.
4. Use the constraint equation to write the objective function in terms of a single variable only.
5. Differentiate the objective function, set it equal to zero, and solve for the stationary points.
6. Test each stationary point using the second derivative test. Or you can use the first derivative test if it's easier.

In the following examples, we'll need to use the formulas for a cylindrical can's volume $V$ and surface area $S$. For a cylinder with radius $r$ and height $h$, its volume is given by the formula

$$
V = \pi r^2 h
$$

If the cylinder is closed at both ends, its surface area $S$ is given by

$$
S = 2πrh + 2πr^{2}
$$

If the cylinder is closed at only one end, its surface area $S$ is

$$
S = 2πrh + πr^{2}

little material as possible to minimize our production costs.

![](images/33/339a377a68f93c78cf99b0f58333ab26c24bff91509dd707d22981d773ef077c.png)

This is yet another type of optimization problem. Let's remind ourselves of the general strategy for optimization problems.

1. Draw a diagram of the situation, introducing variables where necessary.
2. Write down the equation of the quantity that you're trying to maximize or minimize. This is the objective function, and it might include more than one variable.
3. Write down the constraint equation.
4. Use the constraint equation to write the objective function in terms of a single variable only.
5. Differentiate the objective function, set it equal to zero, and solve for the stationary points.
6. Test each stationary point using the second derivative test. Or you can use the first derivative test if it's easier.

In the following examples, we'll need to use the formulas for a cylindrical can's volume $V$ and surface area $S$. For a cylinder with radius $r$ and height $h$, its volume is given by the formula

$$
V = \pi r^2 h
$$

If the cylinder is closed at both ends, its surface area $S$ is given by

$$
S = 2πrh + 2πr^{2}
$$

If the cylinder is closed at only one end, its surface area $S$ is

$$
S = 2πrh + πr^{2}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "67df391f-27a3-55c3-bc1d-46e69a2931e3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 672 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "3c14aa67-65c7-52ad-b74d-223f276e9735" :step/math-academy-id 1290 :step/next {:db/id 17592186101628}} {:db/id 17592186102011 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to construct a cylindrical container with a fixed volume, yet we wish to use as little material as possible to minimize our production costs.

- Then, we solve $7x +11 < -3$:
$\begin{bmatrix}7x + 11 & < - 3 \\ 7x + 11 - 11 & < - 3 - 11 \\ 7x & < - 14 \\ \frac{7x}{7} & < \frac{-14}{7} \\ x & < - 2\end{bmatrix}$

![](images/b6/b6014786331de7693c3a1e0d502ea79fb049252fe9f3ecfcd49a873d996896fe.png)

To find the values of $x$ that satisfy both inequalities, we find where the two solutions overlap:

![](images/2e/2e5425630ece3ab7006378a7930aae0452c3d5261e7bfb579c97daf572b71d22.png)

${5x - 35 \ge 0; 7x > 21$" :question/worked-solution "To solve the system, we need to find the values of $x$ that satisfy both

$$
5x-35 \geq 0
$$

and $7x > 21$ simultaneously.

- First, we solve $5x-35 \geq 0$:
$\begin{bmatrix}5x - 35 & \ge 0 \\ 5x - 35 + 35 & \ge 0 + 35 \\ 5x & \ge 35 \\ \frac{5x}{5} & \ge \frac{35}{5} \\ x & \ge 7\end{bmatrix}$

![](images/48/4875553156dc3e4ec15ecdb6c848fd43d519941123d0d9763d209e9f1d6a52f6.png)

- Then, we solve $7x > 21$:
$\begin{bmatrix}7x & > 21 \\ \frac{7x}{7} & > \frac{21}{7} \\ x & > 3\end{bmatrix}$

![](images/f7/f7a68da2d31f0bfe038252ac0dc9151d81bf854a7d33da591cbaef05f52bda28.png)

To find the values of $x$ that satisfy both inequalities, we find where the two solutions overlap:

![](images/27/27fbd7222a4a02d4a14c17c4043b55a2828e66c2d4dcb019598ea5efef2089e6.png)

Thus, the final solution is

$$
x \geq 7
$$"} {:db/id 17592186064603 :question/id #uuid "6152f535-8bb3-5c5a-ab82-63b316f3b909" :question/math-academy-id "q-218740"} {:db/id 17592186064656 :question/id #uuid "5e282d54-b631-510a-9a44-8555de5a0156" :question/math-academy-id "q-25455"} {:db/id 17592186064895 :question/id #uuid "f1cfa7a0-c14b-5a5f-8da0-46436605de10" :question/math-academy-id "q-51736"} {:db/id 17592186064239 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186063978 :question/id #uuid "0a39d86b-ab9b-5479-9d7b-726247558397" :question/math-academy-id "e-13959"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c9460289-3e48-558e-b149-3e12a25e50a6" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049162} {:db/id 17592186050301}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064471 :question/id #uuid "acc484ba-824c-5a65-8d78-08f4b1ba21e5" :question/math-academy-id "q-102305"} {:db/id 17592186064604 :question/id #uuid "d2607a47-925e-5689-83b2-87182ff342af" :question/math-academy-id "q-218794"} {:db/id 17592186064913 :question/id #uuid "3366d4cd-bafb-5283-92a7-effe58a0ac1f" :question/math-academy-id "q-59506"}] :knowledge-point/title "Flipping the Sign of an Inequality in a System"} {:db/id 17592186063978 :question/id #uuid "0a39d86b-ab9b-5479-9d7b-726247558397" :question/math-academy-id "e-13959" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186064239 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c9460289-3e48-558e-b149-3e12a25e50a6" :knowledge-point/title "Flipping the Sign of an Inequality in a System"}] :question/problem "What is the solution to the following system of inequalities?
${2 - 7x \ge 2; 10x - 3 \ge 7$" :question/worked-solution "To solve the system, we need to find the values of $x$ that satisfy both

$$
2-7x \geq 2
$$

and

$$
10x-3 \geq 7
$$

simultaneously.

- First, we solve $2-7x \geq 2$:
$\begin{bmatrix}2 - 7x & \ge 2 \\ 2 - 7x - 2 & \ge 2 - 2 \\ -7x & \ge 0 \\ (-1) \cdot (-7x) & \le (-1) \cdot 0 \\ 7x & \le 0 \\ \frac{7x}{7} & \le \frac{0}{7} \\ x & \le 0\end{bmatrix}$

![](images/96/96957d6e6c105fd3734dbe478850287c1c8771873b94fedc4ee0ed5cebf41c40.png)

- Then, we solve $10x-3 \geq 7$:
$\begin{bmatrix}10x - 3 & \ge 7 \\ 10x - 3 + 3 & \ge 7 + 3 \\ 10x & \ge 10 \\ \frac{10x}{10} & \ge \frac{10}{10} \\ x & \ge 1\end{bmatrix}$

![](images/9d/9d2d2e7b05bd4bcaf964353266e35bb12f406372ade7255accf6dc3503046f5c.png)

To find the values of $x$ that satisfy both inequalities, we find where the two solutions overlap:

![](images/98/98654d9ff727e680d0e1ba1ff88b9202248aba6a75a5002a01cd9d628cb6c5b3.png)

It turns out that the solutions do not overlap at all. Therefore, no values of $x$ satisfy both inequalities simultaneously. So, there is no solution."} {:db/id 17592186049162} {:db/id 17592186050301} {:db/id 17592186064471 :question/id #uuid "acc484ba-824c-5a65-8d78-08f4b1ba21e5" :question/math-academy-id "q-102305"} {:db/id 17592186064604 :question/id #uuid "d2607a47-925e-5689-83b2-87182ff342af" :question/math-academy-id "q-218794"} {:db/id 17592186064913 :question/id #uuid "3366d4cd-bafb-5283-92a7-effe58a0ac1f" :question/math-academy-id "q-59506"} {:db/id 17592186064240 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186063979 :question/id #uuid "d2726a15-72d6-5c0c-8302-68ba55f8734d" :question/math-academy-id "e-13961"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d3286dfe-5140-5ba7-8e34-c98e63dc15c0" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050734}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064518 :question/id #uuid "d1725c9d-2a3b-503d-bc6c-7ed0dc5d594f" :question/math-academy-id "q-156132"} {:db/id 17592186064605 :question/id #uuid "5b65ad66-5f52-5406-9e2e-007075702256" :question/math-academy-id "q-220299"}] :knowledge-point/title "Systems Containing Compound Inequalities"} {:db/id 17592186063979 :question/id #uuid "d2726a15-72d6-5c0c-8302-68ba55f8734d" :question/math-academy-id "e-13961" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186064240 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d3286dfe-5140-5ba7-8e34-c98e63dc15c0" :knowledge-point/title "Systems Containing Compound Inequalities"}] :question/problem "Find the set of values of $x$ that satisfy $1 \lt 3x-2 \leq 7$ and $2-3x \leq -4$." :question/worked-solution "To solve compound "and" inequalities, we solve each inequality separately and then find their intersection.

- First, we solve $1 \lt 3x-2 \leq 7 \,$:
$\begin{bmatrix}1 & < 3x - 2 \le 7 \\ 1 + 2 & < 3x - 2 + 2 \le 7 + 2 \\ 3 & < 3x \le 9 \\ \frac{3}{3} & < \frac{3x}{3} \le \frac{9}{3} \\ 1 & < x \le 3\end{bmatrix}$

![](images/34/341633f5e132e1ab07af8969161c20443d65aec7e89ce0bc600868504dd19f9b.png)

- Then, we solve $2-3x \leq -4 \,$:

:question/problem "Find the projection of the intersection between the hyperboloid of one sheet 
$(x+3)^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}-2{z}^{2}=1$
 and the plane   $x+2z=-3$ onto the
$xy$-plane." :question/worked-solution "Since we want to find the projection onto the $xy$-plane, we need to eliminate the variable $z.$ First, we solve the equation of the plane for $z$, as follows:

$$
x+2z=-3\,⟹\,z=-\frac{x+3}{2}
$$

Substituting the expression for $z$ into the equation of the hyperboloid, we obtain: 

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3)^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}-2{(-\frac{x+3}{2})}^{2} & =1 \\ (x+3)^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}-\frac{(x+3)^{2}}{2} & =1 \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{4}+\frac{(x+3)^{2}}{2} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the projection of the intersection is the ellipse $\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}+\frac{(x+3)^{2}}{2}=1.$"} {:db/id 17592186198433 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198075 :question/id 17592186199499 :tutorial/content "Now, let's consider the intersection of the elliptic paraboloid 
$z=x^2+y^2$
and the plane 
$z = x+y-\dfrac{1}{4},$
as shown below.

![](images/1d/1d4b8db0985d437807f6e580bc6c2c16cacca1ea7c8e49ed4653717cdb3c9e27.png)

 

Note that the intersection of the paraboloid and plane is given by the solution to the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2} \\ z=x+y-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

- To find the projection of the intersection onto the $xy$-plane, we need to eliminate the variable $z$ from the system. The resulting projection curve will be an ellipse, as depicted below.

![](images/52/520b57cf872ede31d4397d59a833c565147d82a45be1d6b2634f82e1effdff8c.png)

 

- To find the projection of the intersection onto the $xz$-plane, we need to eliminate the variable $y$ from the system. The resulting projection curve will be an ellipse, as depicted below.

![](images/05/059acf1ec5dadaa98b2cd4d4b6c79884e4facc96dd49664abbc247cfba86aaeb.png)

 

- To find the projection of the intersection onto the $yz$-plane, we need to eliminate the variable $x$ from the system. The resulting projection curve will be an ellipse, as depicted below.

![](images/80/80d3042d21d2e7265a40739ae1531ac30b03fea16fa67609a4e1b0eac8559411.png)

$z=x^2+y^2$
and the line with the equation
$x = -y = -z+1.$
The line, paraboloid, and their points of intersection are shown below.

![](images/51/5159ac99a1bc9f73c01df3c2cc2e6fb2093a3d68e00731609d7b62a6fa55149d.png)

 

The trick is to express the equation of the line in parametric form, substitute the parametric equations into the equation of the surface, and solve for the parameter.

So, first, we write the equation of our line in the parametric form:

![](images/01/01357a5c6b72d7c976765aeed04db8afa3e3a80e13095d9be1ea2f2594ae5bf5.svg)

where $t \in (-\infty,\infty).$

Our intersection points must belong to the line and the surface simultaneously. So, substituting the expressions for $x$, $y$, and $z$ from the parametric equation of the line into the equation of the paraboloid, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2} \\ (-t+1) & =(t)^{2}+(-t)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Simplifying this equation, we get

$$
2t^2+t - 1=0.
$$

The solutions to this equation are
$t=\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $t=-1.$ 

Substituting these values back into the parametric equations of the line

- For $t=\dfrac{1}{2}$, we have

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=(\frac{1}{2})=\frac{1}{2} \\ y=-(\frac{1}{2})=-\frac{1}{2} \\ z=-(\frac{1}{2})+1=\frac{1}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

so the first point is $(\dfrac{1}{2},-\dfrac{1}{2},\dfrac{1}{2}).$

- For $t=-1$, we have

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=(-1)=-1 \\ y=-(-1)=1 \\ z=-(-1)+1=2,\end{aligned}
$$

so the second point is $(-1,1,2).$

Therefore, the points of intersection are $(\dfrac{1}{2},-\dfrac{1}{2},\dfrac{1}{2})$ and $(-1,1,2).$
