Transformation"}] :question/problem "Consider the transformation $\mathbf{T}:(u,v,w) \to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation $\mathbf T^{-1}(x,y,z)\to(u(x,y,z), v(x,y,z), w(x,y,z))$ is given by
![](images/f8/f82cf760dee34626c290e29420fbaddb4ef254180087d05bb6fb883f2dc32e75.svg)

Find the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T.$

*Hint: You can assume that $x>0$, $y \ne 0.$*" :question/worked-solution "For a transformation 

![](images/1c/1c2567cd1c2cf28ed17b6dc445025cb60061dc7d7d6c78c960be77f8866ef4a7.svg)

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given $\mathbf T^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\dfrac{\partial (u, v, w)}{\partial (x, y, z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T$ using the relation

$$
\dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (u, v, w)}{\partial (x, y, z)} \right)^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z) = x^2, \qquad 
v(x,y,z) = xy, \qquad
w(x,y,z) = yz.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =2x & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =y & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =x & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =z & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =y\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2x & 0 & 0 \\ y & x & 0 \\ 0 & z & y\end{aligned}| \\  & =2x|\begin{aligned}x & 0 \\ z & y\end{aligned}| \\  & =2x(xy-0) \\  & =2{x}^{2}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\dfrac{\partial (u, v, w)}{\partial (x, y, z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}y & =2\cdot x\cdot (xy) \\  & =2\cdot \sqrt{u}\cdot v \\  & =2v\sqrt{u}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2v\sqrt{u}}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048251} {:db/id 17592186129728 :question/id #uuid "f85af4c0-4520-5614-952b-cb9d6d06c6c9" :question/math-academy-id "q-39300" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186129269 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e290e8b2-7766-55ff-95da-99a3430b18e3" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Jacobian of an Inverse Transformation"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "408e29c9-6522-5467-9ab8-def9fe8cfb65" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\frac{{u}^{2}}{2\sqrt{w}}" :db/id 17592186324490} {:answer/id #uuid "69224e59-e1c5-54cd-8748-b2d597b5cd76" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{w}{u}^{2}}{2}" :db/id 17592186324848} {:answer/id #uuid "7b1e869c-a3b7-584b-8e0f-e99423947eb0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{{u}^{2}}{2\sqrt{w}}" :db/id 17592186325004} {:answer/id #uuid "e98f16dc-8225-5762-aa80-dca5e80b6645" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2{u}^{2}\sqrt{w}}" :db/id 17592186326027} {:answer/id #uuid "fb5ec600-18ee-54e3-bb28-7c22c6783223" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2{u}^{2}\sqrt{w}}" :db/id 17592186326182}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "e98f16dc-8225-5762-aa80-dca5e80b6645" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2{u}^{2}\sqrt{w}}" :db/id 17592186326027} :answer-field/id #uuid "65802821-8118-5ece-8435-a69816ad88f1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186326394}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Consider the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y,z)\to (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{x} \\ \sqrt{y}+z \\ {y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T.$

*Hint: You can assume that $x\ne 0$ and $y>0.$*" :question/worked-solution "For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{x},\,y(x,y,z)=\sqrt{y}+z,\,z(x,y,z)={y}^{2}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =1 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =2y & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} & 1 \\ 0 & 2y & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\begin{vmatrix}\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} & 1 \\ 2y & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}} & =(\frac{1}{x})^{2}\cdot 2\sqrt{{y}^{2}} \\  & ={u}^{2}\cdot 2\sqrt{w} \\  & =2{u}^{2}\sqrt{w}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2{u}^{2}\sqrt{w}}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129751 :question/id #uuid "9ad6bc33-7c9a-5d03-8204-18b81f486eea" :question/math-academy-id "q-39669" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0a3dfa61-4983-5101-a590-b7cae3069606" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186324062} {:answer/id #uuid "5975b6e2-4d63-5522-bc15-85311b4304c4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16" :db/id 17592186324714} {:answer/id #uuid "a5d3c1d8-1ca4-5893-ae40-8a4995898733" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{16}" :db/id 17592186325383} {:answer/id #uuid "c5fd3b47-8f20-518a-a996-2dbd4fa2edc8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{40}" :db/id 17592186325679} {:answer/id #uuid "fcb623d2-5638-5465-9671-82a386df23f7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "40" :db/id 17592186326195}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186325679} :answer-field/id #uuid "5d44cd8a-7ab2-5c59-a740-4c19610ad44c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186326377}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)),$ given that 

$$
u=2x+y,\,v=-x+3y-2z,\,w=3y+4z.
$$" :question/worked-solution "For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =2 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =1 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =3 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =-2 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =3 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2\begin{vmatrix}3 & -2 \\ 3 & 4\end{vmatrix}-1\begin{vmatrix}-1 & -2 \\ 0 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2(12+6)-1(-4-0) \\  & =40.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =1 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =1 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =1 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =-3 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ -3 & 0 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-(-1)\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -3 & 0\end{vmatrix}+1\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(0+3)+1(0-0) \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186281331 :question/id #uuid "4f0a4eb6-83e4-58b7-81d7-e22ca020da04" :question/math-academy-id "q-161801"} {:db/id 17592186281332 :question/id #uuid $$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)={e}^{x},\,v(x,y,z)={e}^{x+y},\,w(x,y,z)={e}^{x+y+z}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & ={e}^{x} & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & ={e}^{x+y} & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & ={e}^{x+y} & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & ={e}^{x+y+z} & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & ={e}^{x+y+z} & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & ={e}^{x+y+z}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}{e}^{x} & 0 & 0 \\ {e}^{x+y} & {e}^{x+y} & 0 \\ {e}^{x+y+z} & {e}^{x+y+z} & {e}^{x+y+z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{x}\begin{vmatrix}{e}^{x+y} & 0 \\ {e}^{x+y+z} & {e}^{x+y+z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{x}({e}^{2x+2y+z}-0) \\  & ={e}^{3x+2y+z}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{3x+2y+z} & ={e}^{x+(x+y)+(x+y+z)} \\  & ={e}^{x}\cdot {e}^{x+y}\cdot {e}^{x+y+z} \\  & =uvw\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{uvw}\end{aligned}

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=xy,\,v(x,y,z)=yz,\,w(x,y,z)=xz.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =y & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =x & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =z & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =y \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =z & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}y & x & 0 \\ 0 & z & y \\ z & 0 & x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =y\begin{vmatrix}z & y \\ 0 & x\end{vmatrix}-x\begin{vmatrix}0 & y \\ z & x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =y(xz-0)-x(0-yz) \\  & =xyz+xyz \\  & =2xyz.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2xyz & =2\sqrt{(xyz)^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{xy(yz)(xz)} \\  & =2\sqrt{uvw}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{uvw}}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186281337 :question/id #uuid "82aa7a5f-aede-5ec9-8984-8cdea4eb6f95" :question/math-academy-id "q-161807" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0626020c-ffd0-5d52-be60-af389fc83a02" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3(uvw)^{1/3}" :db/id 17592186278648} {:answer/id #uuid "57bde7fd-ba02-508b-9c77-edf62367e8ed" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{9(uvw)^{2/3}}" :db/id 17592186279398} {:answer/id #uuid "84467733-f429-5feb-8388-07e2d51f176e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3(uvw)^{3}" :db/id 17592186279778} {:answer/id #uuid "af416bf2-0b93-5782-b6de-1f1c2d402fc0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(uvw)^{2/3}" :db/id 17592186280143} {:answer/id #uuid "c8f31297-6e1d-54c7-be43-6fdd25ab29fd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9}{(uvw)^{2}}" :db/id 17592186280352}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279398} :answer-field/id #uuid "2bbffbbf-30e0-555b-b5e7-55199b3bfffb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186280913}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Consider the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y,z)\to (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z))$ is given by

*Hint: You can assume that $x,y,z\ne 0.$*" :question/worked-solution "For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=y{z}^{2},\,v(x,y,z)=z{x}^{2},\,w(x,y,z)=x{y}^{2}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & ={z}^{2} & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =2yz \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =2xz & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & ={x}^{2} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & ={y}^{2} & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =2xy & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & {z}^{2} & 2yz \\ 2xz & 0 & {x}^{2} \\ {y}^{2} & 2xy & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-{z}^{2}\begin{vmatrix}2xy & {x}^{2} \\ {y}^{2} & 0\end{vmatrix}+2yz\begin{vmatrix}2xz & 0 \\ {y}^{2} & 2xy\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-{z}^{2}(0-{x}^{2}{y}^{2})+2yz(4{x}^{2}yz-0) \\  & ={x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+8{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2} \\  & =9{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}9{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2} & =9{({x}^{3}{y}^{3}{z}^{3})}^{2/3} \\  & =9{(y{z}^{2}\cdot z{x}^{2}\cdot x{y}^{2})}^{2/3} \\  & =9(uvw)^{2/3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
u=x,\,v=2y,\,w=3z.
$$" :question/worked-solution "For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =1 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =2 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(6-0) \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129270 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186128847 :question/id #uuid "b16845a2-5f66-524a-90ea-37f8a8186f8f" :question/math-academy-id "e-11518"} :knowledge-point/id $$

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)={u}^{2}-v,\,y(u,v,w)={u}^{2}+v,\,z(u,v,w)={e}^{w}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & ={e}^{w}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}2u & -1 & 0 \\ 2u & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {e}^{w}\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{w}\begin{vmatrix}2u & -1 \\ 2u & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{w}(2u+2u) \\  & =4u{e}^{w}.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ 4u{e}^{w} & =0 \\ u & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $u=0$ defines the plane $u=0,$ i.e., $vw$-plane."} {:db/id 17592186281338 :question/id #uuid "d47d2404-bd86-5706-ba43-4f015172617a" :question/math-academy-id "q-161809"} {:db/id 17592186281339 :question/id #uuid "f26bca76-37a5-5f68-8e4a-4d9215b02535" :question/math-academy-id "q-161812" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "710d7d7d-97b4-592f-b30c-acf388d38859" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The critical points lie on the parabolic cylinder $v={w}^{2}.$" :db/id 17592186279617} {:answer/id #uuid "76ca4acf-773c-501c-ba6e-25239ada0435" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The critical points lie on the $vw-$plane." :db/id 17592186279651} {:answer/id #uuid "7b363e77-7f40-535f-a3a7-6bd580690682" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The critical points lie on the plane $v=2w.$" :db/id 17592186279692} {:answer/id #uuid "88ce4141-06f6-5738-b4cf-0fb6b9a3a05e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The critical points lie on the planes $v=\pm w.$" :db/id 17592186279813} {:answer/id #uuid "eaed37b4-3321-5a47-9faa-28666138fd1b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The critical points lie on the plane $v=u.$" :db/id 17592186280655}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279813} :answer-field/id #uuid "bcf9576c-0ce8-5723-bb46-cfba69aeb672" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281170}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $T,$ where $T$ is defined as

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=u,\,y(u,v,w)={v}^{3}+{w}^{3},\,z(u,v,w)=v+w.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =3{v}^{2} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =3{w}^{2} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3{v}^{2} & 3{w}^{2} \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}3{v}^{2} & 3{w}^{2} \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(3{v}^{2}-3{w}^{2}) \\  & =3({v}^{2}-{w}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ 3({v}^{2}-{w}^{2}) & =0 \\ {v}^{2}-{w}^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =w & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =v \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & w & v \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\begin{vmatrix}w & v \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}+1\begin{vmatrix}0 & 0 \\ w & v\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}(w-0)+0 \\  & =\frac{w}{2\sqrt{u}}.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ \frac{w}{2\sqrt{u}} & =0 \\ w & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $w=0$ defines the plane $w=0,$ i.e., $uv$-plane."} {:db/id 17592186281341 :question/id #uuid "5ae1d4bd-a84e-5282-96ec-f8259badfc91" :question/math-academy-id "q-161817" the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=u,\,y(u,v,w)=v{e}^{w},\,z(u,v,w)=2u+v+3w.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & ={e}^{w} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =v{e}^{w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =2 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{w} & v{e}^{w} \\ 2 & 1 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}{e}^{w} & v{e}^{w} \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(3{e}^{w}-v{e}^{w}) \\  & ={e}^{w}(3-v).\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ {e}^{w}(3-v) & =0 \\ 3-v & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $T,$ where $T$ is defined as

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{u} \\ {e}^{u+w} \\ uv+w\end{bmatrix}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)={e}^{u},\,y(u,v,w)={e}^{u+w},\,z(u,v,w)=uv+w.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & ={e}^{u} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & ={e}^{u+w} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & ={e}^{u+w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =v & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =u & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}{e}^{u} & 0 & 0 \\ {e}^{u+w} & 0 & {e}^{u+w} \\ v & u & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{u}\begin{vmatrix}0 & {e}^{u+w} \\ u & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{u}(0-u{e}^{u+w}) \\  & =-u{e}^{2u+w}.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ -u{e}^{2u+w} & =0 \\ u & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $u=0$ defines the plane $u=0,$ i.e., $vw$-plane."} {:db/id 17592186406771 :question/id #uuid "84951e54-c705-5b01-85eb-275b777e397c" :question/math-academy-id "q-161810" 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T,$ defined as

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}u{e}^{w} \\ w-u \\ w{e}^{u}-3v\end{bmatrix}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=u{e}^{w},\,y(u,v,w)=w-u,\,z(u,v,w)=w{e}^{u}-3v.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & ={e}^{w} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =u{e}^{w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =1 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =w{e}^{u} & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =-3, & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & ={e}^{u}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}{e}^{w} & 0 & u{e}^{w} \\ -1 & 0 & 1 \\ w{e}^{u} & -3 & {e}^{u}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(-3)(-1)^{3+2}\begin{vmatrix}{e}^{w} & u{e}^{w} \\ -1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =3({e}^{w}+u{e}^{w}) \\  & =3{e}^{w}(1+u).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186281327 :question/id #uuid "27f802ec-0d96-5c3f-9520-b80524648c50" :question/math-academy-id "q-161794"} {:db/id 17592186281328 :question/id #uuid "590673d5-674e-5f87-8a3b-a26381077e85" :question/math-academy-id "q-161796" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186129271 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d433063f-f145-5bf4-8bd4-8d5e5b36b3d8" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Jacobian of a Three-Dimensional Transformation"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "555199b9-aced-5dd0-a7a4-1c3b529e0ad8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{w}" :db/id 17592186279370} {:answer/id #uuid "71d28527-0b0f-581a-b145-41b591816c80" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\frac{uv}{w}" :db/id 17592186279625} {:answer/id #uuid "9bf35eb4-7d06-504d-97d6-6d62c0d12660" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186279976} {:answer/id #uuid "9e2827ef-81bc-5319-a0af-3f83476042b9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{u}{w}-\frac{1}{v}" :db/id 17592186279995} {:answer/id #uuid "f447c433-d789-5722-828c-42983f30e64f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{u}{w}" :db/id 17592186280731}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "f447c433-d789-5722-828c-42983f30e64f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{u}{w}" :db/id 17592186280731} :answer-field/id #uuid "65c51ca4-49aa-5089-b98e-4e0fed70679a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186281007}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T,$ defined as

$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(u\,v\,w),\,y(u,v,w)=u+2w,\,z(u,v,w)=uv.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\frac{1}{u} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =\frac{1}{v} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =\frac{1}{w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =2 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =v & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =u & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{1}{u} & \frac{1}{v} & \frac{1}{w} \\ 1 & 0 & 2 \\ v & u & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{w}(-1)^{1+3}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ v & u\end{vmatrix}+2(-1)^{2+3}\begin{vmatrix}\frac{1}{u} & \frac{1}{v} \\ v & u\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{w}(u-0)-2(1-1) \\  & =\frac{u}{w}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186406772 :question/id #uuid "9eac1497-79c1-5ed3-be68-00cfa0edfef5" :question/math-academy-id "q-39710" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186129271 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d433063f-f145-5bf4-8bd4-8d5e5b36b3d8" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Jacobian of a Three-Dimensional Transformation"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "03b82058-2ed1-5ab3-8be0-f2ccd9e791be" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2uv-2u{v}^{2}-vu" :db/id 17592186406759} {:answer/id #uuid "2b07851c-5666-5e08-93b4-ea52710578c9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2{u}^{2}-2{v}^{3}-vw" :db/id 17592186406761} {:answer/id #uuid "4e04d287-7eaa-501d-ba5e-706a25e1adcd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2vw" :db/id 17592186406764} {:answer/id #uuid "78a6574d-a7a7-5dd3-9372-265b4fd8dfa8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2uv-2u{v}^{2}+vu" :db/id 17592186406765} {:answer/id #uuid "c5d7dba0-5d86-5a7b-97ed-55ed0cf1cb1c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2{u}^{2}-2{v}^{3}+vw" :db/id 17592186406767}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "2b07851c-5666-5e08-93b4-ea52710578c9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2{u}^{2}-2{v}^{3}-vw" :db/id 17592186406761} :answer-field/id #uuid "bc7e9e1f-8201-5457-9ae8-866cb0a50e5b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186406770}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T$ that maps the $uvw$-space into the $xyz$-space by means of the equations

$$
x={u}^{2}+vw,\,y=2-uv,\,z={v}^{2}-w.
$$" :question/worked-solution "For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =w & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =-v & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =-u & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =2v & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}2u & w & v \\ -v & -u & 0 \\ 0 & 2v & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2u(-1)^{1+1}\begin{vmatrix}-u & 0 \\ 2v & -1\end{vmatrix}+(-v)(-1)^{2+1}\begin{vmatrix}w & v \\ 2v & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2u(u-0)+v(-w-2{v}^{2}) \\  & =2{u}^{2}-2{v}^{3}-vw.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186424178 :question/id #uuid "03a9f960-3754-59ca-a7ce-a0ebf6a90fdf" :question/math-academy-id "q-39294"} {:db/id 17592186424179 :question/id #uuid {:db/id 17592186130212 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130457 :tutorial/content "Similar to transformations in the plane, we can also consider transformations of three-dimensional regions.

For example, the transformation

![](images/71/71b4c6b8f2db4890436050206115b94eb57b088be76049cb32667f02986b4f56.svg) 

maps a rectangular prism in Cartesian $uvw$-space onto one-eighth of a sphere in Cartesian $xyz$-space, as shown below.

![](images/3e/3e1ee5a6116d57cc1c3419b55bf0a9701b9f5d4d93931d053ed4a05b83a5d8f0.png)

 

In general, if a transformation

![](images/d1/d175f9eba3a6da7cc7750b3e59fe0e5904df27511a6b64481598e0f0ebfa1f0c.svg) 

is a $C^1$ transformation, meaning that it and its first derivatives are continuous, then the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T}$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

  

For example, to compute the Jacobian determinant of our transformation above, we first calculate the required partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =-u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =-u\operatorname{sin}⁡v & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡v & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v|\begin{aligned}u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w\end{aligned}|+u\operatorname{sin}⁡v|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w\end{aligned}| \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v\cdot {u}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡v\cdot ({cos}^{2}⁡w+{sin}^{2}⁡w)+u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\cdot u{sin}^{2}⁡v\cdot ({cos}^{2}⁡w+{sin}^{2}⁡w) \\  & ={u}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡v+{u}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & ={u}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡v\cdot ({cos}^{2}⁡v+{sin}^{2}⁡v) \\  & ={u}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡v.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's get some practice at computing Jacobians of three-dimensional transformations." :tutorial/id #uuid "610a6348-ed80-507a-b390-560e9bc1e4ef" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7237 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "d8ced6e6-4bb6-52e9-8819-7a54180e8a4f" :step/math-academy-id 43046 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130234}} {:db/id 17592186130213 :step/content {:db/id 17592186129271 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186128848 :question/id #uuid "66d757d2-f2ad-5f0d-b4f1-8d426f4c8351" :question/math-academy-id "e-11579"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d433063f-f145-5bf4-8bd4-8d5e5b36b3d8" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048219} {:db/id 17592186048505} {:db/id 17592186049159}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186129727} {:db/id 17592186129750} {:db/id 17592186281325} {:db/id 17592186281326} {:db/id 17592186281327} {:db/id 17592186281328} {:db/id 17592186406772} {:db/id 17592186424178} {:db/id 17592186424179}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Jacobian of a Three-Dimensional Transformation"} :step/id #uuid "d3c03e1b-973d-566a-96d2-32f746decf45" :step/math-academy-id 43048 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130229}} {:db/id 17592186130229 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130463 :tutorial/content "The **critical points** of a transformation $\mathbf T: \mathbb R^3\longrightarrow\mathbb R^3,$ given by

![](images/0f/0f47dfd79a5147b5628975b26ea21a37288d809fb30a5a90b205ecc7b25ae008.svg)

are the points in Cartesian $uvw$-space where the Jacobian is zero:

$$
\dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)}=0
$$

  

Similar to the two-dimensional case, the transformation $\mathbf T$ is locally non-invertible at the critical points.

Finally, provided that $\mathbf{T}$ is invertible, the connection between the Jacobians of $\mathbf T$ and $\mathbf{T}^{-1}$ is as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\partial (u, v, w)}{\partial (x, y, z)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} \right)^{-1}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "9dd5b9bc-94c3-5fd0-8752-3fa9be521934" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7676 :tutorial/title "The Critical Points of a Transformation"} :step/id #uuid "99520515-6bfa-5265-8e42-e193dc1183f6" :step/math-academy-id 44587 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130211}} {:db/id 17592186130234 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130467 :tutorial/content "The Jacobian determinant of a spatial transformation can be interpreted similarly to the Jacobian of a plane transformation.

As before, the Jacobian describes *local* effects, not global ones. 

Given that $J(u_0,v_0,w_0)$ denotes the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T}$ evaluated at $(u_0, v_0, w_0),$ let's describe $\mathbf T$'s effect on a *tiny* rectangular prism in Cartesian $uvw$-space whose bottom, back left corner is at the point $(u_0,v_0,w_0).$

![](images/31/31c0a7275acdac0dc217e73f3c1e3d9efe504832419c87486cee980e20ea04da.png)

 

It can be shown that, provided that our prism is very small and $(u_0,v_0, w_0)$ is not a critical point of $\mathbf T,$ the image of our prism can be approximated by a parallelepiped. 

The Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T$ evaluated at $(u_0,v_0,w_0)$ describes the following key features between our tiny rectangular prism and its (approximate) image:

- The local *volume* scale factor of $\mathbf T$. 

Suppose the length, width, and height of our rectangular prism are $\delta u,$ $\delta v,$ and $\delta w,$ so its volume is 

$$
\delta V = \delta u \delta v \delta w.
$$

 Then, it can be shown that the approximate parallelepiped in $xyz$-space has a volume equal to 

$$
\left|J(u_0,v_0,w_0)\right| \cdot \delta V,
$$

 as depicted below.

![](images/d6/d669cd5369d33e618ab43cfd3e93ee70c9fea8420b5a829d78826c11524511aa.png)

- Whether the transformation is *locally* orientation-preserving or *locally* orientation-reversing.

If $J(u_0,v_0,w_0) > 0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-preserving. 

Geometrically, this means that the transformation maps a triple of vectors onto a triple with the same orientation (right-handed $\to$ right-handed or left-handed $\to$ left-handed).

![](images/f0/f05f9a79d9156518e948c46f6c67eb5ff31132fd4a088e14219eada7eb49a441.png)

 

If $J(u_0,v_0, w_0) < 0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing.

Geometrically, this means that the transformation maps a triple of vectors onto a triple with the opposite orientation (right-handed $\to$ left-handed or left-handed $\to$ right-handed).

![](images/45/45b08e0fec7114db52a05cb42ed46d7d62baa5b01a5dea37752928348802b205.png)

- Whether the transformation is *locally* invertible or *locally* non-invertible.

If $J(u_0,v_0,w_0) \neq 0,$ the transformation is (locally) invertible.

Geometrically, this means that the transformation maps our tiny rectangular prism (a three-dimensional region) onto a three-dimensional region (i.e., a parallelepiped).

![](images/61/61557eb2d78d468946375b918ab182da518b7cf2c68a1c0a0593c93b991bcf78.png)

 

If $J(u_0,v_0,w_0)= 0,$ the transformation is (locally) non-invertible.

Geometrically, this means that the transformation maps our tiny rectangular prism (a three-dimensional region) onto a two-dimensional region (a parallelogram), a one-dimensional region (a line segment), or a zero-dimensional region (a point).

![](images/72/726ba518de982ddd0b2924a645463b496ed881ead76a652c812c7a164aa684b8.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "10a3ad60-7124-5508-a053-b827183f5a2a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7718 :tutorial/title "Intuition Behind the Jacobian"} :step/id #uuid "ed9fa5db-a7c0-512a-bb14-c0e7e5dcbcd0" :step/math-academy-id 44764 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130213}}] :activity/title "The Jacobian of a Three-Dimensional Transformation" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186129388} {:db/id 17592186130212 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130457 :tutorial/content "Similar to transformations in the plane, we can also consider transformations of three-dimensional regions.

For example, the transformation

![](images/71/71b4c6b8f2db4890436050206115b94eb57b088be76049cb32667f02986b4f56.svg) 

maps a rectangular prism in Cartesian $uvw$-space onto one-eighth of a sphere in Cartesian $xyz$-space, as shown below.

![](images/3e/3e1ee5a6116d57cc1c3419b55bf0a9701b9f5d4d93931d053ed4a05b83a5d8f0.png)

 

In general, if a transformation

![](images/d1/d175f9eba3a6da7cc7750b3e59fe0e5904df27511a6b64481598e0f0ebfa1f0c.svg) 

is a $C^1$ transformation, meaning that it and its first derivatives are continuous, then the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T}$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

  

For example, to compute the Jacobian determinant of our transformation above, we first calculate the required partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =-u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =-u\operatorname{sin}⁡v & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡v & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v|\begin{aligned}u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w\end{aligned}|+u\operatorname{sin}⁡v|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w\end{aligned}| \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v\cdot {u}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡v\cdot ({cos}^{2}⁡w+{sin}^{2}⁡w)+u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\cdot u{sin}^{2}⁡v\cdot ({cos}^{2}⁡w+{sin}^{2}⁡w) \\  & ={u}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡v+{u}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & ={u}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡v\cdot ({cos}^{2}⁡v+{sin}^{2}⁡v) \\  & ={u}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡v.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's get some practice at computing Jacobians of three-dimensional transformations." :tutorial/id #uuid "610a6348-ed80-507a-b390-560e9bc1e4ef" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7237 :tutorial/title are the points in Cartesian $uvw$-space where the Jacobian is zero:

\dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)}=0
$$

  

Similar to the two-dimensional case, the transformation $\mathbf T$ is locally non-invertible at the critical points.

Finally, provided that $\mathbf{T}$ is invertible, the connection between the Jacobians of $\mathbf T$ and $\mathbf{T}^{-1}$ is as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\partial (u, v, w)}{\partial (x, y, z)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} \right)^{-1}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "9dd5b9bc-94c3-5fd0-8752-3fa9be521934" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7676 :tutorial/title "The Critical Points of a Transformation"} {:db/id 17592186130467 :tutorial/content "The Jacobian determinant of a spatial transformation can be interpreted similarly to the Jacobian of a plane transformation.

As before, the Jacobian describes *local* effects, not global ones. 

Given that $J(u_0,v_0,w_0)$ denotes the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T}$ evaluated at $(u_0, v_0, w_0),$ let's describe $\mathbf T$'s effect on a *tiny* rectangular prism in Cartesian $uvw$-space whose bottom, back left corner is at the point $(u_0,v_0,w_0).$

![](images/31/31c0a7275acdac0dc217e73f3c1e3d9efe504832419c87486cee980e20ea04da.png)

 

It can be shown that, provided that our prism is very small and $(u_0,v_0, w_0)$ is not a critical point of $\mathbf T,$ the image of our prism can be approximated by a parallelepiped. 

The Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T$ evaluated at $(u_0,v_0,w_0)$ describes the following key features between our tiny rectangular prism and its (approximate) image:

- The local *volume* scale factor of $\mathbf T$. 

Suppose the length, width, and height of our rectangular prism are $\delta u,$ $\delta v,$ and $\delta w,$ so its volume is 

$$
\delta V = \delta u \delta v \delta w.
$$

 Then, it can be shown that the approximate parallelepiped in $xyz$-space has a volume equal to 

$$
\left|J(u_0,v_0,w_0)\right| \cdot \delta V,
$$

 as depicted below.

![](images/d6/d669cd5369d33e618ab43cfd3e93ee70c9fea8420b5a829d78826c11524511aa.png)

- Whether the transformation is *locally* orientation-preserving or *locally* orientation-reversing.

If $J(u_0,v_0,w_0) > 0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-preserving. 

Geometrically, this means that the transformation maps a triple of vectors onto a triple with the same orientation (right-handed $\to$ right-handed or left-handed $\to$ left-handed).

![](images/f0/f05f9a79d9156518e948c46f6c67eb5ff31132fd4a088e14219eada7eb49a441.png)

 

If $J(u_0,v_0, w_0) < 0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing.

Geometrically, this means that the transformation maps a triple of vectors onto a triple with the opposite orientation (right-handed $\to$ left-handed or left-handed $\to$ right-handed).

![](images/45/45b08e0fec7114db52a05cb42ed46d7d62baa5b01a5dea37752928348802b205.png)

- Whether the transformation is *locally* invertible or *locally* non-invertible.

If $J(u_0,v_0,w_0) \neq 0,$ the transformation is (locally) invertible.

Geometrically, this means that the transformation maps our tiny rectangular prism (a three-dimensional region) onto a three-dimensional region (i.e., a parallelepiped).

![](images/61/61557eb2d78d468946375b918ab182da518b7cf2c68a1c0a0593c93b991bcf78.png)

 

If $J(u_0,v_0,w_0)= 0,$ the transformation is (locally) non-invertible.

Geometrically, this means that the transformation maps our tiny rectangular prism (a three-dimensional region) onto a two-dimensional region (a parallelogram), a one-dimensional region (a line segment), or a zero-dimensional region (a point).

transformation $T,$ where $T$ is defined as

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}{u}^{2}-v \\ {u}^{2}+v \\ {e}^{w}\end{bmatrix}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)={u}^{2}-v,\,y(u,v,w)={u}^{2}+v,\,z(u,v,w)={e}^{w}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & ={e}^{w}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}2u & -1 & 0 \\ 2u & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {e}^{w}\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{w}\begin{vmatrix}2u & -1 \\ 2u & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{w}(2u+2u) \\  & =4u{e}^{w}.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ 4u{e}^{w} & =0 \\ u & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $u=0$ defines the plane $u=0,$ i.e., $vw$-plane."} :step/id #uuid "1059b764-2977-50ff-bfe0-2e03c6d8a3b7" :step/next {:db/id 17592186416649}} {:db/id 17592186416648 :step/content {:db/id 17592186129728 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "408e29c9-6522-5467-9ab8-def9fe8cfb65" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{{u}^{2}}{2\sqrt{w}}" :db/id 17592186324490} {:answer/id #uuid "69224e59-e1c5-54cd-8748-b2d597b5cd76" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{w}{u}^{2}}{2}" :db/id 17592186324848} {:answer/id #uuid "7b1e869c-a3b7-584b-8e0f-e99423947eb0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{u}^{2}}{2\sqrt{w}}" :db/id 17592186325004} {:answer/id #uuid "e98f16dc-8225-5762-aa80-dca5e80b6645" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2{u}^{2}\sqrt{w}}" :db/id 17592186326027} {:answer/id #uuid "fb5ec600-18ee-54e3-bb28-7c22c6783223" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2{u}^{2}\sqrt{w}}" :db/id 17592186326182}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186326027} :answer-field/id #uuid "65802821-8118-5ece-8435-a69816ad88f1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186326394}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "f85af4c0-4520-5614-952b-cb9d6d06c6c9" :question/math-academy-id "q-39300" :question/problem "Consider the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y,z)\to (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z))$ is given by

$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T.$

*Hint: You can assume that $x\ne 0$ and $y>0.$*" :question/worked-solution "For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{x},\,y(x,y,z)=\sqrt{y}+z,\,z(x,y,z)={y}^{2}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =1 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =2y & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} & 1 \\ 0 & 2y & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\begin{vmatrix}\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} & 1 \\ 2y & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}} & =(\frac{1}{x})^{2}\cdot 2\sqrt{{y}^{2}} \\  & ={u}^{2}\cdot 2\sqrt{w} \\  & =2{u}^{2}\sqrt{w}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2{u}^{2}\sqrt{w}}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "8e074033-7ddf-5114-859f-8aff01ee8989" :step/next {:db/id 17592186416647}} {:db/id 17592186416649 :step/content {:db/id 17592186281337 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0626020c-ffd0-5d52-be60-af389fc83a02" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3(uvw)^{1/3}" :db/id 17592186278648} {:answer/id #uuid "57bde7fd-ba02-508b-9c77-edf62367e8ed" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{9(uvw)^{2/3}}" :db/id 17592186279398} {:answer/id #uuid "84467733-f429-5feb-8388-07e2d51f176e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3(uvw)^{3}" :db/id 17592186279778} {:answer/id #uuid "af416bf2-0b93-5782-b6de-1f1c2d402fc0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(uvw)^{2/3}" :db/id 17592186280143} {:answer/id #uuid "c8f31297-6e1d-54c7-be43-6fdd25ab29fd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9}{(uvw)^{2}}" :db/id 17592186280352}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279398} :answer-field/id #uuid "2bbffbbf-30e0-555b-b5e7-55199b3bfffb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186280913}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "82aa7a5f-aede-5ec9-8984-8cdea4eb6f95" :question/math-academy-id "q-161807" :question/problem "Consider the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y,z)\to (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z))$ is given by

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$

$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=y{z}^{2},\,v(x,y,z)=z{x}^{2},\,w(x,y,z)=x{y}^{2}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & ={z}^{2} & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =2yz \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =2xz & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & ={x}^{2} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & ={y}^{2} & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =2xy & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & {z}^{2} & 2yz \\ 2xz & 0 & {x}^{2} \\ {y}^{2} & 2xy & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-{z}^{2}\begin{vmatrix}2xy & {x}^{2} \\ {y}^{2} & 0\end{vmatrix}+2yz\begin{vmatrix}2xz & 0 \\ {y}^{2} & 2xy\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-{z}^{2}(0-{x}^{2}{y}^{2})+2yz(4{x}^{2}yz-0) \\  & ={x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+8{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2} \\  & =9{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}9{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2} & =9{({x}^{3}{y}^{3}{z}^{3})}^{2/3} \\  & =9{(y{z}^{2}\cdot z{x}^{2}\cdot x{y}^{2})}^{2/3} \\  & =9(uvw)^{2/3}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{9(uvw)^{2/3}}\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ 4u{e}^{w} & =0 \\ u & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T.$

*Hint: You can assume that $x,y,z\ne 0.$*" :question/worked-solution "For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=y{z}^{2},\,v(x,y,z)=z{x}^{2},\,w(x,y,z)=x{y}^{2}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & ={z}^{2} & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =2yz \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =2xz & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & ={x}^{2} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & ={y}^{2} & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =2xy & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & {z}^{2} & 2yz \\ 2xz & 0 & {x}^{2} \\ {y}^{2} & 2xy & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-{z}^{2}\begin{vmatrix}2xy & {x}^{2} \\ {y}^{2} & 0\end{vmatrix}+2yz\begin{vmatrix}2xz & 0 \\ {y}^{2} & 2xy\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-{z}^{2}(0-{x}^{2}{y}^{2})+2yz(4{x}^{2}yz-0) \\  & ={x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+8{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2} \\  & =9{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}9{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2} & =9{({x}^{3}{y}^{3}{z}^{3})}^{2/3} \\  & =9{(y{z}^{2}\cdot z{x}^{2}\cdot x{y}^{2})}^{2/3} \\  & =9(uvw)^{2/3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{9(uvw)^{2/3}}\end{aligned}

$$

$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=xy,\,v(x,y,z)=yz,\,w(x,y,z)=xz.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =y & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =x & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =z & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =y \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =z & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}y & x & 0 \\ 0 & z & y \\ z & 0 & x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =y\begin{vmatrix}z & y \\ 0 & x\end{vmatrix}-x\begin{vmatrix}0 & y \\ z & x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =y(xz-0)-x(0-yz) \\  & =xyz+xyz \\  & =2xyz.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2xyz & =2\sqrt{(xyz)^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{xy(yz)(xz)} \\  & =2\sqrt{uvw}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{uvw}}\end{aligned}

$$" :question/worked-solution "For a transformation 

$$

$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)={e}^{u}+v,\,y(u,v,w)=v+w,\,z(u,v,w)=vw.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & ={e}^{u} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =1 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =w & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =v\end{aligned}
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T.$

*Hint: You can assume that $x,y,z>0.$*" :question/worked-solution "For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=xy,\,v(x,y,z)=yz,\,w(x,y,z)=xz.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =y & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =x & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =z & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =y \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =z & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}y & x & 0 \\ 0 & z & y \\ z & 0 & x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =y\begin{vmatrix}z & y \\ 0 & x\end{vmatrix}-x\begin{vmatrix}0 & y \\ z & x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =y(xz-0)-x(0-yz) \\  & =xyz+xyz \\  & =2xyz.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3{v}^{2} & 3{w}^{2} \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}3{v}^{2} & 3{w}^{2} \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(3{v}^{2}-3{w}^{2}) \\  & =3({v}^{2}-{w}^{2}).\end{aligned}

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =1 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =2 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(6-0) \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}

$\begin{bmatrix}12x + 8 & > 44 \\ 12x & > 36 \\ x & > 3\end{bmatrix}$

![](images/e9/e9eec85ca2dd2a9fd01db97a5f281d16fd958e143e048f7ff3c5e7a87dd33f0a.png)

Then, we solve

$$
5x+3 \leq 28
$$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}5x + 3 & \le 28 \\ 5x & \le 25 \\ x & \le 5\end{bmatrix}
$$

![](images/c9/c9cec5cfc0e476fffe4f89f89ff0585992855e8e36fe09778029d5accd2bdc6b.png)

To graph the values of $x$ that satisfy either inequality, we overlay the two graphs on the same number line:

![](images/dd/dd1330c9f2d9dc2140a3e3a4dc37ac269d134c5e367f59c9985ce04d4acd6304.png)

Therefore, the final solution is $-\infty < x < \infty$. We can write this using interval notation as $(-\infty,\infty)$."} {:db/id 17592186115903 :question/id #uuid "59f4234d-7f54-5341-b6b4-e5e2ca156720" :question/math-academy-id "q-55288" Express your answer in interval notation." :question/worked-solution "We start by solving

$$
6x-1 \leq 2
$$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}6x - 1 & \le 2 \\ 6x & \le 3 \\ x & \le \frac{3}{6} \\ x & \le \frac{1}{2}\end{bmatrix}
$$

![](images/dd/dd2c101e02e14a147371bc1b822f3bc86081dd0059ac50ae1f9131909e73e3ad.png)

Then, we solve $5x -1 > 9$:
$\begin{bmatrix}5x - 1 & > 9 \\ 5x & > 10 \\ x & > 2\end{bmatrix}$

![](images/8b/8b252e1c42dcac87072a33b33460a887b6ec3bfa0d1511f05a004935df1911ca.png)

To graph the values of $x$ that satisfy either inequality, we overlay the two graphs on the same number line:

![](images/ac/ac44f335b135463820ec0db9bc04470769fee7aabc8717edcc351893b6d8de47.png)

Therefore, the final solution is

$$
x \leq \dfrac{1}{2}
$$

or $x >2$. We can write this using interval notation as

$$
(- ∞, \frac{1}{2}]∪(2, ∞)
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049986} {:db/id 17592186050229} {:db/id 17592186115575 :question/id #uuid "d49e016f-75f1-58ba-a1d6-f031560b6c52" :question/math-academy-id "q-25419"} {:db/id 17592186115577 :question/id #uuid "61f317f4-c237-5111-9abb-b10f52746c4a" :question/math-academy-id "q-25664"} {:db/id 17592186115323 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186115155 :question/id #uuid "dced871e-e24d-5d06-a4bb-9faa933ecac7" :question/math-academy-id "e-967"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "3e3a4ead-02d0-5023-a7a7-3aaaca19b563" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050734}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186115576 :question/id #uuid "710e74cf-0030-5cf8-afcc-101ba583257c" :question/math-academy-id "q-25484"} {:db/id 17592186115906 :question/id #uuid "657ccae9-03d3-59e9-af36-01df6031e4ca" :question/math-academy-id "q-59512"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Union of Two Linear Inequalities When One Inequality is Compound"} {:db/id 17592186115155 :question/id #uuid "dced871e-e24d-5d06-a4bb-9faa933ecac7" :question/math-academy-id "e-967" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186115323 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "3e3a4ead-02d0-5023-a7a7-3aaaca19b563" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Union of Two Linear Inequalities When One Inequality is Compound"}] :question/problem "Find the set of values of $x$ that satisfy $1 < 5x+6 \leq 11$ or $5x-7 > 8$." :question/worked-solution "We start by solving

$$
1 < 5x+6 \leq 11
$$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & < 5x + 6 \le 11 \\ -5 & < 5x \le 5 \\ -1 & < x \le 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

![](images/69/69948e87bc893a2461ec6e8bb77dd72e77e6d496970e31df899400c42238cd01.png)

Then, we solve $5x-7 > 8$:
$\begin{bmatrix}5x - 7 & > 8 \\ 5x & > 15 \\ x & > 3\end{bmatrix}$

![](images/10/10bb9a3bcc0b13b015649e2dae70a3ff3dcd361f46e6c545182031d6e095ad16.png)

To graph the values of $x$ that satisfy either inequality, we overlay the two graphs on the same number line:

![](images/84/84a05cd47818c9609609c2f02bd026ccadfa77c6641dff82936630bf04fbe77e.png)

Thus, the final solution is

$$
-1 < x \leq 1
$$

or $x > 3$. We can write this using interval notation as

$$
(-1,1] \cup (3,\infty)
$$"} {:db/id 17592186115576 :question/id #uuid "710e74cf-0030-5cf8-afcc-101ba583257c" :question/math-academy-id "q-25484" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186115323 :knowledge-point/id #uuid [{:db/id 17592186116243 :step/content {:db/id 17592186116417 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find all of the values of $x$ that satisfy *either* $4x+2 < 6$ *or*

$$
2x \geq 8
$$

To do this, we solve each inequality individually and then compute the union of the two solutions.

We start by solving $4x+2 < 6$:
$\begin{bmatrix}4x + 2 & < 6 \\ 4x & < 4 \\ x & < 1\end{bmatrix}$

![](images/0d/0d36b8e68d9fd0b33b255502860481eeb525b60382029b17434bfb072cc39da2.png)

Then, we solve

$$
2x \geq 8
$$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2x & \ge 8 \\ x & \ge 4\end{bmatrix}
$$

![](images/ed/edf5665b7cab7f51e3f252601a96d43c6f0cbfc64e5c9b8da81f0ef09d7b2f5a.png)

To graph the values of $x$ that satisfy either inequality, we overlay the two graphs on the same number line:

![](images/5c/5c60839a626f2ba8a0fe4a24f4011af0fa52c00d79fbf80039bcfdbdf0a612c7.png)

Thus, the final solution is $x < 1$ or

$$
x \geq 4
$$

We can write this using interval notation as

$$
(-\infty, 1) \cup [4,\infty)
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6d186c13-c1df-52d0-8ed6-a383185138a9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1428 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "cdc53761-47a4-5dc1-a8a0-b21a01b5b35a" :step/math-academy-id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186115415} {:db/id 17592186116243 :step/content {:db/id 17592186116417 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find all of the values of $x$ that satisfy *either* $4x+2 < 6$ *or*

$$
2x \geq 8
$$

To do this, we solve each inequality individually and then compute the union of the two solutions.

We start by solving $4x+2 < 6$:
$\begin{bmatrix}4x + 2 & < 6 \\ 4x & < 4 \\ x & < 1\end{bmatrix}$

![](images/0d/0d36b8e68d9fd0b33b255502860481eeb525b60382029b17434bfb072cc39da2.png)

Then, we solve

$$
2x \geq 8
$$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2x & \ge 8 \\ x & \ge 4\end{bmatrix}
$$

![](images/ed/edf5665b7cab7f51e3f252601a96d43c6f0cbfc64e5c9b8da81f0ef09d7b2f5a.png)

To graph the values of $x$ that satisfy either inequality, we overlay the two graphs on the same number line:

![](images/5c/5c60839a626f2ba8a0fe4a24f4011af0fa52c00d79fbf80039bcfdbdf0a612c7.png)

Thus, the final solution is $x < 1$ or

$$
x \geq 4
$$

We can write this using interval notation as

$$
(-\infty, 1) \cup [4,\infty)
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6d186c13-c1df-52d0-8ed6-a383185138a9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1428 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "cdc53761-47a4-5dc1-a8a0-b21a01b5b35a" :step/math-academy-id 3201 :step/next {:db/id 17592186116245}} {:db/id 17592186116417 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find all of the values of $x$ that satisfy *either* $4x+2 < 6$ *or*
