17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "$$
\overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}}}=\overset{Q}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}{q}_{11} & {q}_{12} \\ {q}_{21} & {q}_{22} \\ {q}_{31} & {q}_{32}\end{bmatrix}}}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}{r}_{11} & {r}_{12} \\ 0 & {r}_{22}\end{bmatrix}}}.
$$

Consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown above. Given that the columns ${a}_{1},{a}_{2}$ of $A$ are orthogonal, and that the columns ${q}_{1},{q}_{2}$ of $Q$ were obtained by normalizing the columns of $A,$ what is the value of ${q}_{32}\cdot {r}_{22}?$" :question/worked-solution "Since the columns of $A$ are already orthogonal, to construct an orthogonal matrix $Q,$ we simply normalize ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{1} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{‖{a}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\ {q}_{2} & =\frac{{a}_{2}}{‖{a}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, pre-multiplying both sides of $A=QR$ by ${Q}^{T},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}R & ={Q}^{T}\,A \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{2} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{6}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following QR factorization of $A:$

$$
\overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}}}=\overset{Q}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ 0 & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}\end{bmatrix}}}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{2} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{6}\end{bmatrix}}}
$$

Finally, ${q}_{32}\cdot {r}_{22}=-\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}\cdot \sqrt{6}=-2.$"} {:db/id 17592186364613 :question/id #uuid "75e8d7ef-26a5-51d9-ba2c-c43a53de12e6" :question/math-academy-id "q-96029"} {:db/id 17592186380318 :question/id #uuid "999c22e3-00be-5df4-8adf-f0fdfad70b35" :question/math-academy-id "q-95942"} {:db/id 17592186395093 :question/id #uuid "5112a112-d520-578f-a615-69da3e2d4aa0" :question/math-academy-id "q-96019"} {:db/id 17592186395100 :question/id #uuid "a11a1ea5-30ff-5154-92c7-cf0778166ca7" :question/math-academy-id "q-96026" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c73f4b81-f7c2-58b3-ba59-81c1cb4e21d8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186395102} {:answer/id #uuid "2965e000-8ed9-5b43-8807-b337179e3e72" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186395103} {:answer/id #uuid "f728b525-0316-5b5a-bee0-0f67b27c8544" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186395104} {:answer/id #uuid "5578869c-e22f-59c6-b9c4-7f6a4a040091" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186395105} {:answer/id #uuid "db6dd2c4-cdf3-588c-b826-6965e60d9428" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186395106}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186395105} :answer-field/id #uuid "d8d465ac-6125-5625-8e53-c378575651c3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186395101}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "$$

{:db/id 17592186134801 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135097 :tutorial/content "Given the matrix $Q$ in the QR factorization of an $m\times n$ matrix $A,$ how do we find $R?$

Recall that $Q$ has orthonormal columns, so pre-multiplying both sides of $A=QR$ by $Q^T,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}^{T}\cdot A & ={Q}^{T}\cdot QR \\ {Q}^{T}A & ={Q}^{T}QR.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, note that since the columns of $Q$ are orthonormal we have $Q^TQ = I_n.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}^{T}A & =({Q}^{T}Q)R \\ {Q}^{T}A & ={I}_{n}R \\ R & ={Q}^{T}A.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can find $R$ by pre-multiplying $A$ by the transpose of $Q.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "20b6ab0a-cf41-550b-9242-2bb3f84c4917" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5017 :tutorial/title "Computing the Matrix R Given the Matrix Q in a QR Factorization"} :step/id #uuid "eebb9689-f8b3-55e2-8167-e5f5525e382a" :step/math-academy-id 31388 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134798}} {:db/id 17592186134802 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135098 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown below:

![](images/ee/ee731d95c111101559ad135429198dd7e0b14313272f0933b1c706006da2fbd2.svg)

Suppose also that we are given the following system of equations that connects the columns of $Q$ and the columns of $A{:}$  

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{q}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{a}_{1} \\ {q}_{2}=\frac{1}{3}{a}_{2}+3{q}_{1} \\ {q}_{3}=\frac{1}{4}{a}_{3}-2{q}_{1}+{q}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

How do we find $R?$
First, let's rewrite the vectors $\mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2, \mathbf{a}_3$ as a linear combination of the vectors $\mathbf{q}_1, \mathbf{q}_2, \mathbf{q}_3 \mathbin{:}$
![](images/82/824c39c97bb115768856d672b39be8f65d8b4ecbc2ee5d6ccc9f4943594cbacd.svg)

In this new system, the coefficients of $\mathbf{q}_1$ correspond to the first-row entries of $R,$ the coefficients of $\mathbf{q}_2$ correspond to the second-row entries of $R,$ and the coefficients of $\mathbf{q}_3$ correspond to the third-row entries of $R.$ Therefore,

![](images/5b/5ba9887a4d9b47963af171e9275319a2564eca5a4ef8b3ef44978e2ff4b111d9.svg)

To see why this is, we can take the transpose of both sides of $A=QR{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =QR \\ {A}^{T} & =(QR)^{T} \\ {A}^{T} & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T} \\ \overset{{A}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}-\,\,\,\, & {a}_{1} & \,\,\,\,- \\ -\,\,\,\, & {a}_{2} & \,\,\,\,- \\ -\,\,\,\, & {a}_{3} & \,\,\,\,-\end{bmatrix}}} & =\overset{{R}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & 0 \\ -9 & 3 & 0 \\ 8 & -4 & 4\end{bmatrix}}}\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}-\,\,\,\, & {q}_{1} & \,\,\,\,- \\ -\,\,\,\, & {q}_{2} & \,\,\,\,- \\ -\,\,\,\, & {q}_{3} & \,\,\,\,-\end{bmatrix}}}\end{aligned}
$$

If we were to expand this matrix product, we would obtain our system of equations." :tutorial/id #uuid "9a6d9a3e-33d4-52e8-b8b0-98cd20590dd6" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5018 :tutorial/title "Interpreting Relations Between Two Bases as Matrix Multiplication"} :step/id #uuid "fdc0053f-e37d-51ef-835e-365ca5c6da98" :step/math-academy-id 31389 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134732}} {:db/id 17592186134803 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135099 :tutorial/content "Let's now go through the QR factorization algorithm to find the factorization of the matrix

![](images/f0/f0d468f6bce43491b3f97d10185f4393ae8e64198e24bb7708ad66ec57c73df4.svg)

**Step 1**. Orthogonalize the columns of $A$ to get the columns of $Q.$ Using the Gram-Schmidt process, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{1}=\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{bmatrix},\,{q}_{2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**. Compute $R=Q^TA.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}R=\begin{bmatrix}6 & 3 \\ 0 & \sqrt{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 1**. Orthogonalize the columns of $A$ to get the columns of $Q.$ Using the Gram-Schmidt process, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{1}=\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{bmatrix},\,{q}_{2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**. Compute $R=Q^TA.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}R=\begin{bmatrix}6 & 3 \\ 0 & \sqrt{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{q}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{a}_{1} \\ {q}_{2}=\frac{1}{3}{a}_{2}+3{q}_{1} \\ {q}_{3}=\frac{1}{4}{a}_{3}-2{q}_{1}+{q}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

How do we find $R?$
First, let's rewrite the vectors $\mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2, \mathbf{a}_3$ as a linear combination of the vectors $\mathbf{q}_1, \mathbf{q}_2, \mathbf{q}_3 \mathbin{:}$

To see why this is, we can take the transpose of both sides of $A=QR{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =QR \\ {A}^{T} & =(QR)^{T} \\ {A}^{T} & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T} \\ \overset{{A}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}-\,\,\,\, & {a}_{1} & \,\,\,\,- \\ -\,\,\,\, & {a}_{2} & \,\,\,\,- \\ -\,\,\,\, & {a}_{3} & \,\,\,\,-\end{bmatrix}}} & =\overset{{R}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & 0 \\ -9 & 3 & 0 \\ 8 & -4 & 4\end{bmatrix}}}\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}-\,\,\,\, & {q}_{1} & \,\,\,\,- \\ -\,\,\,\, & {q}_{2} & \,\,\,\,- \\ -\,\,\,\, & {q}_{3} & \,\,\,\,-\end{bmatrix}}}\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown above. $$

Now, pre-multiplying both sides of $A=QR$ by ${Q}^{T},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}R & ={Q}^{T}\,A \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ 0 & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 \\ -2 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{6} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{5}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

Now, pre-multiplying both sides of $A=QR$ by ${Q}^{T},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}R & ={Q}^{T}\,A \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{7}{9} & \frac{4}{9} & \frac{4}{9} \\ 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}7 & 0 \\ 4 & 1 \\ 4 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}9 & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

Consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown above. You're given that the system of equations given below connects the columns of $Q$ and the columns of $A.$  

$$

$$

$$
\overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}| & | & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} & {a}_{3} \\ | & | & |\end{bmatrix}}}=\overset{Q}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}| & | & | \\ {q}_{1} & {q}_{2} & {q}_{3} \\ | & | & |\end{bmatrix}}}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 2 & -8 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}}}

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}R & ={Q}^{T}A \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{3} & 2\sqrt{3} \\ 0 & \sqrt{6}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$

Consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown above. Given that the columns ${q}_{1},{q}_{2}$ of $Q$ were obtained from the columns of $A$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, find  the value of ${q}_{12}\cdot {r}_{22}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let ${a}_{1},{a}_{2}$ be the columns of $A.$

First, we find an orthonormal basis of $\text{Col}(A)=\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ using the Gram-Schmidt process.

**Step 1**. We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 3 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.$

**Step 2**. We find the vector ${v}_{2}$ orthogonal to $\text{Span}\{{v}_{1}\}$ using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}{a}_{2} \\  & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}-(-\frac{6}{18})\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 3 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 3 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we normalize ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 3 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\ {q}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute $R:$

$$
\begin{aligned}R & ={Q}^{T}\,A \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 3 & 0 \\ 3 & -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3\sqrt{2} & -\sqrt{2} \\ 0 & 3\sqrt{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following QR factorization of $A:$

$$
\overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 3 & 0 \\ 3 & -2\end{bmatrix}}}=\overset{Q}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}0 & \frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}}}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}3\sqrt{2} & -\sqrt{2} \\ 0 & 3\sqrt{2}\end{bmatrix}}}.
$$

Finally, ${q}_{12}\cdot {r}_{22}=(\frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}})\cdot (3\sqrt{2})=4.$"} :step/id #uuid "aaefce95-2575-5d4e-9758-6032bf02fe49"} {:db/id 17592186442812 :step/content {:db/id 17592186134354 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5efe4aae-2768-528f-a3cc-4c9b9a907391" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186379830} {:answer/id #uuid "a5705d08-f2bc-5a4f-b1ab-65641a5b0ae3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "26" :db/id 17592186379831} {:answer/id #uuid "bf62a0e5-63e3-5e42-889b-986f2738de40" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-20" :db/id 17592186379832} {:answer/id #uuid "e87b5762-481c-57bd-ba1b-c18fef4d4c0f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4" :db/id 17592186379833} {:answer/id #uuid "411c482c-f2e8-5cb9-b82c-84752b240dce" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186379834}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186379831} :answer-field/id #uuid "a20ad309-608a-5c10-aca7-0636d5c13dac" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186379829}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "9fc92fc5-cd9a-5882-b3a5-3c9b7ba00cb3" :question/math-academy-id "q-41417" :question/problem "$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

![](images/c0/c0ed78e2e640611d70263e17a76eb4a13e9e2816efba02494b53e540d38065d6.png)" :question/worked-solution "As $x$ approaches $0$, the value of $f(x)$ approaches $1$. Consequently,

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,0}f(x)= 1\,
$$

Remember, it does not matter that the actual value of $f(0)$ is $2$. All that matters is that as $x$ approaches $0$, the function $f(x)$ *looks like* it is getting closer and closer to $1$."} {:db/id 17592186069093 :question/id #uuid "4b624718-54bc-577c-bda1-017c8cf28e46" :question/math-academy-id "q-16261"} {:db/id 17592186069094 :question/id #uuid "9fa81edb-a127-519d-b9d1-759d92ae8eee" :question/math-academy-id "q-16266"} {:db/id 17592186068795 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186068534 :question/id #uuid "ab95d805-958c-5de3-99bd-41368cc57080" :question/math-academy-id "e-3"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "851c841f-6e27-5f81-8a0d-0f2439ae3e61" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186069274 :question/id #uuid "bbc80124-17c2-585a-8280-2acdc4c9d707" :question/math-academy-id "q-34840"} {:db/id 17592186069276 :question/id #uuid "7a5fdf11-243e-52ee-a4a4-937c2603f07f" :question/math-academy-id "q-34932"} {:db/id 17592186233090 :question/id #uuid "7dee115c-2d20-5ec2-8285-ad5a690a282f" :question/math-academy-id "q-106090"}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying True Statements About Limits"} {:db/id 17592186068534 :question/id #uuid "ab95d805-958c-5de3-99bd-41368cc57080" :question/math-academy-id "e-3" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186068795 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "851c841f-6e27-5f81-8a0d-0f2439ae3e61" :knowledge-point/title "Identifying True Statements About Limits"}] :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true concerning the function $y=f(x)$ whose graph is shown below?

1. $\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,0}f(x)=0$
2. $\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,3}f(x)=0$
3. $\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,-1}f(x)=\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,1}f(x)$

![](images/68/68241f3cd913cd91d10765499dc4ce4398fb3e8a81ec4bcfb65b47c0d77731d6.png)" :question/worked-solution "Let's analyze each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. As $x$ approaches $0$, the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=-1$. Consequently,
$\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,0}f(x)=-1$.
- Statement II is true. As $x$ approaches $3$, the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=0$. Consequently,
$\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,3}f(x)=0$.
- Statement III is false. As $x$ approaches $-1$ the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=2$, and consequently
$\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,-1}f(x)=2$.
Similiarly, as $x$ approaches $1$, the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=-2$, and consequently
$\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,1}f(x)=-2$.
As a result,
$\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,-1}f(x)\ne\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,1}f(x)$.

In conclusion, only statement II is true."} {:db/id 17592186069274 :question/id #uuid "bbc80124-17c2-585a-8280-2acdc4c9d707" :question/math-academy-id "q-34840"} {:db/id 17592186069276 :question/id #uuid "7a5fdf11-243e-52ee-a4a4-937c2603f07f" :question/math-academy-id "q-34932"} {:db/id 17592186233090 :question/id #uuid "7dee115c-2d20-5ec2-8285-ad5a690a282f" :question/math-academy-id "q-106090"} {:db/id 17592186050259} {:db/id 17592186050454} {:activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186069709} :activity/id #uuid "c2e3d487-c981-55e6-ba25-8949d030cfa3" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186050274 :topic/id #uuid "3bdc5470-2e0b-5f3c-9875-854353ddeb19" :topic/math-academy-id 461} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186069709 :step/content {:db/id 17592186069928 :tutorial/content "The **limit** of a function is the value that the function approaches. For example, the function $y=f(x)$ shown below is not defined at $x=2$, as represented by the open circle there $-$ but when we *approach* $x=2$, we see that $f(x)$ *approaches* the value $y=1$.

![](images/f7/f7081d649c6cdfa0a19a0fb2de93b97ee700ad922f34530c7f3e5c2a3228c9fb.png)

As $x$ approaches $2$, the value of $f(x)$ approaches $1$. In other words, the limit of $f(x)$, as $x$ approaches $2$, is $1$. We can express this mathematically as

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 2}f(x)=1 \,
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e52528a2-ed6a-5d07-89d4-1a74d70eb6b9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 138 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "309b25fa-6c05-5421-8f80-e956e2975682" :step/math-academy-id 256 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069713}} {:db/id 17592186069713 :step/content {:db/id 17592186068791 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186068428 :question/id #uuid "282add39-5184-589e-bb7b-b87a59cd41e6" :question/math-academy-id "e-1"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "607443d5-b1dd-56b1-919b-fcc652ac3bc9" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048652} {:db/id 17592186049534}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186069091} {:db/id 17592186069092}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Limit When the Function Value is Not Defined"} :step/id #uuid "01fbff48-2ebc-5e33-a1b9-e271896f5340" :step/math-academy-id 257 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069717}} {:db/id 17592186069714 :step/content {:db/id 17592186068792 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186068533 :question/id #uuid "fb401fbe-a718-5ea7-b598-139ef837b047" :question/math-academy-id "e-2"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e5fe1482-00d6-5738-b56a-8c082912d8d7" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186069093} {:db/id 17592186069094}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Limit When the Limit is Not Equal to the Function Value"} :step/id #uuid "9144fd7b-81d4-5cb5-8051-0619e464002c" :step/math-academy-id 260 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069718}} {:db/id 17592186069717 :step/content {:db/id 17592186069924 :tutorial/content "The limit of a function at some point has **nothing to do** with the value of the function at that point.

For example, the following functions $g(x)$ and $h(x)$ have *different values* at $x=2$, but they have the *same limit* at $x=2$.

![](images/6a/6a73b74072a8a990c91a38553d519f4913370d34ef0251b7e45cc664da40517d.png)

![](images/06/06e150aacae774b4fe883a2750ef13cebbddf2ea871e5a682f2587c47a54615a.png)

The actual values of $g(2)$ and $h(2)$ are irrelevant for determining the limit at $x=2$. All that matters is what values the functions *look like* they are approaching as $x$ approaches $2$.

Near $x=2$, both $g(x)$ and $h(x)$ appear to be approaching $y=1$. Therefore,

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 2}g(x)=1
$$

and

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 2}h(x)=1 \,
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "ea300af0-adfe-5df2-8b4d-ae23430245a7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1333 :tutorial/title "Limit Has Nothing to Do with Function Value"} :step/id #uuid "d21275b2-0542-5145-8c14-535a8c0db329" :step/math-academy-id 2621 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069714}} {:db/id 17592186069718 :step/content {:db/id 17592186068795 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186068534 :question/id #uuid "ab95d805-958c-5de3-99bd-41368cc57080" :question/math-academy-id "e-3"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "851c841f-6e27-5f81-8a0d-0f2439ae3e61" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186069274} {:db/id 17592186069276} {:db/id 17592186233090}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying True Statements About Limits"} :step/id #uuid "0447b7b5-01f2-52cd-851f-84ee0d719836" :step/math-academy-id 263}] :activity/title "The Finite Limit of a Function" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186068988} {:db/id 17592186069709 :step/content {:db/id 17592186069928 :tutorial/content "The **limit** of a function is the value that the function approaches. ![](images/53/536069f862ae1044f9e924714ef3e2327c17b632a1b5da336ffac30f50fcf783.png)" :question/worked-solution "Two vectors are equal if and only if they lie on parallel lines and have both the same magnitude and the same direction.

The vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{e}$ are parallel and have the same direction and magnitude, hence

$$
\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{e}
$$

Similarly, $\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{d}$ are parallel and have the same direction and magnitude, hence

$$
\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{d}
$$

On the other hand,

$$
\mathbf{a} \neq \mathbf{b}
$$

,

$$
\mathbf{a} \neq \mathbf{c}
$$

and

$$
\mathbf{b} \neq \mathbf{c}
$$

because they are not parallel.

Therefore, we get

$$
\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{e}
$$

and

$$
\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{d}
$$

only.

**magnitude.** We can think of a vector as a "directed line segment".

For example, consider a ship that travels $15\:\textrm{km}$ due east. In the diagram below, the ship starts at the point $A$ and ends at the point $B$. This information can be represented as a **vector**, a directed line segment that starts at $A$ and points to $B$, as follows:

![](images/5c/5c12cfd2657f42293b2ee53fd2a4aede2f0325233305be9ac9bc0b5620391654.png)

The vector itself represents the **displacement** of the ship. The magnitude (length) of the vector represents the total distance traveled, and the direction of the vector gives the direction of travel.

The **tail** of the vector is at the point $A$. The **head** of the vector is at the point $B$.

The vector can be written using its endpoints as $\overrightarrow{AB}$. We can also represent vectors using lowercase letters written in bold, such as $\mathbf{a}$, $\mathbf{b}$, $\mathbf{c}$." :tutorial/id #uuid "6ccac1e4-068b-5d32-9511-15bcc9142591" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2899 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "2f547b48-2d83-5acb-bfd1-ba058d79863a" :step/math-academy-id 15682 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097465}} {:db/id 17592186097465 :step/content {:db/id 17592186096640 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186096437 :question/id #uuid "5987eb83-0b8c-54f9-8295-2b25c677c855" :question/math-academy-id "e-4270"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "6a0610a8-fff6-5365-be0f-1f4524fbf7a1" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048587} {:db/id 17592186050563}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186096952} {:db/id 17592186096987}] :knowledge-point/title "Drawing Vectors Representing Displacements"} :step/id #uuid "defe8630-5cba-584a-874a-00e5bedf61b4" :step/math-academy-id 15683 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097466}} {:db/id 17592186097466 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097827 :tutorial/content "Two vectors are **equal** if they have both the same magnitude and the same direction. As an example, let's consider the rule defined by

$$
f(x) = x+3
$$

where $x$ can be any number from the **set** $\{1,2,3,4\}.$ A set is a collection of numbers we can use in our rule. 

Let's calculate the possible values of $f(x)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1) & =1+3=4 \\ f(2) & =2+3=5 \\ f(3) & =3+3=6 \\ f(4) & =4+3=7\end{aligned}
$$

We can represent this rule using a **mapping diagram**, like the one shown below.

![](images/47/4714001592222932934cb7edd5852542a2e990e6680daad85e2db88b9c7cef47.png)

$$

$$

$$
f(x)={x}^{2}{y}^{3},\,x=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix},
$$

calculate ${f}^{′}(x).$" :question/worked-solution "Suppose a transformation $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{m}$ is defined by 

$$
f:\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}{f}_{1}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ {f}_{2}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ ⋮ \\ {f}_{m}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

where ${f}_{1},{f}_{2},…,{f}_{m}$ are scalar functions with $n$ variables. If $f$ is differentiable at $x,$ then the total derivative of $f$ at $x,$ denoted ${f}^{′}(x),$ is given by the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{y}^{3})=2x{y}^{3}, & \,\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}{y}^{3})=3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}2x{y}^{3} & 3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186367755 :question/id #uuid "8b1abcc3-d245-53a5-9c03-cbdd810d6090" :question/math-academy-id "q-163035"} {:db/id 17592186367762 :question/id #uuid From top to bottom, what are the missing entries?" :question/worked-solution "Suppose a transformation $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{m}$ is defined by 

$$
f:\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}{f}_{1}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ {f}_{2}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ ⋮ \\ {f}_{m}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

where ${f}_{1},{f}_{2},…,{f}_{m}$ are scalar functions with $n$ variables. If $f$ is differentiable at $x,$ then the total derivative of $f$ at $x,$ denoted ${f}^{′}(x),$ is given by the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy)=y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy)=x, \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-y)=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-y)=-1, \\ \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy))=y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy),\, & \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy))=x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}y & x \\ 2x & -1 \\ y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy) & x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Thus, the missing entries are $x,\,$ $2x,\,$ and $y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy).$"} {:db/id 17592186401412 :question/id #uuid "e4436f3f-18fe-5775-815d-04fe166d17a2" :question/math-academy-id "q-163100"} $$
f:\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}{f}_{1}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ {f}_{2}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ ⋮ \\ {f}_{m}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

where ${f}_{1},{f}_{2},…,{f}_{m}$ are scalar functions with $n$ variables. If $f$ is differentiable at $x,$ then the total derivative of $f$ at $x,$ denoted ${f}^{′}(x),$ is given by the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{x}+y)={e}^{x},\, & \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x}+y)=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{x} & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Evaluating $f$ and its derivative at $x=a=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},$ we have

$$
f(a)=2,\,{f}^{′}(a)=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The tangent to $f$ at $x=a$ is given by

$$
z-f(a)={f}^{′}(a)(x-a).
$$

Substituting $f(a),$ ${f}^{′}(a),$ and $a$ in the equation above, we obtain

$$
z-2=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1\end{bmatrix}(\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}).
$$

Therefore, the sum of the missing values is

$$
2+1+1=4.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186281584 :question/id #uuid "723c2fc9-85ff-54eb-a36d-e043eb14286d" :question/math-academy-id "q-163056"} {:db/id 17592186281585 :question/id #uuid "0b9a1de6-0ca7-5f4f-b40d-58cbe6ce207e" :question/math-academy-id "q-163058"} {:db/id 17592186281589 :question/id #uuid "1f8309ca-8cff-5376-85e1-fbcd4f2e85f6" :question/math-academy-id "q-163075" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "253a5862-fe76-59bf-bc9f-e5b4c2c81cb1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2+\frac{\pi }{4}" :db/id 17592186278922} {:answer/id #uuid "38badd4c-30f8-554d-b11b-dbcc78a85dd3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186279087} {:answer/id #uuid "6d9f3b1d-5608-5c20-993b-fb7acb5da074" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7" :db/id 17592186279590} {:answer/id #uuid "a4996288-fed0-5a92-95cf-6f46d536635d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186280051} {:answer/id #uuid "d76a9632-4cec-5ffa-99d2-34ae09bdb959" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186280496}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279590} :answer-field/id #uuid "c588e84a-c201-5164-ad12-e6f62f15b38b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281179}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Consider the function $f:{R}^{2}\to R,$ defined as

$$
f:\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}{f}_{1}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ {f}_{2}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ ⋮ \\ {f}_{m}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

where ${f}_{1},{f}_{2},…,{f}_{m}$ are scalar functions with $n$ variables. If $f$ is differentiable at $x,$ then the total derivative of $f$ at $x,$ denoted ${f}^{′}(x),$ is given by the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\operatorname{tan}⁡x)=\frac{y}{{cos}^{2}⁡x},\, & \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y\operatorname{tan}⁡x)=\operatorname{tan}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{y}{{cos}^{2}⁡x} & \operatorname{tan}⁡x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Evaluating $f$ and its derivative at $x=a=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\pi }{4} \\ 2\end{bmatrix},$ we have

$$
f(a)=2,\,{f}^{′}(a)=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The tangent to $f$ at $x=a$ is given by

$$
z-f(a)={f}^{′}(a)(x-a).
$$

Substituting $f(a),$ ${f}^{′}(a),$ and $a$ in the equation above, we obtain

$$
z-2=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1\end{bmatrix}(\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\pi }{4} \\ 2\end{bmatrix}).
$$

Therefore, the sum of the missing values is

$$

$$

If the tangent to $f$ at $a=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ is given by

what is the sum of the missing values?" :question/worked-solution "Suppose a transformation $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{m}$ is defined by 

$$
f:\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}{f}_{1}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ {f}_{2}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ ⋮ \\ {f}_{m}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

where ${f}_{1},{f}_{2},…,{f}_{m}$ are scalar functions with $n$ variables. If $f$ is differentiable at $x,$ then the total derivative of $f$ at $x,$ denoted ${f}^{′}(x),$ is given by the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+xy)=2x+y,\, & \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+xy)=x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}2x+y & x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Evaluating $f$ and its derivative at $x=a=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},$ we have

$$
f(a)=2,\,{f}^{′}(a)=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The tangent to $f$ at $x=a$ is given by

$$
z-f(a)={f}^{′}(a)(x-a).
$$

Substituting $f(a),$ ${f}^{′}(a),$ and $a$ in the equation above, we obtain

$$
z-2=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & -2\end{bmatrix}(\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}).
$$

Therefore, the sum of the missing values is

$$
2+(-3)+(-2)=-3.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186367776 :question/id #uuid "b09db73d-f8e6-5800-82db-d1d7aaa24e92" :question/math-academy-id "q-163072"} {:db/id 17592186367783 :question/id #uuid "f9d94cbd-ee2b-5982-acfb-18c8cc38370a" :question/math-academy-id "q-163073" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "78256e55-f9c0-5f25-9bce-75879edc9fd2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186367785} {:answer/id #uuid "ba371be4-a3c4-507f-8f66-4f2055137231" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186367786} {:answer/id #uuid "f4193f0d-676e-5937-aff3-0523d50d7633" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186367787} {:answer/id #uuid "14823d05-96e6-5666-b344-a9dccb8d3e57" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186367788} {:answer/id #uuid "6f5b3af7-e5e3-5a46-ba00-2dda1f55acee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186367789}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186367786} :answer-field/id #uuid "c371aaec-d4e5-5c39-a2b8-4eb96f2445c2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186367784}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Consider the function $f:{R}^{2}\to R,$ defined as

If the tangent to $f$ at $a=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ is given by

$$
z-∗=\begin{bmatrix}∗ & ∗\end{bmatrix}(\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix})
$$

what is the sum of the missing values?" :question/worked-solution "Suppose a transformation $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{m}$ is defined by 

$$
f:\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}{f}_{1}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ {f}_{2}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ ⋮ \\ {f}_{m}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

where ${f}_{1},{f}_{2},…,{f}_{m}$ are scalar functions with $n$ variables. If $f$ is differentiable at $x,$ then the total derivative of $f$ at $x,$ denoted ${f}^{′}(x),$ is given by the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+1})=-\frac{2xy}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}},\, & \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+1})=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2xy}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}} & \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Evaluating $f$ and its derivative at $x=a=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},$ we have

$$
f(a)=0,\,{f}^{′}(a)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & \frac{1}{2}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The tangent to $f$ at $x=a$ is given by

$$
z-f(a)={f}^{′}(a)(x-a).
$$

Substituting $f(a),$ ${f}^{′}(a),$ and $a$ in the equation above, we obtain

$$
z-0=\begin{bmatrix}0 & \frac{1}{2}\end{bmatrix}(\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}).
$$

Therefore, the sum of the missing values is

$$
0+0+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186367790 :question/id #uuid "08e9a1c4-09e3-536e-9e2b-e51736b93226" :question/math-academy-id "q-163074"} {:db/id 17592186434998 :question/id #uuid $$
f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1),\,x=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}.
$$

If the tangent to $f$ at $a=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}$ is given by

$$
z-∗=\begin{bmatrix}∗ & ∗\end{bmatrix}(\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix})

what is the sum of the missing values?" :question/worked-solution "Suppose a transformation $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{m}$ is defined by 

$$
f:\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}{f}_{1}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ {f}_{2}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ ⋮ \\ {f}_{m}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

where ${f}_{1},{f}_{2},…,{f}_{m}$ are scalar functions with $n$ variables. If $f$ is differentiable at $x,$ then the total derivative of $f$ at $x,$ denoted ${f}^{′}(x),$ is given by the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)=\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1},\, & \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)=\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1} & \frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Evaluating $f$ and its derivative at $x=a=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix},$ we have

$$
f(a)=\operatorname{ln}⁡6,\,{f}^{′}(a)=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{3} & \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The tangent to $f$ at $x=a$ is given by

$$
z-f(a)={f}^{′}(a)(x-a).
$$

Substituting $f(a),$ ${f}^{′}(a),$ and $a$ in the equation above, we obtain

$$
z-\operatorname{ln}⁡6=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{3} & \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}(\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}).
$$

Therefore, the sum of the missing values is

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡6+(-\frac{1}{3})+\frac{2}{3}=\operatorname{ln}⁡6+\frac{1}{3}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186198414 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198056 :question/id #uuid "f3540571-9159-50b4-a46c-4cf28a454602" :question/math-academy-id "e-12484"} :knowledge-point/id $$
f:\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}{f}_{1}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ {f}_{2}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ ⋮ \\ {f}_{m}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

where ${f}_{1},{f}_{2},…,{f}_{m}$ are scalar functions with $n$ variables. If $f$ is differentiable at $x,$ then the total derivative of $f$ at $x,$ denoted ${f}^{′}(x),$ is given by the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & =\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{1})+{x}_{2})=\frac{1}{{x}_{1}},\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{1})+{x}_{2})=1 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & =\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{2}^{2}+1)=0,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{2}^{2}+1)=2{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}^{-1} & 1 \\ 0 & 2{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

$$
f(a)=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix},\,{f}^{′}(a)=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-1} & 1 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}.

$$

$$
f(x)≈\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-1} & 1 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}(x-\begin{bmatrix}e \\ -1\end{bmatrix}).
$$

$$

4169} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186199335 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199487 :tutorial/content "We've spent some time studying so-called **plane transformations** of the form

$$
\mathbf T: \mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2.
$$

In this lesson, we'll generalize our understanding of derivatives to transformations (or functions) of the form 

$$
\boldsymbol f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m.
$$

To motivate the discussion, we start by considering functions of one variable. 

Recall that a function $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is **differentiable** at a point $x = a$ if there exists a number $f'(a)$, called the **derivative** of $f$ at $a$, such that

$$
f'(a) = \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a}.
$$

We can restate this definition by applying basic algebraic properties of limits.

Since the left-hand side, $f'(a)$, is just a constant, we can rewrite the equation as

$$
\lim_{x \to a} f'(a) = \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a},
$$

using the fact that the limit of a constant is the constant itself.

Bringing all terms to one side, we obtain

$$
\lim_{x \to a} \left( \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a} - f'(a) \right) = 0,
$$

which can be rearranged as

$$
\lim_{x \to a} \left( \frac{f(x) - f(a) - f'(a)(x - a)}{x - a} \right) = 0.
$$

This final expression tells us that the difference between $f(x)$ and its *linear approximation* $f(a) + f'(a)(x - a)$ becomes negligible relative to $x - a$ as $x$ approaches $a$.

In other words, not only does $f(x)$ become close to $f(a) + f'(a)(x-a)$ near $a$, but the error between them shrinks *faster than* the distance $|x - a|$ itself.

Let's see how we can generalize this definition to vector-valued functions." :tutorial/id #uuid "a9769637-9fcb-5829-817e-f82930d6d99b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7762 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} 17592186199340 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199488 :tutorial/content "The equation of the tangent plane to a surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $(x_0,y_0,z_0),$ where $z_0=f(x_0,y_0),$ is given by

$$
z - z_0 = (x-x_0) \cdot \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0) \cdot \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0).
$$

Let's express this equation in terms of the total derivative.

Writing our multivariable function $f:\mathbb R^2 \to \mathbb R$ as $f\left(\mathbf x \right),$ where ![](images/88/88f9f758bffba384670449973c5c89edae05c67268d2914a12801b21b60a319f.svg) the total derivative of $f$ is given by

![](images/56/56dc34676135e9c35b9e08cff732715c5d878d4a19f4fee6625384460ed6ee5f.svg)

Let ![](images/ca/ca5b0074c216a3235f015d7b96dece9ffc6fc50eecbdd0b5e97dfbd89eb446fa.svg) Then, we can re-write the equation of the tangent plane as a matrix equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-{z}_{0} & =(x-{x}_{0})\cdot \frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\cdot \frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}) \\ z-{z}_{0} & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}) & \frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}x-{x}_{0} \\ y-{y}_{0}\end{bmatrix} \\ z-f({x}_{0},{y}_{0}) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}) & \frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})\end{bmatrix}\cdot (\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{0} \\ {y}_{0}\end{bmatrix}) \\ z-f(a) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(a) & \frac{∂f}{∂y}(a)\end{bmatrix}\cdot (x-a) \\ z-f(a) & ={f}^{′}(a)(x-a)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane to $f:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ at $\mathbf x = \mathbf{a},$ in matrix form, is given by

$$
z - f(\mathbf a) = \boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf a)(\mathbf x - \mathbf a).
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "15747496-662a-5601-8abc-953fd6f5a43b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7764 :tutorial/title "The Tangent Plane to the Graph of a Scalar Function"} :step/id #uuid "67589fc2-05c5-57f9-9944-a77ae10109f1" :step/math-academy-id 44948 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199338}} {:db/id 17592186199341 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199489 :tutorial/content "If $f:\mathbb R \to \mathbb R$ is differentiable at $x=a,$ then for points close to $x=a,$ we have the linear approximation

$$
f(x) \approx f(a) + f'(a)(x-a).
$$

We have a similar result for transformations of the form $\boldsymbol{f}:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m.$

If $\boldsymbol f:\mathbb R^n \to \mathbb R^m$ is differentiable at $\mathbf x=\mathbf a,$ then for points close to $\mathbf x=\mathbf a,$ we have the linear approximation

$$
\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf x) \approx \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf a) + \boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf a)(\mathbf x - \mathbf a).
$$

 

Notice that this approximation for $\boldsymbol f$ is affine. Thus, if a function is differentiable at a point $\mathbf x = \mathbf a,$ it is **locally affine** in a neighborhood of $\mathbf x = \mathbf a.$ 

Let's see some examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "4f9fb273-0149-5dca-a967-7bb027abab86" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7765 :tutorial/title "Affine Approximations of Vector Functions"} :step/id #uuid "322a9f6a-d0e4-5c2f-b7dd-5ac1d040f24a" :step/math-academy-id 44949 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199339}} {:db/id 17592186199362 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199495 :tutorial/content "Suppose that a transformation (or function) $\boldsymbol f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ is defined by 

![](images/cd/cd9132d6a0e934349ae58a0718e6320cba3dd8ae84de7df2e3fb98b391256b57.svg) 

where $f_1,f_2,\ldots,f_m$ are scalar functions of $n$ variables. 
We say that $\boldsymbol{f}$ is **differentiable** at a point $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ if there exists an $m \times n$ matrix $\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a})$, called the **total derivative** of $\boldsymbol{f}$ at $\mathbf{a}$, such that

$$
\lim_{\mathbf{x} \to \mathbf{a}}
\frac{
\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}) - \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{a}) - \boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a})
}{
||\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}||
}
= \mathbf{0}.
$$

In other words, near $\mathbf{a}$, the function $\boldsymbol{f}$ is well-approximated by the linear map

$$
\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{a}) + \boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}),
$$

and the error between $\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x})$ and this linear approximation becomes negligible compared to the distance $\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}\|$ as $\mathbf{x}$ approaches $\mathbf{a}$.

If $\boldsymbol{f}$ is differentiable at $\mathbf{x},$ then the total derivative of $\boldsymbol f$ is given by the matrix

![](images/6b/6bd7bcfb4e48c1833ff57c614bb18f469ca0a17e8a6e29d730b9e940c2f58984.svg)

Note the following:

- We sometimes refer to $\boldsymbol f'(\mathbf x)$ simply as **the derivative** of $\boldsymbol f(\mathbf x).$

- For scalar-valued functions of the form $f: \mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R,$ the total derivative is the *transpose* of the gradient vector:

$$
\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf a) = \left(\nabla f \right)^T(\mathbf a)
$$

- For vector-valued functions $\boldsymbol f: \mathbb R\to\mathbb R^n$ of a single parameter $t,$ the total derivative at $t=a$ is the usual column vector containing the partial derivatives of the components of $f{:}$
![](images/27/27651b3ca026cad63ee6cbbd88162d3ce85b9afc642986daf0ae76c6519bdc38.svg)

- For functions of the form $\boldsymbol f: \mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2,$ the *determinant* of this matrix is the corresponding Jacobian: 

$$
\det\left(\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf a)\right)  = \dfrac{\partial (f_1,f_2)}{\partial (x_1,x_2)}
$$

Similarly, for functions of the form $\boldsymbol f: \mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3,$ the *determinant* of this matrix is the corresponding Jacobian: 

$$
\det\left(\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf a)\right)  = \dfrac{\partial (f_1,f_2,f_3)}{\partial (x_1,x_2,x_3)}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "fb0be5f3-0f3d-5c1f-81f5-97faa1864dc1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7793 :tutorial/title "Defining the Total Derivative"} :step/id #uuid "19886282-4967-5610-ab9e-7c0b0a12ce44" :step/math-academy-id 45103 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199336}}] :activity/title "The Derivative of a Multivariable Function" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186198497} {:db/id 17592186199335 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199487 :tutorial/content "We've spent some time studying so-called **plane transformations** of the form

17592186199340 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199488 :tutorial/content "The equation of the tangent plane to a surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $(x_0,y_0,z_0),$ where $z_0=f(x_0,y_0),$ is given by

$$
z - z_0 = (x-x_0) \cdot \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0) \cdot \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0).
$$

Let's express this equation in terms of the total derivative.

Writing our multivariable function $f:\mathbb R^2 \to \mathbb R$ as $f\left(\mathbf x \right),$ where ![](images/88/88f9f758bffba384670449973c5c89edae05c67268d2914a12801b21b60a319f.svg) the total derivative of $f$ is given by

![](images/56/56dc34676135e9c35b9e08cff732715c5d878d4a19f4fee6625384460ed6ee5f.svg)

Let ![](images/ca/ca5b0074c216a3235f015d7b96dece9ffc6fc50eecbdd0b5e97dfbd89eb446fa.svg) Then, we can re-write the equation of the tangent plane as a matrix equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-{z}_{0} & =(x-{x}_{0})\cdot \frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\cdot \frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}) \\ z-{z}_{0} & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}) & \frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}x-{x}_{0} \\ y-{y}_{0}\end{bmatrix} \\ z-f({x}_{0},{y}_{0}) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}) & \frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})\end{bmatrix}\cdot (\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{0} \\ {y}_{0}\end{bmatrix}) \\ z-f(a) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(a) & \frac{∂f}{∂y}(a)\end{bmatrix}\cdot (x-a) \\ z-f(a) & ={f}^{′}(a)(x-a)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane to $f:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ at $\mathbf x = \mathbf{a},$ in matrix form, is given by

$$
z - f(\mathbf a) = \boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf a)(\mathbf x - \mathbf a).
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "15747496-662a-5601-8abc-953fd6f5a43b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7764 :tutorial/title "The Tangent Plane to the Graph of a Scalar Function"} :step/id #uuid "67589fc2-05c5-57f9-9944-a77ae10109f1" :step/math-academy-id 44948 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199338}} {:db/id 17592186199338 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198413 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198055 :question/id #uuid "db0be438-94fe-52de-9daf-60d1727ce7b9" :question/math-academy-id "e-12479"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0e90349c-33ae-5b60-9d0d-7542dfebbbc7" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050293}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198636} {:db/id 17592186198653} {:db/id 17592186281584} {:db/id 17592186281585} {:db/id 17592186281589} {:db/id 17592186281590} {:db/id 17592186281591} {:db/id 17592186367776} {:db/id 17592186367783} {:db/id 17592186367790} {:db/id 17592186434998}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Tangent Plane to the Graph of a Scalar Function in Matrix Form"} :step/id #uuid "cc985165-12b8-5db0-9db3-3f6ef902bc46" :step/math-academy-id 44926 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199341}} {:db/id 17592186199341 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199489 :tutorial/content "If $f:\mathbb R \to \mathbb R$ is differentiable at $x=a,$ then for points close to $x=a,$ we have the linear approximation

$$
f(x) \approx f(a) + f'(a)(x-a).
$$

We have a similar result for transformations of the form $\boldsymbol{f}:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m.$

If $\boldsymbol f:\mathbb R^n \to \mathbb R^m$ is differentiable at $\mathbf x=\mathbf a,$ then for points close to $\mathbf x=\mathbf a,$ we have the linear approximation

$$
\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf x) \approx \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf a) + \boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf a)(\mathbf x - \mathbf a).
$$

 

Notice that this approximation for $\boldsymbol f$ is affine. Thus, if a function is differentiable at a point $\mathbf x = \mathbf a,$ it is **locally affine** in a neighborhood of $\mathbf x = \mathbf a.$ 

Let's see some examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "4f9fb273-0149-5dca-a967-7bb027abab86" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7765 :tutorial/title "Affine Approximations of Vector Functions"} :step/id #uuid "322a9f6a-d0e4-5c2f-b7dd-5ac1d040f24a" :step/math-academy-id 44949 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199339}} {:db/id 17592186199339 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198414 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198056 :question/id #uuid "f3540571-9159-50b4-a46c-4cf28a454602" :question/math-academy-id "e-12484"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9f09fc28-bdce-554f-98f5-019d34542a13" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049012}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198635} {:db/id 17592186198656} {:db/id 17592186281597} {:db/id 17592186281598} {:db/id 17592186281617} {:db/id 17592186281618} {:db/id 17592186367797} {:db/id 17592186367818} {:db/id 17592186367832} {:db/id 17592186442218}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding an Affine Approximation of a Vector Function"} :step/id #uuid "2a4a2d6d-09ba-598c-aec7-fedd75d2da7e" :step/math-academy-id 44947} {:db/id 17592186199488 :tutorial/content "The equation of the tangent plane to a surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $(x_0,y_0,z_0),$ where $z_0=f(x_0,y_0),$ is given by

Let's see some examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "4f9fb273-0149-5dca-a967-7bb027abab86" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7765 :tutorial/title "Affine Approximations of Vector Functions"} {:db/id 17592186199495 :tutorial/content "Suppose that a transformation (or function) $\boldsymbol f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ is defined by 

![](images/cd/cd9132d6a0e934349ae58a0718e6320cba3dd8ae84de7df2e3fb98b391256b57.svg) 

where $f_1,f_2,\ldots,f_m$ are scalar functions of $n$ variables. 
We say that $\boldsymbol{f}$ is **differentiable** at a point $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ if there exists an $m \times n$ matrix $\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a})$, called the **total derivative** of $\boldsymbol{f}$ at $\mathbf{a}$, such that

$$
\lim_{\mathbf{x} \to \mathbf{a}}
\frac{
\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}) - \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{a}) - \boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a})
}{
||\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}||
}
= \mathbf{0}.
$$

In other words, near $\mathbf{a}$, the function $\boldsymbol{f}$ is well-approximated by the linear map

$$
\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{a}) + \boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}),
$$

and the error between $\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x})$ and this linear approximation becomes negligible compared to the distance $\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}\|$ as $\mathbf{x}$ approaches $\mathbf{a}$.

If $\boldsymbol{f}$ is differentiable at $\mathbf{x},$ then the total derivative of $\boldsymbol f$ is given by the matrix

![](images/6b/6bd7bcfb4e48c1833ff57c614bb18f469ca0a17e8a6e29d730b9e940c2f58984.svg)

Note the following:

- We sometimes refer to $\boldsymbol f'(\mathbf x)$ simply as **the derivative** of $\boldsymbol f(\mathbf x).$

- For scalar-valued functions of the form $f: \mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R,$ the total derivative is the *transpose* of the gradient vector:

$$
\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf a) = \left(\nabla f \right)^T(\mathbf a)
$$

- For vector-valued functions $\boldsymbol f: \mathbb R\to\mathbb R^n$ of a single parameter $t,$ the total derivative at $t=a$ is the usual column vector containing the partial derivatives of the components of $f{:}$
![](images/27/27651b3ca026cad63ee6cbbd88162d3ce85b9afc642986daf0ae76c6519bdc38.svg)

- For functions of the form $\boldsymbol f: \mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2,$ the *determinant* of this matrix is the corresponding Jacobian: 

$$
\det\left(\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf a)\right)  = \dfrac{\partial (f_1,f_2)}{\partial (x_1,x_2)}
$$

Similarly, for functions of the form $\boldsymbol f: \mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3,$ the *determinant* of this matrix is the corresponding Jacobian: 

$$
\det\left(\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf a)\right)  = \dfrac{\partial (f_1,f_2,f_3)}{\partial (x_1,x_2,x_3)}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "fb0be5f3-0f3d-5c1f-81f5-97faa1864dc1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7793 :tutorial/title "Defining the Total Derivative"} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046659} :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186442221} :activity/id #uuid "fe2bd770-056c-540f-8c4f-31dd27239fe4" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186049962 :topic/id #uuid "220386bf-4147-5f25-bbd8-b3b4f855f1a0" :topic/math-academy-id 4169} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186442219 :step/content {:db/id 17592186367783 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "78256e55-f9c0-5f25-9bce-75879edc9fd2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186367785} {:answer/id #uuid "ba371be4-a3c4-507f-8f66-4f2055137231" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186367786} {:answer/id #uuid "f4193f0d-676e-5937-aff3-0523d50d7633" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186367787} {:answer/id #uuid "14823d05-96e6-5666-b344-a9dccb8d3e57" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186367788} {:answer/id #uuid "6f5b3af7-e5e3-5a46-ba00-2dda1f55acee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186367789}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186367786} :answer-field/id #uuid "c371aaec-d4e5-5c39-a2b8-4eb96f2445c2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186367784}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "f9d94cbd-ee2b-5982-acfb-18c8cc38370a" :question/math-academy-id "q-163073" :question/problem "Consider the function $f:{R}^{2}\to R,$ defined as

$$
f(x)=\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+1},\,x=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}.
$$

If the tangent to $f$ at $a=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ is given by

$$
z-∗=\begin{bmatrix}∗ & ∗\end{bmatrix}(\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix})
$$

what is the sum of the missing values?" :question/worked-solution "Suppose a transformation $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{m}$ is defined by 

$$
f:\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}{f}_{1}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ {f}_{2}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ ⋮ \\ {f}_{m}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

where ${f}_{1},{f}_{2},…,{f}_{m}$ are scalar functions with $n$ variables. If $f$ is differentiable at $x,$ then the total derivative of $f$ at $x,$ denoted ${f}^{′}(x),$ is given by the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+1})=-\frac{2xy}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}},\, & \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+1})=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2xy}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}} & \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Evaluating $f$ and its derivative at $x=a=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},$ we have

$$
f(a)=0,\,{f}^{′}(a)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & \frac{1}{2}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The tangent to $f$ at $x=a$ is given by

$$
z-f(a)={f}^{′}(a)(x-a).
$$

Substituting $f(a),$ ${f}^{′}(a),$ and $a$ in the equation above, we obtain

$$
z-0=\begin{bmatrix}0 & \frac{1}{2}\end{bmatrix}(\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}).
$$

Therefore, the sum of the missing values is

$$
0+0+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "1cc56c04-dae4-5804-9f0a-0ad43a3a6deb" :step/next {:db/id 17592186442223}} {:db/id 17592186442220 :step/content {:db/id 17592186442218 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "18b3a6d3-2922-5952-9dd5-688afdd0e22e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186442212} {:answer/id #uuid "3b47b2e0-7b7d-5338-9d25-ced74e84a6e9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186442213} {:answer/id #uuid "5f1bfc1c-98a1-5b2b-8c25-93072e2631fd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{2}+4" :db/id 17592186442214} {:answer/id #uuid "ec4d1f97-e95b-5ef1-8ea5-17d2a475dba0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{2}" :db/id 17592186442215} {:answer/id #uuid "f115dc76-a7c4-5fcd-bfa9-03dec29e7b4d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186442216}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186442212} :answer-field/id #uuid "d6d03c68-c527-56d7-8eec-20b909744859" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186442217}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "afc538b7-6818-5bf5-a45c-82af4af91e85" :question/math-academy-id "q-163159" :question/problem "Consider the transformation $f:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2},$ defined as

$$
f(x)=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}} \\ {e}^{{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}^{2}}\end{bmatrix},\,x=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

If the linear approximation of $f$ at  $a=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}$ is given by

$$
f(x)≈\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ ∗\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}∗ & 1 \\ 1 & ∗\end{bmatrix}(x-\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}),
$$

what is the sum of the missing values?" :question/worked-solution "Suppose a transformation $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{m}$ is defined by 

$$
f:\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}{f}_{1}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ {f}_{2}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ ⋮ \\ {f}_{m}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

where ${f}_{1},{f}_{2},…,{f}_{m}$ are scalar functions with $n$ variables. If $f$ is differentiable at $x,$ then the total derivative of $f$ at $x,$ denoted ${f}^{′}(x),$ is given by the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & =\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({e}^{{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}})=2{x}_{1}{e}^{{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}},\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({e}^{{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}})={e}^{{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & =\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({e}^{{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}^{2}})={e}^{{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}^{2}},\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({e}^{{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}^{2}})=-2{x}_{2}{e}^{{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}2{x}_{1}{e}^{{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}} & {e}^{{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}} \\ {e}^{{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}^{2}} & -2{x}_{2}{e}^{{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Evaluating $f$ and its derivative at $x=a=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix},$ we have

$$
f(a)=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{f}^{′}(a)=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The linear approximation of $f$ at $x=a$ is given by

$$
f(x)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a).
$$

Substituting $f(a),$ ${f}^{′}(a),$ and $a$ in the equation above, we obtain

$$
f(x)≈\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}(x-\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}).
$$

Therefore, the sum of the missing values is

where ${f}_{1},{f}_{2},…,{f}_{m}$ are scalar functions with $n$ variables. If $f$ is differentiable at $x,$ then the total derivative of $f$ at $x,$ denoted ${f}^{′}(x),$ is given by the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{bmatrix}.

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\operatorname{tan}⁡x)=\frac{y}{{cos}^{2}⁡x},\, & \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y\operatorname{tan}⁡x)=\operatorname{tan}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{y}{{cos}^{2}⁡x} & \operatorname{tan}⁡x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

$$

$$

$$
z-f(a)={f}^{′}(a)(x-a).
$$

$$
z-2=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1\end{bmatrix}(\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\pi }{4} \\ 2\end{bmatrix}).
$$

what is the sum of the missing values?" :question/worked-solution "Suppose a transformation $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{m}$ is defined by 

$$
f:\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}{f}_{1}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ {f}_{2}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ ⋮ \\ {f}_{m}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

where ${f}_{1},{f}_{2},…,{f}_{m}$ are scalar functions with $n$ variables. If $f$ is differentiable at $x,$ then the total derivative of $f$ at $x,$ denoted ${f}^{′}(x),$ is given by the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\operatorname{tan}⁡x)=\frac{y}{{cos}^{2}⁡x},\, & \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y\operatorname{tan}⁡x)=\operatorname{tan}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{y}{{cos}^{2}⁡x} & \operatorname{tan}⁡x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Evaluating $f$ and its derivative at $x=a=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\pi }{4} \\ 2\end{bmatrix},$ we have

$$
f(a)=2,\,{f}^{′}(a)=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The tangent to $f$ at $x=a$ is given by

$$
z-f(a)={f}^{′}(a)(x-a).
$$

Substituting $f(a),$ ${f}^{′}(a),$ and $a$ in the equation above, we obtain

$$
z-2=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1\end{bmatrix}(\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\pi }{4} \\ 2\end{bmatrix}).
$$

Therefore, the sum of the missing values is

$$
2+4+1=7.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "ef05c0b5-9fcd-53ae-8c36-9e2f672c2758" :step/next {:db/id 17592186442222}} {:db/id 17592186442220 :step/content {:db/id 17592186442218 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "18b3a6d3-2922-5952-9dd5-688afdd0e22e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186442212} {:answer/id #uuid "3b47b2e0-7b7d-5338-9d25-ced74e84a6e9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186442213} {:answer/id #uuid "5f1bfc1c-98a1-5b2b-8c25-93072e2631fd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{2}+4" :db/id 17592186442214} {:answer/id #uuid "ec4d1f97-e95b-5ef1-8ea5-17d2a475dba0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{2}" :db/id 17592186442215} {:answer/id #uuid "f115dc76-a7c4-5fcd-bfa9-03dec29e7b4d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186442216}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186442212} :answer-field/id #uuid "d6d03c68-c527-56d7-8eec-20b909744859" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186442217}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "afc538b7-6818-5bf5-a45c-82af4af91e85" :question/math-academy-id "q-163159" :question/problem "Consider the transformation $f:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2},$ defined as

$$
f:\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}{f}_{1}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ {f}_{2}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ ⋮ \\ {f}_{m}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

where ${f}_{1},{f}_{2},…,{f}_{m}$ are scalar functions with $n$ variables. If $f$ is differentiable at $x,$ then the total derivative of $f$ at $x,$ denoted ${f}^{′}(x),$ is given by the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & =\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({e}^{{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}})=2{x}_{1}{e}^{{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}},\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({e}^{{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}})={e}^{{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & =\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({e}^{{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}^{2}})={e}^{{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}^{2}},\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({e}^{{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}^{2}})=-2{x}_{2}{e}^{{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}2{x}_{1}{e}^{{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}} & {e}^{{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}} \\ {e}^{{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}^{2}} & -2{x}_{2}{e}^{{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Evaluating $f$ and its derivative at $x=a=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix},$ we have

$$
f(a)=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{f}^{′}(a)=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The linear approximation of $f$ at $x=a$ is given by

$$
f(x)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a).
$$

Substituting $f(a),$ ${f}^{′}(a),$ and $a$ in the equation above, we obtain

$$
f(x)≈\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}(x-\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}).
$$

Therefore, the sum of the missing values is

$$
1+2+2=5.
